statement_full_latex: Put $V=T_{\B}$, $D=T_{\dR}$ and $H=\operatorname{gr}_F D$. On the weight $n$ part, $\operatorname{gr}^p_F D$ is assigned bidegree $(p,n-p)$. The actual maps have types \[ \alpha:V_{\C}\longrightarrow D_{\C},\qquad \beta:D_{\C}\longrightarrow H_{\C},\qquad \gamma=(\beta\alpha)^{-1}:H_{\C}\longrightarrow V_{\C}. \] They are tensor isomorphisms; $\beta$ is the projection of each Hodge summand onto its associated-graded summand. Write \[ G=\Aut^\otimes(V),\quad G'=\Aut^\otimes(D),\quad B'=\Aut^\otimes(D,F),\quad U'=\ker\bigl(B'\longrightarrow\Aut^\otimes(H)\bigr). \] The normalized splitting space \[ Q=\{s:D\xrightarrow{\sim}H\text{ tensor and filtered}: \operatorname{gr}(s)=\id_H\} \] is a $U'$-torsor. Geometrically the filtration and bigrading spaces are $G/B$ and $G/L$, where $B$ and $L$ are the transported parabolic and Levi stabilizers. With $g=\dim G$, $b=\dim B$, $l=\dim L$, $u=\dim U$, one has \[ g=l+2u,\qquad b=l+u,\qquad g-b=u. \] The morphism $\BigSpace\to\Fil$ is a torsor under the relative unipotent group over $\Fil$ whose fibre at $F$ is $R_u(\operatorname{Stab}(F))$. Every fibre has dimension $u$.

In short frames, \[ \lambda^2h(E')=Nh(E)+S_C,\qquad \lambda^2\upsilon_p(E')=N\upsilon_p(E)+S_C. \] For $h\in\Qb$, fix an embedding of a number field containing $h$ and the isogeny data into $\mathbf C_p$. Normalize $v_p(p)=1$. Suppose $h$ is integral at the chosen place and $h\ne\upsilon_p(E)$, and put $b=v_p(h-\upsilon_p(E))\ge0$. Choose, once over $K$, \'etale parameters $X,Y$ at the identity such that \[ X(e)=Y(e)=0,\qquad D_aX(e)=1,\qquad D_aY(e)=0. \tag{A.4.40a} \] Write the actual formal graph as $Y=\phi_a(X)=\sum_{n\ge2}b_nX^n\in K[[X]]$. Outside a finite set of places, put \[ \mathcal B_a=\{v:K_{p_v}+aH_{p_v}\ne0\pmod v\},\qquad d_v=[K_v:\Q_{p_v}]. \] For the absolute value normalized by $\|p\|_v=p^{-d_v}$, the geometric size of this precise embedded formal curve satisfies \[ S_v(\widehat C_a)=\|p\|_v^{1/(p-1)}\quad(v\in\mathcal B_a), \qquad S_v(\widehat C_a)\ge\|p\|_v^{1/(p(p-1))} \quad(v\notin\mathcal B_a). \tag{A.4.40b} \] Consequently its adelic size product is zero. In particular this formal leaf fails the A-analyticity condition in Bost--Chambert-Loir's Definition~3.7. For Andr\'e's normalization $|p|_v=p^{-d_v/d}$ and his arithmetic coefficient invariant $\tau$, the same fixed graph satisfies \[ \tau(\phi_a)\ \ge\ \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac1T \sum_{\substack{v\in\mathcal B_a\\p_v\le T}} \frac{d_v}{d}\log p_v \ \ge\ \frac1{4d}>0. \tag{A.4.40c} \] Thus the zero-$\tau$ hypothesis of Andr\'e's Theorem~5.4.3 fails for this actual graph. statement: The profinite free group of the thrice-punctured sphere contains a specified nontrivial, nonperipheral element not conjugate to any discrete element whose every conjugated power has integral homology whenever it lies in any finite-cover subgroup, showing that these tests do not recognize discrete conjugacy without producing a Galois transporter.

statement_full_latex: Let \(X=\mathbf P^1(\C)\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\), with basepoint \(1/2\), and let \(F=\pi_1^{\mathrm{top}}(X,1/2)=\langle x,y\rangle\), where \(x,y\) are the usual positive loops around \(0,1\). Put \(G=\widehat F\), identified with the geometric \'{e}tale fundamental group by the actual finite-cover comparison. For an open subgroup \(H\subset G\), let \(Y_H\) be its pointed cover and put \[ F_H=F\cap H,\qquad \Lambda_H=F_H^{\mathrm{ab}}=H_1(Y_H(\C),\Z),\qquad H^{\mathrm{ab}}=\Lambda_H\otimes\widehat\Z. \tag{E.2.27a} \] There is a fully specified element \(g\in G\) with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item \(g\) is not conjugate in \(G\) to any element of \(F\). \item For every open \(H\), every \(m\in\Z\), and every \(t\in G\) such that \(tg^mt^{-1}\in H\), \[ \operatorname{ab}_H(tg^mt^{-1})\in\Lambda_H \subset\Lambda_H\otimes\widehat\Z. \tag{E.2.27b} \] \item \(g\neq1\), its image in \(G^{\mathrm{ab}}\) is zero, and \(g\) lies in no conjugate of a cusp inertia subgroup. \end{enumerate} The image of (E.2.27b) under the actual filling map also belongs to the integral homology lattice of the smooth compactification of \(Y_H\). Thus these element-to-homology maps, even for all powers and all finite-cover lifts, do not recognize a discrete conjugacy class. The construction supplies an element of \(G\); it does not supply the Galois automorphism and compatible full transporter required in E.2.22.

statement: For a finitely generated free group, the subgroup H_int defined by its discrete virtually abelian quotients is their actual inverse limit, and a continuous profinite automorphism preserves all affine integral cover-homology lattices exactly when one inner adjustment preserves H_int, equivalently when its generator images lie there, with proper-to-affine boundary and Galois issues left separate.

statement_full_latex: Let \(F=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle\) be a specified discrete free group of finite rank, and put \(G=\widehat F\). For each open normal subgroup \(N\subset G\), set \[ \begin{aligned} K_N&=F\cap N,& A_N&=K_N/[K_N,K_N],\\ D_N&=\overline{[K_N,K_N]}^{\,G},& \Gamma_N&=F/[K_N,K_N],\\ P_N&=G/D_N,& Q_N&=G/N=F/K_N. \end{aligned} \tag{E.2.28a} \] The group \(\Gamma_N\) embeds in \(P_N\). Define the actual subgroup and its displayed inverse-limit realization by \[ \mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}} =\bigcap_N\pi_N^{-1}(\Gamma_N)\subset G, \qquad \mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\simeq\varprojlim_N\Gamma_N, \quad \pi_N:G\longrightarrow P_N. \tag{E.2.28b} \] For an open subgroup \(U\subset G\), write \(\Lambda_U=(F\cap U)^{\mathrm{ab}}\subset U^{\mathrm{ab}}\). This is the integral homology lattice of its actual finite cover of the bouquet of \(r\) circles. For a continuous automorphism \(\alpha\) of \(G\), the following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item The actual induced map \(U^{\mathrm{ab}}\to \alpha(U)^{\mathrm{ab}}\) carries \(\Lambda_U\) onto \(\Lambda_{\alpha(U)}\) for every open \(U\). \item The same assertion holds on the integral lattices \(A_N\) for one characteristic cofinal chain of open normal subgroups. \item There is one element \(h\in G\) such that \((\operatorname{ad}(h)\alpha)(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}) =\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\). \end{enumerate} Furthermore, an actual continuous automorphism \(\beta\) of \(G\) preserves \(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\) if and only if \(\beta(x_j)\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{int}}\) for \(1\leq j\leq r\). For the punctured curve of E.2.22 this characterizes preservation of all \emph{affine} integral homology lattices, up to one actual inner adjustment. Passing from the proper-homology condition in E.2.22 to this affine condition requires the vanishing of the boundary-extension classes identified below. The discrete-representative and Galois requirements remain open.

statement: The explicit A5-cover of the thrice-punctured sphere has genus nine and homology ranks (61,43,18) for affine, boundary and proper parts, and admits a profinite automorphism acting by an integral equivariant matrix I+60N that fails to preserve the boundary module, so even this integral action gives neither a proper-homology endomorphism nor a Galois action.

statement_full_latex: Let \(U=\mathbb P^1_{\overline{\Q}}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\), fix \(F=\langle X,Y\rangle=\pi_1^{\mathrm{top}}(U(\mathbb C))\), and specify the quotient \[ \pi:\widehat F\longrightarrow H=A_5,\qquad X\longmapsto x=(123),\quad Y\longmapsto y=(12345). \tag{E.2.29a} \] Products of permutations act as compositions of functions. Let \(Y_H\to U\) be its actual connected Galois cover, let \(C_H\) be its smooth compactification, and put \[ \begin{aligned} L&=H_1(Y_H(\mathbb C),\Z),\\ P&=\langle\text{oriented boundary classes}\rangle\subset L,\\ W&=H_1(C_H(\mathbb C),\Z)=L/P . \end{aligned} \] There is an actual continuous automorphism \(\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(\widehat F)\) with \(\pi\alpha=\pi\) and \(\alpha^{\mathrm{ab}}=1\) such that its action on \(\ker(\pi)^{\mathrm{ab}}=\widehat L\) is the completion of an integral \(H\)-equivariant automorphism \(\gamma\) of \(L\), but \(\gamma(P)\not\subset P\). In particular this action does not induce an endomorphism of the fixed proper-homology quotient \(W\). The construction has \[ g(C_H)=9,\quad \#(C_H\setminus Y_H)=44,\quad \operatorname{rank}L=61,\quad \operatorname{rank}P=43,\quad \operatorname{rank}W=18 . \tag{E.2.29b} \] It supplies an integral matrix \(N\), an actual boundary class \(b\in P\), and an integral functional \(q:L\to\Z\) with \[ N^2=0,\quad \gamma=I+60N,\quad q(P)=0,\quad qNb=19440,\quad q\gamma b=1166400 . \tag{E.2.29c} \] The same failure holds for every positive power of \(\alpha\). statement_full_latex: Let \(F=\langle x,y\rangle\) be the specified topological fundamental group of \(X=\mathbf P^1(\C)\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\), put \(z=(xy)^{-1}\), and put \(G=\widehat F\). For every open normal subgroup \(N\subset G\), let \(Y_N\) be the actual regular cover, let \(C_N\) be its smooth compactification, and define \[ \begin{aligned} K_N&=F\cap N,& A_N^c&=H_1(C_N,\Z),\\ L_N&=\ker(K_N\longrightarrow A_N^c),& J_N&=\overline{L_N}^{\,G},\\ \Gamma_N^c&=F/L_N,&P_N^c&=G/J_N,& Q_N&=G/N. \end{aligned} \tag{E.2.30a} \] There are actual embeddings and inverse-limit identifications \[ \Gamma_N^c\hookrightarrow P_N^c=\widehat{\Gamma_N^c}, \qquad \mathcal H_c:=\bigcap_N(\pi_N^c)^{-1}(\Gamma_N^c) \simeq\varprojlim_N\Gamma_N^c\subset G, \quad \pi_N^c:G\longrightarrow P_N^c. \tag{E.2.30b} \] The subgroup \(\mathcal H_c\) is self-normalizing in \(G\). statement_full_latex: Let $k$ be any commutative ring, including rings with torsion, and let $M,N$ be arbitrary $k$-modules. A homogeneous polynomial law $f:M\rightsquigarrow N$ of degree $d\geq0$ means a family of maps \[ f_R:R\otimes_k M\longrightarrow R\otimes_k N \qquad(R\in\operatorname{CAlg}_k) \] natural in the commutative $k$-algebra $R$, with $f_R(rx)=r^d f_R(x)$. It is not merely its function $f_k$ on $k$-points. There is a natural isomorphism of $k$-modules \[ \operatorname{Pol}^d_k(M,N) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_k(\Gamma^d_k M,N). \tag{A1.1} \] Here $\Gamma^d$ is the degree-$d$ part of the universal divided-power algebra; $\Gamma^0 M=k$, $\Gamma^1M=M$. The isomorphism sends $u$ to $(1\otimes u)\gamma_{d,R}$. Divided powers commute with arbitrary scalar extension and satisfy \[ \Gamma^d(M\oplus N)\simeq \bigoplus_{a+b=d}\Gamma^a M\otimes_k\Gamma^b N. \tag{A1.2} \] The exact references are Roby, Theorem IV.1, pp.~266--267, Theorem III.3, p.~262, and Theorem III.4, pp.~262--263 \cite{Roby1963}. If $Y$ is forward tame in $X$, then the ordinary homotopy types satisfy \[ X\simeq Y\mathbin{\cup^h}_{H}U. \tag{B2.4} \] Quinn proves a controlled strict relative version in \cite[Lemma 2.4(2)]{Quinn1988}, using his controlled holink and mapping-cylinder convention. We give a separate proof of (B2.4) that does not identify that cylinder topology with the ordinary quotient-cylinder topology. Let $N$ range over the open neighborhoods of $Y$. The numerable open cover $X=N\cup U$ gives, naturally in $N$, the homotopy-pushout equivalence $N\cup^h_{N\setminus Y}U\simeq X$. A fixed tame deformation gives an equivalence $\{N\}_N\simeq\operatorname{const}Y$ in prospaces: for any target neighborhood $N$, shrink to the points whose entire deformation lies in $N$. The same fixed deformation and the explicit endpoint-preserving path homotopy of C4.02 give $\{N\setminus Y\}_N\simeq\operatorname{const}H$. Those formulas need only tameness of this pair; the fibration part of the HSS definition is not used. The comparison uses the natural zigzag through paths wholly contained in $N$, so its endpoint maps and the homotopy between the two maps to $X$ are the original ones. The finite span colimit in $\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal S)$ is computed on these synchronized levels, because filtered colimits of spaces commute with finite simplicial limits. Replacing the two pro-germs by their constant equivalents therefore gives $\operatorname{const}X\simeq \operatorname{const}(Y\cup^h_HU)$. The constant embedding is fully faithful, proving (B2.4). In the usual quotient double-cylinder model, the associated map to $X$ is induced by the continuous path evaluation $H\times[0,1]\to X$. Quinn's Definition 3.1 adds, for each incident pair of strata, that $e_0$ is a fibration. That is the precise normal-fibration analogue of 151/032, once a deleted tube has been compared with the holink. It is not the whole definition: forward tameness remains a separate hypothesis. The fibration condition alone does not imply tameness. For the Hawaiian earring with $Y$ its common point, $e_0$ is a fibration because its target is a point. But $Y$ is not tame: a neighbourhood deformation into $Y$ would null-homotope every sufficiently small circle in $X$, while retraction of $X$ onto any one of those circles shows its fundamental loop is nonzero. statement_full_latex: At $n=1$, (B3.1) is the equivalence between constructible stacks in groupoids and homotopy-coherent $2$-functors from the exit-path $2$-category to groupoids. It is also the restriction of \cite[Theorem 7.14]{Treumann2009} from category-valued to groupoid-valued stacks: the value at each object is the stalk category, so the condition that these values are groupoids is preserved in both directions. His Theorem 7.13 proves compatibility with open-cover descent. The set-valued level, by contrast, is $n=0$: it retains $\pi_0$ of each exit mapping space. Thus L3's phrase ``truncated at $\pi_1$ of the links'' is one level too high if it means that link $\pi_1$ survives as automorphisms of exiting arrows. Those automorphisms first appear in the stack level. For $(S^2,\{p\})$, the two-stratum exit category can be represented by two objects and cross mapping space $S^1$: the open stratum is contractible, and its attaching holink has the homotopy type of $S^1$. Taking $\pi_0$ makes a single arrow, while the fundamental groupoid of that mapping space retains $\mathbb Z$. This is exactly the difference seen by the gerbes. One should also distinguish two uses of gluing. A general constructible stack is a closed--open system (B3.2), with a possibly noninvertible functor to nearby data. An $A$-banded gerbe is locally equivalent to $BA$ at every point of $X$. Its gluing over an honest open tube and $U$ uses an \emph{equivalence} on their overlap, as in 151/042. statement_full_latex: \label{b5.5.-flatness-forest-comparisons-and-verdier-hypercovers} \textbf{Status: Refuted for the proposed ``strictly between'' description.} A hypercover condition agreeing with Verdier's cannot in general lie between the manuscript's forest conditions and flatness. For \(A=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\), the ordinary Cech nerve \(U_n=\{0,1\}^{n+1}\) of a cover of a point is a hypercover, and its realization is the contractible nerve of the indiscrete groupoid on two objects. Yet Hyp \(2'\) fails. Take in \(\Delta\) the span \([0]\leftarrow[1]\to[2]\), with the first map constant and the second selecting endpoints 0,2. The corresponding fiber product contains \((0,(0,1,0))\). A cocone must have a monotone map \([2]\to[m]\) with equal endpoint values, hence a constant map. Every tuple lifted from a completing cone is therefore constant in those three positions. The displayed element has no lift. In particular full (Hyp) fails as well. Conversely, \(\Delta[1]\) is a flat functor on \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\): its extension is evaluation at \([1]\). It is not a hypercover of a point, because its degree-one matching map omits the ordered pair of vertices \((1,0)\). Thus even flatness and Verdier's condition are incomparable for ordinary simplicial indexing. The failure of ``between'' persists for symmetric indexing. Put \(U(S)=\operatorname{Cont}(\Delta(S),\mathbf R)\), with maps by affine precomposition. Every continuous boundary map to \(\mathbf R\) extends to the simplex by coning from the barycenter and interpolating to zero; compactness gives continuity at the barycenter. Hence the ordinary simplicial restriction is a hypercover of a point. For the finite-set span \(1\leftarrow2\to3\), with the right map selecting vertices 0,2, take zero on \(\Delta^0\) and \[b(t_0,t_1,t_2)=t_1(t_0-t_2).\] They agree on edge 02. Any amalgamating finite-set map identifies vertices 0,2, so its affine map takes \((1/2,1/2,0)\) and \((0,1/2,1/2)\) to the same point. A lifted function must have equal values there; \(b\) has values \(1/4,-1/4\). Thus Hyp \(2'\) fails. Exact rational computation checks this obstruction on 30 amalgams; the argument proves it for every target cardinality. There is nevertheless a one-way implication specific to symmetric indexing: full (Hyp) implies the hypercover condition. By B5.4 its system is \(U(S)=E^S\) with \(E\to1\) epic. The simplicial restriction is the Cech nerve of this epimorphism; every positive matching map is an isomorphism. The symmetric continuous-simplex example just given proves the converse false. Thus ordinary flatness and hypercovers are incomparable, whereas symmetric flatness is strictly stronger than hypercovers; in either case hypercovers need not satisfy the forest conditions. Over sets there is also an explicit ordinary-index classification: flat functors \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}\) are precisely nerves of nonempty linear orders. Indeed a flat functor is a filtered colimit of the covariant representables \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}}([n],-)=\Delta[n]\). A filtered colimit of finite ordinals and monotone maps is a linear order: comparisons and antisymmetry are witnessed at a common stage. Nerves commute with filtered colimits, since finite strings use finite limits of sets. Conversely a linear order is the filtered union of its nonempty finite suborders. The filtered-colimit characterization follows from the cofiltered element-category argument in B5.4. \(\square\) This corrects \path{study/readings/151_001-017_INTEGRATION.md} lines 61--68, 78--83, and \path{study/readings/151_001-017.md} lines 303--309. The assertion that the comparison scheme lies strictly between forest conditions and flatness is not a valid requirement for the desired Verdier comparison.

statement_full_latex: \label{b6.2.-a-complete-replacement-is-available-in-the-primary-literature} \textbf{Status: Known, with a direct translation to the manuscript generators.} Grandis, \emph{Finite sets and symmetric simplicial sets}, §3 and Theorem 4.2 \cite{B56Grandis2001}, gives a complete presentation of finite cardinals by all elementary cofaces, codegeneracies and adjacent transpositions, subject to the cosimplicial, symmetric-group and mixed interchange relations. His §5 restricts the presentation to nonempty finite cardinals. Thus a complete corrected presentation is obtained by adding all these translated relations to the manuscript generators. Here are explicit substitution words, including their arities. Write \(c_i^{(m)}=(i\ i+1\ \cdots\ m)\in\mathfrak S_m\), with \(c_m^{(m)}=1\). For the coface \(d_i^{(n)}:n\to n+1\) omitting \(i\), and the codegeneracy \(e_i^{(n)}:n+1\to n\) identifying \(i,i+1\), set \[ d_i^{(n)}=c_i^{(n+1)}\delta_n\quad(1\le i\le n+1),\qquad e_i^{(n)}=c_i^{(n)}K_n\bigl(c_i^{(n+1)}\bigr)^{-2} \quad(1\le i\le n). \tag{B6.2.1} \] Adjacent transpositions are \(s_i=(i\ i+1)\), already present in the symmetric groups. The first word fixes positions before \(i\) and moves every later old position one step to the right. In the second word, the source permutation fixes \(k<i\), sends \(i,i+1\) to \(n,n+1\), and sends \(k>i+1\) to \(k-2\); \(K_n\) merges the last two, and the output cycle puts the merged value back in position \(i\). Thus these are exactly the indicated finite-set maps. Crucially, the last words recover the old generators literally: \(d_{n+1}^{(n)}=\delta_n\) and \(e_n^{(n)}=K_n\). For a completely explicit enlarged relation scheme, use (B6.2.1) in all the following formulas, whenever their arities are positive and well typed; dimension superscripts are suppressed: \[ d_i d_j=d_{j+1}d_i\ (i\le j),\qquad e_j e_i=e_i e_{j+1}\ (i\le j), \] \[ e_jd_i= \begin{cases} d_i e_{j-1},&i<j,\\ 1,&i=j\text{ or }i=j+1,\\ d_{i-1}e_j,&i>j+1; \end{cases} \] \[ s_i^2=1,\quad s_i s_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_i s_{i+1},\quad s_i s_j=s_j s_i\ (i<j-1), \] \[ \begin{array}{lll} s_i d_j=d_j s_i &(i<j-1),&s_i e_j=e_j s_i\quad(i<j-1),\\ s_i d_i=d_{i+1},&&s_i e_i=e_{i+1}s_i s_{i+1},\\ s_i d_j=d_j s_{i-1}&(i>j),&s_i e_j=e_j s_{i+1}\quad(i>j), \end{array} \qquad e_i s_i=e_i. \tag{B6.2.2} \] These are Grandis's (3), (10), (12), (13), with indices shifted from zero-based to one-based notation. The omitted mixed cases follow by \(s_i^2=1\), exactly as in Grandis. The group equations are redundant if the complete groups \(\mathfrak S_n\) and their multiplication laws are retained as the manuscript prescribes. We verify carefully that no unspoken defining equations are missing. Let \(P\) be Grandis's presented category on positive cardinals and let \(Q\) be the category on the manuscript generators with their group laws, the valid manuscript equations, and all of (B6.2.2) after the substitutions (B6.2.1). Substitution defines a functor \(F:P\to Q\), because every defining relation of \(P\) has explicitly been imposed in \(Q\). This functor is surjective on every hom-set: its image contains \(\delta_n\) and \(K_n\) literally and contains all adjacent transpositions, which generate each of the already imposed symmetric groups. The finite-set interpretation gives \(G:Q\to\mathsf F\), because every imposed relation holds for these functions. The composite \(GF\) is the standard interpretation of Grandis's generators and is an isomorphism by Theorem 4.2 and §5. For faithfulness of \(G\), choose lifts \(u,v\) in \(P\) of two parallel arrows of \(Q\). Equality of their \(G\)-images gives \(GF(u)=GF(v)\), hence \(u=v\), and hence equality of the arrows in \(Q\). Fullness follows from the same composite. Thus \(Q\cong\mathsf F\), with exactly the requested old generators. This proof does not assume that generator substitutions are inverses without checking their defining equations. The auxiliary script \texttt{check\_B6\_translation.py} verifies all 168 coface and codegeneracy words for \(1\le n\le12\); the explicit coordinate argument above proves the formulas in every arity. We make no minimality claim for this enlarged relation list. Write the three objects \(E_0,E_1,E_2\) for cardinalities \(1,2,3\), respectively, and abbreviate \[p=p_0:E_1\to E_0,\quad d=\delta_0:E_0\to E_1, \quad q=p_{12}:E_2\to E_1,\quad e=\delta_1:E_1\to E_2.\] The groups are \(\mathfrak S_2\) and \(\mathfrak S_3\). In the coordinate interpretation, let \[\sigma(x,y)=(y,x),\quad \rho(x,y,z)=(y,z,x), \quad\sigma_1(x,y,z)=(x,z,y),\quad\sigma_3(x,y,z)=(y,x,z).\] Thus \(\sigma_i\) fixes coordinate \(i\). The corrected list is \[pd=1,\quad \sigma d=d,\quad qe=\sigma,\quad q\rho e=dp, \quad q\rho^2e=1,\] \[\sigma_1e=e,\quad q\sigma_3=\sigma q,\quad ged=ed\ (g\in\mathfrak S_3), \quad pq\sigma_1=pq,\] together with the group equations. The coordinate maps \[p(x,y)=x,\quad d(x)=(x,x),\quad q(x,y,z)=(x,y),\quad e(x,y)=(y,x,x)\] satisfy them. These maps and the permutations generate all maps between sets of cardinalities at most three, by elementary inclusion and retraction factorization. Hence the presented category \(Q\) maps surjectively on hom-sets to \(\mathsf F_{\le3}^{\mathrm{op}}\). We now prove injectivity by a terminating reduction and exact hom-set bounds. First combine adjacent permutations. A path which rises from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\) and immediately returns has a segment \(qge\). Every \(g\in\mathfrak S_3\) is \(\rho^i h\) with \(h\in\langle\sigma_1\rangle\). Since \(he=e\), the three relations \(q\rho^ie\in\{\sigma,dp,1\}\) eliminate this segment. A path rising from \(E_0\) to \(E_1\) and returning has a segment \(p\sigma^\epsilon d=p d=1\). These replacements terminate: order words first by the number of \(q,e\) transitions and then by the number of \(p,d\) transitions. A first replacement lowers the first count; a second lowers the second without increasing the first. Every surviving path descends in height and then ascends, with at most one valley. Paths through \(E_0\) are constant maps: on the output side \(\sigma d=d\) and \(ged=ed\) erase all output permutations. On the input side, there is one form from \(E_0\), at most two forms \(p\sigma^\epsilon\) from \(E_1\), and at most three forms \(pqh\) from \(E_2\), because \(pq\sigma_1=pq\). A path with valley \(E_1\) from \(E_2\) to \(E_2\) is \(ge\sigma^\epsilon qh\). The stabilizer relation \(\sigma_1e=e\) leaves three choices for the coset of \(g\); the equation \(q\sigma_3=\sigma q\) moves the two-element left stabilizer of \(h\) into the central \(\sigma^\epsilon\), leaving three choices for its coset. Thus there are at most \(3\cdot2\cdot3=18\) forms of rank two. The same calculation gives at most six rank-two maps each from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\) or from \(E_2\) to \(E_1\). Finally there are at most two invertible forms at \(E_1\) and six at \(E_2\). Collecting these bounds, with source cardinality indexing rows and target cardinality columns, gives \[\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\2&4&8\\3&9&27\end{pmatrix}.\] The entries are exactly \(a^b=|\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf F^{\mathrm{op}}}(a,b)|\). Since the functor was already surjective on each hom-set, each bound is attained and it is bijective on each hom-set. It is the identity on objects, hence an isomorphism of categories. The program enumerates all 56 maps, verifies this matrix, checks the rank decomposition and every corrected relation. The reduction proof supplies completeness, which checking the relations in the target alone would not establish. \(\square\) The doubtful alternatives must remain separate. On 151/005, the last relation is transcribed \(p_0p_{12}\sigma_{\text{unsure }1|3}=p_0p_{12}\). The \(1\) reading is the corrected presentation just proved. The \(3\) reading says that first-coordinate and second-coordinate projections agree, and is false already on \((0,1,0)\). On 151/003, the transcribed \(\sigma_3e=e\) is false: the two maps have coordinate values \((x,y,x)\) and \((y,x,x)\). The final list on 151/005 instead has \(\sigma_1e=e\), which is true. Retaining every literal 151/003 equation together with 151/005 therefore gives a false presentation. These checks confirm the mathematical correction SA10-K151a-01 and complete the earlier partial verification SA10-R151a-08. Independent inspection of original 151/003 (PDF page 3, printed p.~2) confirms the boxed subscript \(3\); inspection of the middle box on 151/005 (PDF page 5, printed p.~4) confirms subscript \(1\). The final 151/005 subscript is a dense short mark and remains visually unresolved between the two supplied readings. Thus the mathematical conclusions for both readings are retained; no paleographic certainty is claimed for that final mark.

statement_full_latex: \label{c1.02-proved-under-fibrancy-the-complete-segal-object} Let C be an internal category in compactly generated spaces, graded by a finite poset I. Suppose C\ensuremath{{}_{0}}=\ensuremath{\coprod}\ensuremath{{}_{i}}\ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{{}_{i}}, C\ensuremath{{}_{1}}=\ensuremath{\coprod}\ensuremath{{}_{i}}\ensuremath{\le}\ensuremath{{}_{j}}\ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{{}_{ij}}, \ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{{}_{ii}}=\ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{{}_{i}} consists exactly of identities, and each strict source \ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{{}_{ij}}\ensuremath{\to}\ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{{}_{i}} is a Hurewicz fibration. The ordinary nerve has Segal maps that are homeomorphisms onto iterated ordinary pullbacks. A pullback along a Hurewicz fibration computes a homotopy pullback. Thus its nerve is a Segal object in the infinity-category of spaces. The functor to N(I) takes equivalences to identities. Every equivalence therefore lies over i=i. That summand consists only of identities, and all identities are equivalences. Hence \(C_0\to N(C)_1^{\mathrm{eq}}\) is an equivalence, proving completeness. If ``Segal space'' is defined to require Reedy fibrancy, take a Reedy fibrant replacement. The raw nerve need not be Reedy fibrant. For the identity-only category on S\ensuremath{{}^{1}} it is constant, and its first matching map is S\ensuremath{{}^{1}}\ensuremath{\to}S\ensuremath{{}^{1}}\ensuremath{\times}S\ensuremath{{}^{1}}, the diagonal. A pair of unequal paths starting at the same point cannot lift through this diagonal. This proves completeness, not the geometric identification with Exit(X). That identification requires a separate comparison; an equivalence of realizations alone does not imply it.

statement_full_latex: \label{c1.03-proved-the-simultaneous-cone-construction} This supplies an explicit completion of the postponed construction, rather than attributing unspecified transition maps to /043. Let \(\Sigma:\operatorname{Drap}(I)^{op}\to\mathrm{Top}\) be the flag diagram of the deployed category, including flags of length zero. For a nonempty flag \(e=\{i_0<\cdots<i_n\}\), write \(e_{\le a}=\{i\in e:i\le a\}\). A pair \((d,e)\) means \(d\subset e\setminus\{\max e\}\); the empty \(d\) is allowed. Put \(a_0<\cdots<a_p=\max e\) for the elements of \(d\cup\{\max e\}\), so \(p=|d|\), not necessarily the length of \(e\). Define the simultaneous mapping cylinder \[ C(d,e)=\operatorname{hocolim}\bigl( \Sigma_{e_{\le a_p}}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow \Sigma_{e_{\le a_0}}\bigr), \] using the ordinary thick simplicial mapping-cylinder model. Explicitly it is the quotient of \[ \coprod_{k=0}^{p}\Sigma_{e_{\le a_k}}\times\Delta^k \] that identifies the face omitting the last vertex with its image under \(\Sigma_{e_{\le a_k}}\to\Sigma_{e_{\le a_{k-1}}}\), and makes the analogous identifications on all nested subfaces. Faces omitting a nonfinal vertex remain boundary faces. In particular \(C(\varnothing,e)=\Sigma_e\); for one cut it is the mapping cylinder of the indicated projection, called a mapping cone in the manuscript's convention. There are three kinds of maps, generating the transition diagram. \begin{itemize} \tightlist \item If \(d\subset d'\subset e\setminus\{\max e\}\), the inclusion of the selected vertices gives \(C(d,e)\to C(d',e)\). \item For \(f=d\cup\{\max e\}\subset e\), the restriction maps \(\Sigma_{e_{\le a}}\to\Sigma_{f_{\le a}}\) give \(C(d,e)\to C(f\setminus\{\max f\},f)\). \item For each selected \(a\in d\), the initial-prefix cylinder already present as a face has its canonical map \(C(d\cap e_{<a},e_{\le a})\to C(d,e)\). These maps identify internal prefix blocks with their standalone objects in the diagram. \end{itemize} All relations among these maps are those induced by inclusions of flags and functoriality of \(\Sigma\). This can equivalently be taken as the image diagram with the maps above, imposing every commuting square that follows from the displayed inclusions. The colimit of this diagram is canonically homeomorphic to the ordinary realization of the strict nerve: \[ \operatorname{colim}_{(d,e)}C(d,e) \;\cong\; \left(\coprod_{\varnothing\ne e\in\operatorname{Drap}(I)} \Sigma_e\times\Delta^{|e|-1}\right)/\sim . \]

statement_full_latex: \label{c1.04-proved-under-the-corrected-hypotheses-incidence-groupoids} Here are the construction and the category in which the moduli version holds. For finite-depth smooth Thom--Mather data, perform the successive cuts in a linear order in which every lower stratum is cut before the strata above it, retaining every new boundary. At the stage of label \(i\), the cut-open closure of its stratum is \(\Sigma_i\). The face of \(\Sigma_j\) over an incidence \(i<j\) is \(\Sigma_{ij}\), and its source is the retained link-bundle projection to \(\Sigma_i\). A longer flag \(d=(i_0<\cdots<i_n)\) defines \[ \Sigma_d=\Sigma_{i_0i_n}\cap\cdots\cap\Sigma_{i_{n-1}i_n}. \] Removing a nonfinal entry gives the inclusion of intersections. Removing a final entry gives the appropriate source projection restricted to that intersection. Projection control identifies all composites with the same source and target, so these maps define the contravariant flag functor. The inverse-image identities make its Segal squares cartesian. Proper stratified link bundles and their base changes prove the initial-segment fibrancy; the incoming target faces have their specified commuting collars. The empty-index case gives the empty space and the empty category. A one-stratum deployment is its fundamental infinity-groupoid. The hypotheses needed in C1.B3 hold for this construction: a cut or an intersection of faces retains the same iterated boundary fibrations, their proper source bundles, and the restrictions of the commuting collars. C2.05 derives this closure property from the iterated-fibration resolution theorem. In the conically smooth formulation it is supplied by AFT, \emph{Local structures on stratified spaces}, Theorem 7.3.8 (full unzip), Proposition 7.3.10 (the blow-up square), and Proposition 8.2.5 (the tubular presentation) \cite{C_AFT}. Thus C1.B3 identifies the resulting complete Segal object with the full exit category in that class. C1.01 explains why the weaker literal mapping-cone data in \S{}8 do not imply this result without equisingularity. For \(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}\), use the following finite incidence category, retaining automorphisms. Its objects are stable graphs \(\Gamma\) of type \((g,n)\), with labelled legs, vertex genera, and stability at every vertex. An arrow is a specified edge contraction \(c:\Gamma\to\Gamma'\), together with its identification of the contracted graph with \(\Gamma'\); graph isomorphisms are arrows as well. Composition contracts the union of the specified edge sets. Contracting a loop raises the genus of its vertex; contracting an edge joining two vertices merges them and adds their genera. The open stratum is the orbifold \[ \mathcal S_\Gamma= \left[\prod_{v\in V(\Gamma)}\mathcal M_{g(v),n(v)} \big/\operatorname{Aut}(\Gamma)\right]. \] Equivalently one may keep half-edge labels throughout and then form the indicated finite groupoids. Fixed contractions preserve which node branches are involved; an orbit-poset does not. Use the cutting construction in smooth universal deformation charts. Looijenga's Theorem 9.13 \cite{C_Looijenga} supplies the chart and its finite automorphism action; its boundary parameters \(q_e\) are indexed by the actual nodes. The ordinary real oriented blow-up writes \(q_e=r_e\exp(i\theta_e)\). To obtain the full deployment with a boundary hypersurface for every strict stratum incidence, further blow up its corner faces successively in increasing dimension. Locally this replaces the face lattice by its flag lattice. In a normal coordinate space with \(r\) nodes, the outgoing link before resolution is the coordinate-stratified sphere \(S^{2r-1}\); the source fibre of the full deployment is its recursively resolved link. For \(r=1\) this is a circle. For \(r>1\), radial-ratio coordinates and their faces are also retained, so identifying this full link with only \((S^1)^r\) would discard data. The ordinary oriented blow-up and the full flag deployment are related by these explicit further corner blow-ups. For a composable chain of specified contractions, take the corresponding flag-face space in these charts and its groupoid of chart identifications and graph automorphisms. Denote the resulting orbifold by \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_d\). Face and source maps are the preceding geometric maps with their equivariant identifications. In simplicial degree \(k\), take the disjoint union over contraction chains of length \(k\), modulo their isomorphism groupoids. Thus fibre products are homotopy fibre products of groupoids/spaces, not orbit-set fibre products. Local transverse product collars and proper link bundles show the Segal comparisons are equivalences. The maps glue because changes of deformation chart preserve the labelled normal-crossings incidences and their resolved boundary fibrations. The source and target maps therefore define a Segal object in orbifold homotopy types. There are two equivalent descriptions of its completion. In the classifying-space construction take the classifying space of the entire groupoid of chains in every degree, with isomorphisms at every vertex and commuting identifications on each arrow. Replacing only the object set by classifying spaces, while leaving the raw arrow sets unchanged, would not suffice. For example, for one object with automorphism group \(G\), the groupoid of length-\(k\) strings is \[ G^k\mathbin{/\mkern-6mu/}G^{k+1}. \] The action changes the trivializations at each vertex. It is transitive with stabilizer a diagonal copy of \(G\), so its classifying space is \(BG\) in every degree. The degree-zero degeneracy to the equivalence subspace in degree one is therefore an equivalence. This is the Rezk classifying-diagram construction. Applied to the entire incidence diagram, with homotopy fibre products for compositions, it gives a complete-Segal model. Equivalently take the Rezk completion of the raw incidence/action-category nerve. A raw group nerve with one discrete object is not already complete when its automorphism group is nontrivial, and discarding that group is not completion. Choose the compatible boundary fibrations and collar data once on the orbifold resolution, and pull them back to each atlas chart. These data can be constructed equivariantly: normal-crossings blow-ups preserve incidence labels, invariant metrics and connections exist by finite-group averaging and orbifold partitions of unity, and the iterated collar construction proceeds on the preserved boundary fibrations. A change of chart consequently preserves the pulled-back structures. Independent arbitrary collar choices are not being asserted to agree. The chartwise source maps are representable proper locally trivial bundles, so their pullbacks compute the needed homotopy fibre products after passage to atlas chain groupoids. Define the orbifold exit category by descent from an orbifold atlas: take the colimit in infinity-categories of the exit categories of its simplicial atlas and its chart identifications. On a finite quotient chart \([U/G]\), this is \(\operatorname{Exit}(U)\mathbin{/\mkern-6mu/}G\). The atlas definition is independent of the atlas. For a surjective stratum-preserving local diffeomorphism \(V\to U\), cover \(U\) by opens admitting stratum-preserving local sections. A section supplies an extra degeneracy in the augmented \v{C}ech diagram, making its image under the exit functor a split augmented simplicial diagram. Its colimit is the exit category of that open. Exit open-cover excision \cite[Theorem A.7.1]{LurieHA} and interchange of colimits globalize the equivalence to \(U\). Two atlases have a common refinement given by their fibre product; applying the preceding argument in both directions of its bisimplicial atlas identifies the two colimits. For \([U/G]\), the atlas nerve is \(U\times G^\bullet\), giving precisely the homotopy-orbit category just displayed, including ineffective isotropy. The comparison of C1.B3 is natural for the face maps, source maps, and isomorphisms. It is consequently an equivariant equivalence on every deformation chart and on every atlas intersection. Taking the displayed colimit gives \[ \widehat{N\boldsymbol\Sigma}\simeq \operatorname{Exit}_{\mathrm{orb}}(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}), \] where the hat denotes complete-Segal localization. The proof is categorical descent of chartwise equivalences; equality of classifying-space realizations alone is not used. Realization gives the homotopy type of the orbifold, with its finite isotropy. On a level cover on which all stabilizers act freely, the same construction gives the ordinary space and its ordinary exit category. For coarse moduli spaces, finite orbit quotients commute with the explicit topological colimits of C1.03, so their cone realization still recovers the coarse space. However quotienting can destroy source fibrancy and can make the stated strata nonmanifolds; C3.03 gives a concrete interior obstruction in genus four. Thus the orbifold exit comparison cannot simply be transferred to the boundary-only coarse stratification. One may instead refine its strata by the isotropy/quotient singularity type and apply the ordinary conical theorem to that refined structure. Fixed contractions alone do not perform that refinement. For the basic case \(\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,4}\cong\mathbb P^1\), the ordinary space has three point strata. Its open object is a sphere with three open discs removed, its point objects are those three points, and its three arrow spaces are the three boundary circles. The source on each circle maps to its point object; the target is the corresponding boundary embedding. Gluing the three mapping cylinders fills the three holes by discs, giving \(S^2\). Thus the cut-open convention does satisfy the presentation in this case; taking the open stratum or a boundary circle as its point object would be a different datum. This verifies the specific inherited \((0,4)\) comparison independently. Empty labels may be deleted, and disconnected strata may be kept as disjoint unions. A grading need not be injective on components: a strictly increasing grading can merge incomparable components, but their actual incidences and disjoint incoming branches must remain in the diagram. The orbifold formulation allows ineffective actions as well. A stabilizer that acts trivially on a deformation chart still contributes its classifying space; quotienting by its kernel would change the stack and its exit category. In particular the vertex moduli factors retain their own automorphisms in addition to graph automorphisms. No divisibility or dense-order assumption on the indexing order is made or needed. Finally this is a homotopy and exit-category presentation, not the missing topos gluing theorem of A.1. The successive cylinders retain the entire face-incidence diagram and its coherence. The manuscript's pair/triple stones omit actual iterated neighbourhood intersections, as the counterexample of A.1 shows. Taking all complete flag-intersection pro-topoi and their \v{C}ech descent maps gives the topos reconstruction there; taking only the homotopy types or only the global stratum-poset forgets information needed for arbitrary sheaves. These are different functors applied to the geometric descent diagram, and their colimit claims have been proved in their respective categories.

statement_full_latex: \label{c4.04-refuted-hss-alone-gives-conical-collars} Quinn's example \cite[p.452]{Quinn1988} is the shrinking hedgehog \[ X=\bigvee_{n\ge1}[0,1/n],\qquad Y=\{0\}, \] with the metric \(|s-t|\) on one arm and \(s+t\) on distinct arms. Thus the two-step filtration is homotopically stratified in Quinn's general definition. It has no mapping-cylinder neighborhood of \(Y\). Every neighborhood contains all sufficiently short arms, including their terminal endpoints, and these endpoints converge to \(Y\). A terminal endpoint of an arm cannot be an interior point of any embedded interval in \(X\). Hence every such endpoint would have to lie on the outer level \(r=1\). Continuity is contradicted by their convergence to the apex \(r=0\). The same argument applies after making the cylinder smaller. Therefore \(\Sigma_d\) in the actual collar/mapping-cylinder sense need not exist for a general HSS. Equations (51), (56), (57), (69), the holink comparison, and the finite spectral sequence have the independent pro-homotopy proofs above. statement_full_latex: \label{c4.06-proved-the-canonical-normal-crossings-comparison} The notation here is checked in the original scans 147/173--177 \cite{C_Grothendieck147}. The normal-crossings branches give \(Q\) a local decomposition into complex lines, with transitions allowed to permute those lines. Write \(Q^*\) for the complement of all coordinate hyperplanes. Thus its fibre is \((\mathbb C^*)^r\), not \(\mathbb C^r\setminus\{0\}\). For rank zero, the empty coordinate arrangement has complement the whole zero bundle; the torus fibre is a point. The same argument then applies without a puncture, and an empty base gives the empty equivalence. Page175(290) defines \(E^*=q^{-1}(Q^*)\); (291) describes \(E^*\to Q^*\) as a torsor for the pulled-back additive bundle \(A\). The quotient map \(q:E^*\to Q^*\) is a canonical homotopy equivalence. Choose a Hermitian splitting \(E=A\oplus Q\); then \((a,v)\mapsto((1-t)a,v)\) contracts the kernel and proves the claim. Splittings form an affine space, so their homotopies identify all inverse choices. The map \(q\) itself does not depend on a splitting. The sector tube \(V^{d_0'}_{d_*,d_0''}\) is, by definition of the normal-crossings incidence sector, the neighborhood germ of \(B\) in the \(E\)-directions, with precisely the coordinates belonging to \(Q\) required to be nonzero. Its pro-homotopy type has a canonical comparison with \(E^*\). Here is a construction and a check of its ambiguity. For a simple normal crossings divisor, use its divisor line bundles with defining sections. Choose an ordinary smooth tubular projection onto the intersection \(B\) and connections on those line bundles. Parallel transport identifies their restrictions on a small neighborhood with their pullbacks from \(B\); the tuple of defining sections then has differential the normal-coordinate isomorphism along \(B\). The inverse function theorem, after variable-radius shrinking, gives an adapted tubular germ from the direct sum of the normal lines to the original space. It takes every coordinate hyperplane and every flag subbundle to the corresponding divisor incidence. This constructs the required sector comparison. Normalize each adapted tubular germ to have identity derivative on the intrinsic normal bundle, by composing with the inverse of its fibrewise normal derivative. This preserves the coordinate arrangement and the flag subbundles. Arbitrary normal-bundle automorphisms are not being declared homotopic to the identity. If a kernel block has no chosen line decomposition, retain its coordinates from an ordinary tubular chart and use the defining sections in the quotient block; the same inverse-function argument respects every flag subbundle. If \(\Phi,\Psi\) are two adapted tubular germs with the same normal derivative, their transition \(g=\Psi^{-1}\Phi\) fixes the zero section and has identity normal derivative. Fibre dilations give \[ g_t=\delta_{1/t}\,g\,\delta_t\quad(t>0),\qquad g_0=\mathrm{id}. \] Taylor's formula in normal coordinates shows this is a continuous, indeed smooth, family of germs through \(t=0\); its tangential displacement tends to zero and its normal derivative tends to the identity. Every \(g_t\) preserves the coordinate-hyperplane arrangement. Restricting to sufficiently small variable-radius neighborhoods makes the family defined for all \(t\in[0,1]\). The same construction works for parameter families. Hence the induced comparison on the sector has a unique homotopy class, compatible with refinements and changes of tubular choices. This supplies the canonical meaning that the manuscript explicitly leaves unresolved below (294). The small-sector pro-germ also compares explicitly with the entire punctured bundle. For a bundle norm and a positive continuous radius function \(\eta\) on the base, the inclusion \(\{v\in E^*:\|v\|<\eta(\pi v)\}\hookrightarrow E^*\) is a homotopy equivalence. An inverse up to homotopy is \[ v\longmapsto \frac{\eta(\pi v)}{\eta(\pi v)+\|v\|}v. \] Interpolation of its strictly positive scalar factor with \(1\) supplies both inverse homotopies and preserves every coordinate nonvanishing condition. Such variable-radius disk neighborhoods are cofinal by the tubular chart and paracompactness of the base. Their natural inclusions therefore identify the sector prospace with the constant space \(E^*\), coherently under shrinking. Combining it with \(q\) gives the precise statement \[ V^{d_0'}_{d_*,d_0''} \ \simeq\ \left.\check N_{d_*,(d_0',d_0'')}^{\,*}\right|_{D_{d_*}^*}. \] The ambiguity is homotopy, not a distinguished homeomorphism of neighborhoods. A Hermitian norm further retracts each punctured line to its unit-circle bundle, giving the corresponding torus bundle; metrics form a convex space of choices. For normal crossings with branch monodromy, perform the construction on the finite local branch-label cover. The normal line bundles and the quotient map descend equivariantly, as does the homotopy-class comparison, because the coordinate arrangement and the dilation are invariant under branch permutations. On a Deligne--Mumford orbifold chart finite-group averaging supplies invariant auxiliary metrics and connections. Thus the result is canonical in the incidence/orbifold category. statement_full_latex: \label{c5.02-refuted-in-all-three-categories-automatic-transversality} Use \(I=\{0<1<2\}\), \[ \Sigma_0=\{*\},\quad \Sigma_1=\mathbb R\times[0,\infty),\quad \Sigma_2=\mathbb R\times[0,\infty)^2. \] Write \((x,t,r)\) on the last space and take \[ \Sigma_{01}=\mathbb R\times\{0\},\quad \Sigma_{12}=\{r=0\},\quad \Sigma_{02}=\{t=0\}. \] All targets are face inclusions and \(s_{01},s_{02}\) are constant. The incoming faces are closed, properly embedded, and transversely collared. Their intersection is \(\{t=r=0\}=s_{12}^{-1}\Sigma_{01}\), and projection control holds because both maps to \(\Sigma_0\) are constant. Thus the induced relation is a topological order with finite totally ordered lower intervals; every bare algebraic and face condition in the proposed implication holds. The source is not assumed fibrant in the general Scholium or its /062 margin. Yet \(s_{12}\) is not transverse to the base boundary in the collar-product meaning explicitly used at /025--027 and /031. Its boundary restriction maps the whole \(x\)-axis to \((0,0)\). If a collar-product description existed near that axis, the image of a small collar neighborhood would lie in a one-dimensional collar through that point. In either example the image of every sufficiently small neighborhood of \((0,0)\) contains a nonempty open two-dimensional wedge: in the smooth example \(|u|<\delta t\), and in the PL example \(|u|<t\). A one-dimensional embedded collar cannot contain an open subset of a two-dimensional manifold, by invariance of dimension. Thus the specified collar-product transversality fails even topologically. This terminology must be retained: the smooth map does satisfy ordinary differential transversality to the target boundary, which is a weaker requirement here. A sufficient extra hypothesis is local triviality of the entire boundary diagram over the base collar, with its trivializations preserving all its faces. Pulling that diagram back along the collar's product coordinate then gives compatible product collars. This is the strong equisingularity qualification in /039; an unspecified use of ``fibrant'' must not be substituted for it. Even adding raw proper Hurewicz fibrancy does not imply the smooth product-collar condition. Take \(\Sigma_0=\{*\}\), \(\Sigma_1=[0,1]\), \(\Sigma_2=[0,1]^2\), \(\Sigma_{01}=\{0,1\}\), \(\Sigma_{12}=[0,1]\times\{0,1\}\), and \(\Sigma_{02}=\{0,1\}\times[0,1]\). statement_full_latex: \label{c5.03-refuted-in-top-automatic-manifold-fibres} Let \(H\) be the Poincare homology three-sphere and \(F=\Sigma H\) its suspension. Then \(F\) is a compact polyhedron which is not a topological manifold: near either suspension vertex the punctured neighborhood is \(H\times(0,\epsilon)\), whose nontrivial fundamental group cannot become that of a punctured four-ball. More precisely the nested punctured cone neighborhoods all induce isomorphisms on that nontrivial group, whereas a four-manifold has a basis of punctured simply-connected ball neighborhoods. Cannon's double-suspension theorem gives \(\Sigma^2H\cong S^5\). Removing the two outer suspension points gives \(F\times\mathbb R\cong S^4\times\mathbb R\): the image of those two points can be sent to the north and south poles by a homeomorphism of \(S^5\). Consequently \(E=F\times S^1\) is a closed topological five-manifold, since it is locally \(F\times\mathbb R\). Take \(\Sigma_0=S^1,\ \Sigma_1=E\times[0,1]\), with incoming face \(\Sigma_{01}=E\times\{0,1\}=\partial\Sigma_1\), and source projection to \(S^1\). This is a proper locally trivial topological bundle, with fibre \(F\amalg F\). Both object spaces are manifolds and the target is the whole boundary. All triple, order, and transversality conditions are vacuous. The fibre is not a manifold. This disproves the mixed-fibre implication at /051 and /063 even with genuine bundles, not merely homotopy fibrations. The precise primary statements used here are Cannon \cite[Theorem 1.5, p.833; Corollary 3.6, p.838]{C_Cannon}.

statement_full_latex: \label{c5.07-refuted-in-top-connected-components-suffice} The word ``connected'' in /068--071 cannot be replaced silently by ``path-connected.'' Even all the stated finiteness, properness, local-immersion, and collared-target conditions permit a strict arrow within one connected component. The following example also satisfies the stronger bordant-target condition of /063, not just the nowhere-dense condition of /069. Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^2\) be a compact, nondegenerate hereditarily indecomposable continuum, for example the plane pseudoarc constructed by R. H. Bing, \emph{Concerning hereditarily indecomposable continua}, Example 1, printed pp.43--44 \cite{C_Bing1951}. Every path in \(K\) is constant. Indeed, a nonconstant path has a nondegenerate image continuum. Uniform continuity partitions its domain into finitely many consecutive intervals whose image continua all have diameter smaller than that whole image. The image would then be a finite union of proper continua with connected successive unions. Indecomposability rules this out, by induction on the number of pieces. Choose a continuous map \(q:[1,\infty)\to\mathbb R^2\) whose cluster set at infinity is exactly \(K\), with \(\operatorname{dist}(q(t),K)\to0\). Here is an explicit existence construction. Fix a point of \(K\). For each positive integer \(n\), choose a finite \(1/n\)-net in \(K\). Its open \(1/n\)-neighbourhood in the plane is connected and hence path-connected. On \([n,n+1]\), let \(q\) traverse a piecewise linear loop, based at the fixed point, which visits every point of that net and stays in that neighbourhood. Concatenation is continuous. These visits show that every point of \(K\) is a cluster point; the neighbourhood bound excludes any other cluster point. Set \[ C=\{(q(t),1/t):t\ge1\}\subset\mathbb R^3, \qquad P=C\cup(K\times\{0\}). \] The height coordinate identifies \(C\) with the ray \([1,\infty)\). The space \(P\) is its compact closure, hence is a connected compact metric space of finite covering dimension at most three. The dimension bound can be checked directly: for any finite open cover of this compact subset of \(\mathbb R^3\), choose a sufficiently fine triangulation of \(\mathbb R^3\). Its vertex open-star cover restricts to a refinement on \(P\), by the Lebesgue number of the given cover; each point lies in at most four such stars, the vertices of its carrier simplex. This is the defining covering-dimension bound. Its single connected component is open. Write \(b=(q(1),1)\); its neighbourhood with height greater than \(1/(1+\epsilon)\) is a collar \([0,\epsilon)\) of the point \(b\). Choose \(a\in K\times\{0\}\). The path component of \(a\) in \(P\) is the singleton \(\{a\}\). To verify this, suppose a path starting in the remainder enters \(C\). An interval component of the inverse image of \(C\) has a finite left endpoint at which the height is zero. On that interval the corresponding ray parameter tends to infinity at its left endpoint. By the intermediate value theorem, the image of every sufficiently short interval after that endpoint contains an entire tail \([T,\infty)\) of ray parameters. Continuity of the path would therefore force the whole tail of \(q\) to converge to the same remainder point. This contradicts its nondegenerate cluster set \(K\). A path remaining in the remainder is constant by the preceding indecomposability argument. Give \(P\) the order with relation \[ R=\Delta_P\cup\{(a,b)\}\subset P\times P. \] This is a closed partial order. Its strict relation consists of one point, which is a clopen component of \(R\); the other component is \(\Delta_P\cong P\). Every lower interval is totally ordered and has at most two elements. Both projections \(s,b:R\to P\) are proper because the domain is compact. The target projection is a local embedding: it is the identity on the diagonal component and the embedding of a point on the strict component. The strict target image \(\{b\}\) is nowhere dense and collared. Thus its family of incoming boundary germs is transverse; there is at most one such germ at any point. The source projection is a Hurewicz fibration, including its full lifting property for arbitrary parameter spaces. Given a map \(g:Z\to R\) and a homotopy \(H:Z\times[0,1]\to P\) with \(H(z,0)=s(g(z))\), let \(Z_e\) be the inverse image of the isolated strict arrow. This is clopen in \(Z\). On \(Z_e\), each path \(H(z,-)\) starts at \(a\), so it is constant; lift it constantly to the strict arrow. On \(Z\setminus Z_e\), lift by \((H(z,t),H(z,t))\in\Delta_P\). These continuous lifts agree with the initial map and glue across the clopen partition. Source transversality to the target collar is also satisfied: on the identity component it is the identity, while the strict component maps to \(a\), outside a chosen collar of \(b\). Nevertheless \(a<b\) lie in the same connected component of \(P\). The map to the one-point set of connected components is not strictly increasing. This refutes the unrestricted TOP conclusion of /070 and therefore the equivalence claimed in /071 in that scope. The additional monomorphism condition for distinct components is vacuous here and cannot repair it. No doubtful transcription is used: the original /070--071 explicitly says connected components, as does the open-component assumption on /068. The exact correction proved in C5.01 is to use open, path-connected components; in particular it applies to manifolds and locally path-connected PL spaces. Another sufficient correction, which can use connected components without local path-connectedness, is to require the proper source map to be open. Here is the additional proof. Suppose a strict arrow has source and target in the same open connected component \(D\). The strict arrows whose targets lie in \(D\) form a clopen subspace of \(R\). Their source image is open by openness of \(s\), and closed by properness; it meets \(D\), so it contains all of \(D\). Thus every point of \(D\) has a strict successor in \(D\). Starting at one point gives arbitrarily long strict chains in its compact upper interval. Proper local injectivity of the target projection makes the cardinalities of lower intervals locally bounded, hence bounded on that compact upper interval, a contradiction. The same open-and-closed image argument aligns middle objects to prove transitivity of the component relation. Cycles would give a strict chain returning to a component and then the same contradiction. Total ordering of the pointwise lower intervals gives the proper-injective target comparison of C5.01. A locally trivial source bundle is open, so this correction applies to the strong equisingular interpretation too.

Let a topological category have Hausdorff object and arrow spaces, open manifold components of its object space, proper locally embedding target map \(b\), Hurewicz source map \(s\), and locally nowhere-dense target image of the strict arrows. Assume every invertible arrow is an identity. Then the induced relation on object components is a partial order, and every nonidentity arrow connects distinct components. Here is a full proof which avoids the manuscript's dimension inequalities. The identity section is closed by Hausdorffness and open by local injectivity of \(b\): near an identity, both that section and a sufficiently small arrow neighbourhood lie in a target-injective chart, so the only arrow in that chart with a given nearby target is its identity. Hence strict arrows form a clopen subspace. Source lifting along a path cannot change from a strict arrow to an identity, and target continuity keeps its target in one component. It follows that the existence of an arrow from one component to another is independent of which source point in the first component is prescribed. This also proves transitivity by lifting the second arrow along a path joining the intermediate endpoints. Suppose a strict arrow has source and target in the same connected \(n\)-manifold component \(D\), allowing boundary or corners. Move its source by path lifting into the interior of \(D\); connected manifold components are path-connected and have nonempty interior, with the dimension-zero case interpreted directly. The target remains in \(D\). Restrict to strict arrows whose source and target lie in \(D\). Over a sufficiently small open coordinate ball \(U\subset D\), a contraction of \(U\) to a point and the Hurewicz lifting property give a continuous section \(\sigma:U	o R^{<}\) of \(s\). Starting from a constant arrow lift proves this for arbitrary parameter space \(U\); the lift stays strict and its target stays in \(D\). Shrink \(U\) around a point so that \(\sigma(U)\) is contained in one target-injective neighbourhood. Then \(b\sigma:U	o D\) is injective, because \(\sigma\) is a section and \(b\) is injective on that neighbourhood. Choose a target corner chart and include its orthant in \(\mathbb R^n\). Invariance of domain makes the image of \(b\sigma\) open in \(\mathbb R^n\); it cannot meet the boundary of that orthant, and hence is open in \(D\). This contradicts the locally nowhere-dense strict target image. Thus no strict arrow has both endpoints in one component. This argument includes dimension zero directly: a nonempty image in a discrete component is open. If there are arrows from \(D\) to \(E\) and back, path lifting aligns their middle endpoints. Write the resulting arrows as \(u:d	o e\) and \(v:e	o d'\), with \(d,d'\in D\). The composite \(vu\) must be an identity by the preceding paragraph, so \(d'=d\). The composite \(uv\), with endpoints in \(E\), must likewise be an identity. Thus \(u\) and \(v\) are inverse; the assumption on invertible arrows forces \(D=E\). This proves antisymmetry. If the category is an ordered space with totally ordered lower intervals, the extra componentwise monomorphism statement and incomparable-face disjointness follow exactly as in C5.01; no extra monomorphism axiom is needed. The same categorical proof applies to finite-dimensional locally finite PL object spaces, even if they are polyhedra rather than manifolds, provided the arrow charts are PL and the target map is a PL local embedding. These are the category-specific assumptions used in the PL-image argument below. For an alleged strict arrow within a component of maximal dimension \(n\), use source path lifting to move its source into the interior of a maximal \(n\)-simplex; this is an open \(n\)-ball. A local source section embeds that ball into a target-injective strict arrow chart. The locally rare PL target image contains no \(n\)-simplex and has local dimension at most \(n-1\). For completeness this cannot contain an embedded \(n\)-ball: a compact sub-ball meets only finitely many target simplices; the closed preimages of these simplices cover it, so one has interior by the Baire theorem. That gives an injective map from an open \(n\)-ball into a Euclidean space of dimension at most \(n-1\), contradicting invariance of domain after inclusion into \(\mathbb R^n\). The remaining component-order argument is unchanged. The TOP counterexample C5.07 explains why arbitrary connected finite-dimensional components do not admit this argument. 	extbf{Doubtful and ill-typed readings.} The original /051, /062, /063, /067, /070, and /071 scans have been opened visually \cite{C_Grothendieck150}. statement_full_latex: Let $P$ be a finite poset and let $\mathcal C_\bullet$ be a complete Segal object in spaces, conservative over $N(P)$. Let $i\in P$ be minimal, let $A=\mathcal C_i$ (an $\infty$-groupoid), and let $\mathcal D=\mathcal C|_{P\setminus\{i\}}$. Let $\mathcal M$ be the category of arrows of $\mathcal C$ whose source is in $A$ and whose target is in $\mathcal D$. Morphisms in $\mathcal M$ are commutative squares, with the source-side arrow necessarily an equivalence. Write $q:\mathcal M\to A$ and $p:\mathcal M\to\mathcal D$ for the source and target functors. Then there is a canonical pushout formula in $\operatorname{Cat}_\infty$ \[ \mathcal C\simeq A\mathbin{\coprod}_{\mathcal M\times\{0\}} (\mathcal M\times[1]) \mathbin{\coprod}_{\mathcal M\times\{1\}}\mathcal D. \tag{C1.B1} \] The maps from the two endpoints are $q$ and $p$, respectively. The comparison is induced by the tautological natural transformation from the source to the target of an arrow.

statement_full_latex: Suppose the deployment is a finite graded topological category with object spaces $\Sigma_j$, arrow spaces $\Sigma_{jk}$ for $j<k$, and identities only within each object space. Suppose its source maps $s_{jk}:\Sigma_{jk}\to\Sigma_j$ are fibrations and the flag identities and control equations are \[ \Sigma_{ijk}=s_{jk}^{-1}(\Sigma_{ij})\subset\Sigma_{jk}, \qquad s_{ik}=s_{ij}s_{jk}\quad\hbox{on }\Sigma_{ijk}. \tag{C1.B3} \] Here $\Sigma_{ij}\hookrightarrow\Sigma_j$ is the target inclusion, and $s_{jk}$ in the second equation is restricted to $\Sigma_{ijk}\to\Sigma_{ij}$. Define a topological category $M_i$ with objects $\coprod_{j>i}\Sigma_{ij}$, arrows $\coprod_{i<j<k}\Sigma_{ijk}$, and the induced source, target and composition maps. Then, after passing to complete Segal objects, $M_i$ is the $\mathcal M$ of C1.B1. Its target functor $p:M_i\to\mathcal D$ is a left fibration. Its source functor $q:M_i\to\Sigma_i$ is well defined by the control equation.

statement_full_latex: The space $|P|$ is homotopy equivalent to $S^2$. The action $\tau$ is free and there is a homotopy equivalence \[ |P|/\langle\tau\rangle\simeq\mathbb {RP}^{2}. \] More precisely, for every old element $g$ the map \[ \Pi_g:P\longrightarrow Q_g:=\{g^+,g^-\}\oplus\mathcal E(M/g) \] is a $\tau$-equivariant homotopy equivalence on order complexes. Here $\oplus$ means the ordinal sum: the two incomparable symbols $g^+,g^-$ lie below every element of $\mathcal E(M/g)$. statement_full_latex: \label{C.01} Let $M$ be a simple, uniform oriented matroid of rank three on $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with a fixed chirotope $\chi_M$. For a non-loop, non-parallel, same-rank extension by an element $p$, put \[ q_{ij}=\chi(i,j,p)\quad (1\leq i<j\leq n). \] The zero pairs of $q$ form a matching in the complete graph on $[n]$. Conversely, we obtain every such extension by enumerating matchings, assigning signs to the remaining pairs, and retaining precisely the assignments satisfying the chirotope axioms on $[n]\cup\{p\}$. We quotient by reorientation of $p$ by requiring the first nonzero coordinate of $q$, in lexicographic pair order, to be positive. \emph{Proof.} If $q_{ij}=q_{ik}=0$ for distinct $i,j,k$, then $p$ lies in both rank-two flats spanned by $\{i,j\}$ and $\{i,k\}$. Their union has rank three because $M$ is uniform. Submodularity bounds the rank of their intersection by one. That intersection contains $i$ and $p$, so the non-loop $p$ is parallel to $i$, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus the zero pairs are disjoint. Every extension therefore occurs in our candidate list. We define the remaining triples by alternation, set repeated triples to zero, and leave triples in $[n]$ equal to $\chi_M$. The full signed basis-exchange axiom is then a necessary and sufficient chirotope test, so accepting exactly its solutions introduces no extra candidates. Multiplication of all $q_{ij}$ by $-1$ is exactly reorientation of $p$. No allowed vector is zero, and hence each orbit has exactly one representative with the stated normalization. \hfill$\square$ For reproducibility, our fast enumerator first checks the necessary three-term Grassmann--Pl\"ucker sign relations \[ \bigl\{ \chi(a,b,c)\chi(a,d,e), -\chi(a,b,d)\chi(a,c,e), \chi(a,b,e)\chi(a,c,d) \bigr\}. \] Each such set must either be zero or contain both signs. This is \emph{only a filter}: a second, independent program checks the full signed basis-exchange axiom on every surviving assignment. Explicitly, for every ordered basis $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ and every ordered basis $y=(y_1,y_2,y_3)$ it verifies that at least one $i$ satisfies \[ \chi(y_i,x_2,x_3) \chi(y_1,\ldots,y_{i-1},x_1,y_{i+1},\ldots,y_3) =\chi(x_1,x_2,x_3)\chi(y_1,y_2,y_3). \] It suffices to choose $x_1$ in each unordered basis, put the other two entries in increasing order, and use increasing $y$: permutations of the remaining entries multiply both sides by the same sign. We thus check the full axiom, not merely its three-term consequence. For $n=6$, the number of candidates, before this filtering, is \[ \sum_{k=0}^{3} \frac{6!}{(6-2k)!\,2^k k!}\,2^{15-k-1}=354304. \] The programs are \texttt{counts\_extensions.py}, its C++ inner loop \texttt{counts\_extensions.cpp}, and \texttt{counts\_independent\_check.py}. Their input and complete accepted sign-vector lists accompany the paper.

statement_full_latex: \label{C.03} We count the literal gen--gen inertia arcs of cote 154/120 independently of the formula $s_1=2s_0$. Here are the complete rules used by the checker, including the endpoint convention. Realize the rank-two chirotope $q$ by oriented rays $w_i$ in an oriented plane and order the $2n$ signed rays $\epsilon w_i$ cyclically. Equal signed rays form packets. For a two-element packet $(\epsilon,i),(\eta,j)$, choose $k$ outside its unoriented parallel class and order the first label before the second exactly when \[ -\eta\,\chi_M(i,j,k)q_{ik}=+1. \tag{C.1} \] The rank-two sign order and (C.1) suffice to construct the complete boundary word. The global reversal of this word has no effect on any count or gluing. To verify (C.1), use local affine representatives $a_i=(w_i,z_i)$ and $a_j=(\lambda w_i,z_j)$. At the endpoint in direction $J(\epsilon w_i)$ of a sufficiently large circle, the angular displacement has sign and relative order determined by $\epsilon z_i/\lVert w_i\rVert$. Moreover \[ \det(a_i,a_j,a_k) =-(z_j-\lambda z_i)\det(w_i,w_k). \] For equal signed rays $\operatorname{sgn}\lambda=\epsilon\eta$; substitution gives (C.1). This calculation is local to the restriction on $\{i,j,k,p\}$ and does not assert a realization of the whole extension. The two packets over the same vertex have reversed orders, as required by the disk construction. Each zero pair gives two generization intervals $G$, one in each packet. For two adjacent endpoint labels $(\epsilon,i),(\eta,j)$ that belong to no $G$ packet, the interval is an ordinary specialization interval $S$ precisely when, for every $k\notin\{i,j\}$, \[ \chi_M(i,j,k)q_{ij} =\epsilon q_{ik}=\eta q_{jk}. \tag{C.2} \] Indeed, the first expression is the side of line $k$ containing $v_{ij}$ in the affine chart $p>0$. The other expressions are its sides at the two endpoint rays. Agreement says that $k$ cuts neither segment from $v_{ij}$ to those endpoints. Since two pseudolines cross at most once and the boundary endpoints are adjacent, this is equivalent to the intervening triangle being empty. Its collapse is exactly the permitted specialization. The independent checker confirms that the resulting pairs are exactly those obtained by replacing one nonzero coordinate of $q$ by zero in the exhaustive extension list. For a possible exceptional sweep at $D_i$, the criterion is \[ q_{ab}\chi_M(a,b,i)=r\in\{+1,-1\} \quad\hbox{for every }a,b\ne i. \tag{C.3} \] The common sign says that every base vertex off $D_i$ lies on the same side of $D_i$ in the affine chart $p>0$. The other side is an empty corridor. Its boundary interval lies on the side with sign $-r$, and is shortened past the adjacent ordinary transition intervals. Its position among the intervals is obtained from that boundary subarc; the program uses its midpoint. When $q$ has one zero pair, (C.3) is tested at the two lines through that vertex and inserts the exceptional interval between the appropriate two $G$ intervals. When $q$ has at least two zero pairs, there is no such exceptional interval, since a zero pair avoiding $i$ would violate (C.3). These rules are exhaustive: the manuscript's ordinary transitions are exactly the empty triangles and the parallel packets (154/035--038), and its exceptional transitions are exactly the empty corridors (154/036--038, together with the stable sweeps in $\mathcal X_2$, 154/005). Consecutive $G$ intervals in the complete cyclic list are therefore precisely the gen--gen inertia arcs. Every boundary word and transition interval is recorded in the boundary-certificate JSON files.

statement_full_latex: Lead L2 is false: all $2^\nu$ stable generizations are present in $\mathcal X$. Its true replacement is the following explicit cellular description. Subdivide every ordinary cube of $\overline T(M)$ by its coordinate midplanes. Its vertices are the centers of the original cube faces, hence ordinary extension labels; its edges are the ordinary cover relations. Replace each parallel polygon by the M\"obius band of E4, subdivided as described below. In this CW model of $B(M)$ the dual quadrangulation $\mathcal X^\vee$ is an embedded subcomplex containing the entire one-skeleton. Specifically, if $\sigma$ has distinct zero coordinates $i,j$ and resolving them with specified signs gives $\sigma_i,\sigma_j,\sigma_{ij}$, its diamond is \[ \sigma<\sigma_i<\sigma_{ij},\qquad \sigma<\sigma_j<\sigma_{ij}. \] The associated quadrangle is the union of these two closed order-complex triangles. It occurs in the ordinary part of the dual manuscript map exactly when the specified transition ports at $i,j$ are adjacent in the full boundary cycle of its disk. This construction specifies the ordinary quadrangles and their attaching maps. The exceptional part consists of the entire subdivided M\"obius bands. Their rectangular cells are indexed by the original flags $(v,e)$, and their four vertices are $U_e^+,S_v^+,S_v^-,U_e^-$ in that cyclic order. Thus there are specified comparison maps \[ \mathcal X\cong\mathcal X^\vee \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ }B(M) \xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }\overline T(M). \] Here $\iota$ is a cellular subcomplex inclusion and induces a surjection on fundamental groups; $\beta$ is the continuous blow-down collapsing each inserted M\"obius core circle to its parallel point. The inclusion $\iota$ is a homotopy equivalence exactly when no ordinary position passes through three old vertices. In that case it is an identification of the indicated CW spaces.

statement_full_latex: Let $K$ be a nonempty finite abstract simplicial complex whose realization is a closed PL manifold. The ordered finite list of simplices of $K$ is all the input in the following construction. There are explicit countable simplicial groups \[ G^{\mathrm{PL}}(K),\qquad G^{\mathrm{SA}}(K) \tag{A.131.1} \] with the following effective properties. Their simplices are finite integer strings; membership, equality, and degeneracy are decidable. Multiplication, inversion, faces and degeneracies are given by total algorithms. The construction also gives a computable simplicial homomorphism $G^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)\to G^{\mathrm{SA}}(K)$. For every real closed field $R$, coefficient extension gives weak equivalences \[ G^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)\longrightarrow P_{\mathrm{PL},R}(|K|_R), \qquad G^{\mathrm{SA}}(K)\longrightarrow P_{\mathrm{SA},R}(|K|_R), \tag{A.131.2} \] where the source is realized over the real algebraic numbers. All families are homeomorphisms of the total product with the parameter simplex, preserve that entire parameter, fix the bottom pointwise, and preserve the free top setwise. For each $r\ge0$, the algorithm in the proof outputs a complete countable presentation $\Pi_r^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)$, respectively $\Pi_r^{\mathrm{SA}}(K)$, for the entire homotopy group \[ \pi_rP_{\mathrm{PL},R}(|K|_R),\qquad \pi_rP_{\mathrm{SA},R}(|K|_R). \tag{A.131.3} \] For $r\ge1$ these groups are based at the identity; translation identifies the corresponding groups on any other component. Here ``outputs'' means that one uniform algorithm enumerates all specified generators and relators. For $r\ge1$ it may instead enumerate an integer relation matrix for the abelian group. For an arbitrary fixed o-minimal expansion, $\Pi_0^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)$ also presents the stipulated definable component group. If every component of $|K|$ has dimension at least five, (A.131.1) gives a weak model for the real TOP concordance space as well, and $\Pi_r^{\mathrm{PL}}(K)$ presents its homotopy groups for all $r$. For the empty complex and empty base, take the constant one-element simplicial group; every component and homotopy group is trivial. These are complete effective countable presentations and whole simplicial models. No terminating word problem, finite presentation, finite invariant-factor description, or efficient complexity bound is asserted. No higher weak equivalence from PL to SA or to an arbitrary o-minimal expansion is inferred.

statement_full_latex: Let $\mathcal M\preccurlyeq\mathcal N$ be an elementary extension of o-minimal structures in the same language, both expanding real closed fields. Let $B$ be a closed bounded definable manifold over $\mathcal M$. Then extension of definitions induces a weak equivalence of simplicial groups \[ P_{\mathrm{def},\mathcal M}(B) \longrightarrow P_{\mathrm{def},\mathcal N}(B_{\mathcal N}). \] The groups use homeomorphisms of the total product with a parameter simplex; they preserve that parameter, fix the bottom pointwise and preserve the free top. All defining parameters in the relevant structure are permitted. More generally, extension gives the same weak equivalence for the simplicial automorphism group of any closed bounded definable set with finitely many marked definable subsets, each required to be preserved setwise or fixed pointwise. If $B$ is given by a finite rational PL model, the square with the PL coefficient-extension map commutes. Hence the comparison from PL is a weak equivalence over $\mathcal M$ if and only if it is a weak equivalence over $\mathcal N$. Corresponding injectivity, surjectivity, or isomorphism assertions in each homotopy degree are equivalent as well.

statement_full_latex: Let $B$ be a compact real PL manifold without boundary, all of whose components have dimension at most two. The natural map from the simplicial group of jointly PL concordances to the singular complex of the compact-open topological concordance group is a weak equivalence: \[ P_{\mathrm{PL}}(B)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sing}P_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B). \tag{A.134.1} \] Both groups fix $B\times\{0\}$ pointwise and leave the top free. For components of dimension zero or one these spaces are weakly contractible. For every closed PL surface $F$, the natural comparison $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{PL}}(F)\to \operatorname{Sing}\operatorname{Homeo}(F)$ is a weak equivalence as well. Together with A.131, this gives the explicit recursive whole-space TOP model and recursive homotopy-group presentations in these base dimensions. The empty base has the one-element simplicial group. No statement about base dimension four, or about higher PL--semialgebraic comparison, is included here.
