statement_full_latex: Let $B$ be a closed compact real PL four-manifold. All PL families below are jointly PL and preserve the parameter projection; all TOP spaces are replaced by their singular complexes. Set \[ \begin{aligned} A_C&=\operatorname{Aut}_C(B),\\ P_C&=\operatorname{Aut}_C(B\times I\text{ rel }B\times\{0\}),\\ H_C&=\operatorname{Aut}_C(B\times I\text{ rel }B\times\partial I), \qquad C\in\{\mathrm{PL},\mathrm{TOP}\}, \end{aligned} \] and let $F_A,F_P,F_H$ be the based homotopy fibres of the respective natural maps from PL to TOP, taken over the identity. Top restriction induces a map $F_P\to F_A$ with homotopy fibre \[ F_H\simeq \operatorname{Map}(B,K(\mathbb Z/2,1)). \tag{A.135.1} \] Here the mapping space is unbased, pointed by the constant map. Consequently there is a based homotopy-fibre sequence \[ \operatorname{Map}(B,K(\mathbb Z/2,1)) \longrightarrow F_P\longrightarrow F_A. \tag{A.135.2} \] In particular $\pi_jF_P\to\pi_jF_A$ is an isomorphism for $j\ge3$, and there is the exact segment \[ \begin{aligned} 0&\longrightarrow\pi_2F_P\longrightarrow\pi_2F_A \longrightarrow H^0(B;\mathbb Z/2)\\ &\longrightarrow\pi_1F_P\longrightarrow\pi_1F_A \longrightarrow H^1(B;\mathbb Z/2)\\ &\longrightarrow\pi_0F_P\longrightarrow\pi_0F_A. \end{aligned} \tag{A.135.3} \] The last line is understood with its usual pointed-set exactness. This identifies the fully boundary-fixed comparison fibre and reduces the free-top comparison to the ordinary four-manifold automorphism comparison. It does not assert that $F_A$ or $F_P$ is contractible, that the original comparison is surjective on components, or that all relative PL structures have the original PL isomorphism type. The connecting maps and any resulting extension data in (A.135.3) remain unevaluated; the abstract homotopy type of $F_A$ alone does not determine $F_P$.

statement_full_latex: For a closed compact real PL four-manifold $B$, use the based comparison fibres $F_A$ and $F_P$ of A.135. There is a specified map of based homotopy types \[ \beta_B:F_A\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}(B,K(\mathbb Z/2,2)) \tag{A.136.1} \] obtained by looping product with a line on sliced PL structures and then applying the open five-dimensional classification with its standard PL lift. It satisfies \[ F_P\simeq\operatorname{hofib}_0(\beta_B). \tag{A.136.2} \] In particular the last line of (A.135.3) extends to the exact pointed-set sequence \[ H^1(B;\mathbb Z/2)\longrightarrow\pi_0F_P \longrightarrow\pi_0F_A \xrightarrow{\pi_0\beta_B}H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2). \tag{A.136.3} \] The image of $\pi_0F_P$ consists exactly of the classes with zero obstruction $\pi_0\beta_B$. A class of $F_A$ represented by a PL automorphism $a$ and a TOP isotopy $\gamma$ from the identity to $a$ has obstruction equal to the relative PL-structure class of the cylinder homeomorphism $(x,u)\mapsto(\gamma_u(x),u)$, in $H^3(B\times I,B\times\partial I;\mathbb Z/2) =H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)$, using the standard PL structure as origin. This describes all components and all higher homotopy groups of the \emph{based comparison fibre} in terms of the actual map $\beta_B$. It does not evaluate that map in general, determine the abstract four-manifold automorphism comparison, or determine the cokernel of $\pi_0P_{\mathrm{PL}}(B)\to\pi_0P_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)$. In particular it does not supply a model for TOP concordance components that have no PL representative. The homotopy type of $F_A$ alone is insufficient without $\beta_B$.

statement_full_latex: Let $B$ be a closed compact real PL four-manifold. Write $c_A:A_{\mathrm{PL}}\to A_{\mathrm{TOP}}$ and $c_P:P_{\mathrm{PL}}\to P_{\mathrm{TOP}}$ for the ordinary-family comparisons of A.135, and $e$ for top restriction. Define the subgroup \[ I_B=(\pi_0e)^{-1} \bigl(\operatorname{im}(\pi_0c_A)\bigr) \subseteq\pi_0P_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B), \qquad J_B=\operatorname{im}(\pi_0\beta_B) \subseteq H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2), \tag{A.137.1} \] where $\beta_B$ is the map specified in A.136. There is a well-defined homomorphism \[ \lambda_B:I_B\longrightarrow H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)/J_B \quad\hbox{such that}\quad \ker\lambda_B=\operatorname{im}(\pi_0c_P). \tag{A.137.2} \] No surjectivity of $\lambda_B$ is asserted. In particular $\operatorname{im}(\pi_0c_P)$ is normal in $I_B$ and \[ I_B/\operatorname{im}(\pi_0c_P) \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)/J_B. \tag{A.137.2a} \] Thus this quotient is a finite elementary abelian $2$-group, of order at most $2^{\dim_{\mathbb Z/2}H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)}$. Here is an explicit definition. Given $h\in P_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)$ whose component belongs to $I_B$, choose a TOP isotopy $\gamma$ from its top map $f=e(h)$ to a PL map $a$. Lift this endpoint change to a bottom-fixed isotopy of the cylinder and let $h_\gamma$ be its final composite with $h$, so that $e(h_\gamma)=a$. Put \[ \kappa(h_\gamma) =[\,(h_\gamma)_*\alpha_N\,]-[\,\alpha_N\,] \in H^3(N,\partial N;\mathbb Z/2) \cong H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2),\qquad N=B\times I, \tag{A.137.3} \] using the relative PL-structure classification with the standard structure $\alpha_N$ as origin. Then $\lambda_B([h])$ is the class of (A.137.3) modulo $J_B$. Product collars are imposed before taking the relative class. Consequently $h$ is TOP-isotopic, through bottom-fixed ordinary concordances with free top, to a PL concordance if and only if its top is TOP-isotopic to a PL map and the class (A.137.3) is zero modulo $J_B$. If $H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)=0$, the endpoint condition is the only condition. The empty-base case has trivial groups throughout. This is a criterion for the complete image on components. It leaves both the ordinary four-dimensional endpoint-image predicate and $J_B$ unevaluated in general. It does not claim that vanishing of a stable boundary obstruction makes a four-dimensional homeomorphism isotopic to PL, or that every TOP concordance component is represented by a PL concordance.

statement_full_latex: Let $K$ be a closed bounded definable set in an o-minimal expansion of a real closed field $R$. Fix finitely many graph-formula formats and retain exactly the parameters defining homeomorphisms of $K$ with any prescribed finite list of definable marked-set or boundary conditions. Let $\mathcal H$ be the definable quotient by equality of the whole maps. For nonempty $K$ put \[ d(h,g)=\max_{x\in K}\|h(x)-g(x)\| +\max_{x\in K}\|h^{-1}(x)-g^{-1}(x)\|. \tag{A.138.1} \] Then $(\mathcal H,d)$ is definably homeomorphic to a definable subset of Euclidean space. For every $h_0\in\mathcal H$ and $\epsilon>0$, there are a definable $d$-open neighbourhood $U$ of $h_0$, a $\delta>0$ with $B_d(h_0,\delta)\subseteq U$, and a definable contraction $C:U\times I\to U$ such that \[ C(h,0)=h,\qquad C(h,1)=h_0,\qquad C(h_0,s)=h_0, \qquad U\subseteq B_d(h_0,\epsilon). \tag{A.138.2} \] Evaluation and inverse evaluation throughout this contraction are jointly definable and continuous. Thus it is a contraction through actual homeomorphisms satisfying the same marked conditions. The empty-set case is trivial. In contrast, if $p:[0,1]\to R$ is continuous and affine on at most $m$ intervals, where $m\ge1$ is an ordinary finite integer, then \[ \max_{x\in[0,1]}|x^2-p(x)|\ge\frac1{8m^2}. \tag{A.138.3} \] Over a non-Archimedean real closed field, a positive infinitesimal $\epsilon$ therefore admits no finite PL $\epsilon$-approximation of the semialgebraic homeomorphism $x\mapsto x^2$. Nevertheless this homeomorphism is semialgebraically isotopic to the identity relative to the two endpoints. The contraction neighbourhood in (A.138.2) depends on the fixed formula formats. The statement supplies neither a uniform contraction over the union of all formats nor a higher PL-to-semialgebraic concordance comparison.

statement_full_latex: Let $B$ be a connected closed oriented real PL four-manifold, and retain $I_B,J_B,\lambda_B$ and $c_P$ from A.137. Put $\pi=\pi_1(B)$ and let $\mathbb Z_{(2)}$ denote the integers localized at the prime $2$. Define \[ \begin{split} \delta_* &: H_2(B;\mathbb Z/2)\longrightarrow H_1(B;\mathbb Z_{(2)}),\\ L_B&=\mathrm{PD}_B^{-1}(\ker\delta_*) \subseteq H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2), \end{split} \tag{A.140.1} \] where $\delta_*$ is the Bockstein for $0\to\mathbb Z_{(2)}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z_{(2)} \to\mathbb Z/2\to0$, and $\mathrm{PD}_B$ is mod-$2$ Poincar\'e duality. Suppose that the assembly summand of Orson--Powell--Randal-Williams, Definition~5.8, is zero: \[ I_2:H_2(\pi;\mathbb Z_{(2)}) \longrightarrow L^q_6(\mathbb Z[\pi])_{(2)}, \qquad I_2=0. \tag{A.140.2} \] Then \[ \operatorname{im}\lambda_B \supseteq (L_B+J_B)/J_B. \tag{A.140.3} \] In particular, if $H_1(B;\mathbb Z_{(2)})$ has no $2$-torsion, $\lambda_B$ is surjective and A.137 becomes the isomorphism \[ I_B/\operatorname{im}(\pi_0c_P) \cong H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)/J_B. \tag{A.140.4} \] This does not evaluate the endpoint-image condition defining $I_B$ or the subgroup $J_B$ in general. If $B$ is simply connected, both of those restrictions disappear on the TOP concordance component group, and \[ \pi_0P_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)=1, \qquad J_B=H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2). \tag{A.140.5} \] There is the stronger ordinary-loop assertion. If $\gamma$ is a based TOP loop of automorphisms of $B$, let $T_\gamma(x,t)=(\gamma_t(x),t)$ and define \[ \eta_B:\pi_1 A_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)\longrightarrow H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2), \qquad \eta_B[\gamma]=\kappa(T_\gamma). \tag{A.140.6} \] For simply connected $B$ this homomorphism is surjective and vanishes on the image of $\pi_1A_{\mathrm{PL}}(B)$. Consequently the ordinary automorphism comparison $A_{\mathrm{PL}}(B)\to A_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)$ is not surjective on $\pi_1$ whenever $H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)\ne0$. In particular this holds for the finite PL manifold $S^2\times S^2$. This last statement concerns automorphisms of the base; it is not an additional conclusion about the homotopy groups of $P_{\mathrm{PL}}(B)\to P_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)$. statement_full_latex: Let $B$ be a connected closed oriented real PL four-manifold. Let $j:W\hookrightarrow B$ be a compact connected simply connected codimension-zero PL submanifold, with collared boundary. The boundary may be empty, in which case $W=B$. Write \[ j_!:H^2(W,\partial W;\mathbb Z/2) \longrightarrow H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2) \] for extension by zero, and write $\mathrm{PD}_W$ for relative Poincar\'e--Lefschetz duality. For an ordinary based TOP loop $\gamma$ of automorphisms of $B$, define \[ \eta_B:\pi_1 A_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)\longrightarrow H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2), \qquad \eta_B[\gamma]=\kappa_B(T_\gamma), \qquad T_\gamma(x,t)=(\gamma_t(x),t). \] This is the A.136 trace homomorphism, also displayed in (A.140.6); its definition does not require an assembly hypothesis. Retain $I_B,J_B,c_P$ from A.137. Then \[ \operatorname{im}\eta_B\supseteq\operatorname{im}j_! =\mathrm{PD}_B^{-1}\!\left( \operatorname{im}\bigl(j_*:H_2(W;\mathbb Z/2) \to H_2(B;\mathbb Z/2)\bigr)\right). \tag{A.141.1} \] Every class in the displayed subgroup is realized by an ordinary TOP loop on $B$ that is the identity outside $\operatorname{int}W$ and on one common collar of $\partial W$ throughout the loop. No assembly hypothesis on $\pi_1(B)$ is imposed. If $j_*$ on $H_2(-;\mathbb Z/2)$ is onto, then \[ \operatorname{im}\eta_B=J_B=H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2), \qquad \operatorname{im}(\pi_0c_P)=I_B. \tag{A.141.2} \] In that case the automorphism comparison $A_{\mathrm{PL}}(B)\to A_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B)$ fails to be surjective on $\pi_1$ whenever $H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2)\ne0$. In particular (A.141.2) holds for \[ B=C\mathbin{\#}D, \] where $C$ is a closed connected simply connected oriented PL four-manifold and $D$ is a closed connected oriented PL four-manifold with $H_2(D;\mathbb Z/2)=0$. The equality $\operatorname{im}(\pi_0c_P)=I_B$ retains the endpoint condition: a TOP concordance component is in the PL image exactly when its top is TOP-isotopic to a PL automorphism. We do not assert that this endpoint condition is automatic for these nonsimply connected $B$, and do not compute either whole concordance space or $\pi_0P_{\mathrm{PL}}(B)$.

statement_full_latex: Let \(M\) be any o-minimal expansion of a real closed field. All sets, maps, homotopies, compactness assertions, and products below are definable over \(M\). Here compact means definably compact. Let \(f:K\to Y\) be a continuous surjection between compact definable sets. If \(Y\ne\varnothing\) and \(d=\dim Y\), there are a compact definable set \(R\), a continuous surjection \(q:R\to Y\), an integer \(1\le m\le d+1\), and a continuous map \[ \ell:R\longrightarrow J_m(f),\qquad \pi\ell=q, \tag{157.1} \] where \(J_m(f)\) is the labelled \(m\)-fold fibrewise join of \(f\). The map \(q\) is universally a definable homotopy equivalence: for every continuous map \(T\to Y\) from a compact definable set, \(R\times_YT\to T\) is a definable homotopy equivalence. If \(Z\subset Y\) is closed and \(b:Z\to J_a(f)\) is a continuous section of its join projection, the resolution can be enlarged to a compact \(R'\) containing \(Z\) as a closed subspace, with \(q'|_Z=\operatorname{id}_Z\), a universal homotopy equivalence \(q':R'\to Y\), and a map \[ \ell':R'\longrightarrow J_{m+a}(f),\qquad \pi\ell'=q',\qquad \ell'|_Z=b \tag{157.2} \] (the last equality uses the last \(a\) slots). In particular, for \(Y=P=[0,1]^k\), \(Z=\partial P\), there is a continuous definable \(w:P\to J_{m+a}(f)\) with \(w|_{\partial P}=b\), and \(\pi w\) is definably homotopic to \(\operatorname{id}_P\) relative to \(\partial P\). For the following metric consequence impose an additional hypothesis, which is not supplied by the topological assertion. Suppose \(C_p\), \(p\in P\), is a bounded Hausdorff-continuous definable family of nonempty compact subsets of a fixed \(M^n\). Suppose there is a compact definable \(K\) and a Lipschitz surjection \(\phi:K\to P\) such that \(s\mapsto C_{\phi(s)}\) is Hausdorff-Lipschitz. The convex homotopy from \(\operatorname{id}_P\) to \(g\) fixes \(\partial P\). Then the comparison on $\pi_0H$ is onto, so (A.163.2) extends to \[ 0\longrightarrow H^1(B;\mathbb Z/2) \longrightarrow\pi_0H_{\mathrm{PL}} \longrightarrow\pi_0H_{\mathrm{TOP}}\longrightarrow0. \tag{A.163.4} \] The central evaluation hypothesis is automatic when $Z(\pi)=0$. Under these additional assumptions the ordinary-loop contribution \[ \eta_B:\pi_1\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{TOP}}(B) \longrightarrow\pi_0F_A \xrightarrow{\pi_0\beta_B}H^2(B;\mathbb Z/2) \tag{A.163.5} \] from A.136 is zero. Thus its fully boundary-fixed component comparison has kernel $(\mathbb Z/2)^4$ and is surjective; its fundamental-group comparison is surjective with kernel $\mathbb Z/2$, and its comparisons in degrees at least two are isomorphisms. Also $\eta_{T^4}=0$. More generally, the assembly and Whitehead-group hypotheses for (A.163.2)--(A.163.3) hold for every such $B$ whose fundamental group is word-hyperbolic or acts properly, cocompactly and isometrically on a finite-dimensional CAT(0) space. Thus the stated relative kernel, fundamental-group exact sequence, and higher isomorphisms hold on this entire explicitly specified class. The extra conclusion (A.163.4) still requires the stated realization of central elements by PL loops; it holds in particular when the centre is trivial. These statements concern the fully boundary-fixed cylinder and the ordinary-loop part of $\beta_B$. They do not compute the free-top comparison fibre $F_P$, the whole map $\beta_B$, or the endpoint-image condition in A.137.

statement_full_latex: Let $X$ be a definable set in a fixed o-minimal expansion of a real closed field, and let $\Phi$ be a finite family of closed definable subsets of $X$. There is a unique coarsest finite partition $\mathcal P(X;\Phi)$ satisfying the following requirements: its strata are locally closed PL manifolds, each of a single dimension; each stratum closure is a union of strata; the sets in $\Phi$ are unions of strata; and for every closed union $Y$ of strata, the non-PL-manifold locus $\operatorname{Sing}_{\rm PL}(Y)$ is a union of strata. Dimension may differ between strata. One may instead require connected strata (definably connected over a general real closed field); this class also has a unique coarsest partition. Both versions are preserved by definable homeomorphisms of the marked data $(X;\Phi)$. Their dimension filtration \[ X_{\le k}=\bigcup_{\substack{S\in\mathcal P(X;\Phi)\\\dim S\le k}}S \quad(-1\le k\le\dim X) \] is closed and canonical, with pure-dimensional PL-manifold layers after empty layers are omitted. If a closed filtration $\varnothing=Y_{-1}\subset Y_0\subset\cdots\subset Y_s=X$ is given, take $\Phi=\{Y_0,\ldots,Y_s\}$ and insert, in lexicographic order, the closed sets \[ E_{j,k}=Y_{j-1}\cup(Y_j\cap X_{\le k}), \qquad 0\le j\le s,\quad -1\le k\le\dim X. \] Omitting repetitions gives a canonical regular equidimensional filtration compatible with the preassigned one. The coarseness assertion concerns the stated class of partitions; it is not the false least-fine assertion among all weak filtrations.

Put \[ M=S^2_R=\{x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in R^3: x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\},\qquad h(x)=x_1, \] and let $X=R^2\times M\times R$, with coordinates $(a,b,x,u)$. Let $F\subset\mathbb R^m$ and $G\subset\mathbb R^n$ be compact definable closed topological surfaces, and let $q:F\to G$ be a continuous definable surjection whose point inverses are cell-like in the classical topological sense. Then there are $\epsilon>0$ and a jointly definable continuous map \[ k:(0,\epsilon]\times G\longrightarrow F \] such that each $k_s$ is a homeomorphism and \[ \lim_{s\downarrow0}\sup_{y\in G}\|q(k_s(y))-y\|=0. \tag{A5.16.4} \] Equivalently, $q$ is the endpoint of a definable continuous family $h_s:F\to G$ with $h_0=q$ and $h_s$ a homeomorphism for every $s>0$. Consequently the associated double mapping-cylinder projection is definably locally trivial at its central parameter.

statement_full_latex: Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be abelian categories and let $T:\mathcal B\longrightarrow\mathcal A$ be an additive left exact functor. Write $\mathcal C_T$ for the category of triples $(F,G,u)$ with $F\in\mathcal A$, $G\in\mathcal B$, and $u:F\to TG$. A morphism $(a,b)$ satisfies $T(b)u=u'a$. Then $\mathcal C_T$ is abelian and has the recollement functors \[ \begin{array}{lll} i^*(F,G,u)=F,&i_*F=(F,0,0),&i^!(F,G,u)=\ker u,\\ j_!G=(0,G,0),&j^*(F,G,u)=G,&j_*G=(TG,G,1). \end{array} \] Their adjunctions are $i^*\dashv i_*\dashv i^!$ and $j_!\dashv j^*\dashv j_*$. Both $i_*$ and $j_!,j_*$ are fully faithful, and $\ker j^*=\operatorname{im}i_*$. The functors $i^*,i_*,j_!,j^*$ are exact; $i^!,j_*$ are left exact. There are natural exact sequences \[ 0\to j_!j^*C\to C\to i_*i^*C\to0, \qquad 0\to i_*i^!C\to C\to j_*j^*C \to i_*\operatorname{coker}u\to0. \] For the displayed triples on 121/039, take $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Sh}_\Lambda(Y)$, $\mathcal B=\operatorname{Sh}_\Lambda(X)$, and $T=p_*i^{-1}$. The adjunction $p^{-1}\dashv p_*$ identifies $u$ with the manuscript's $\alpha:p^{-1}F\to i^{-1}G$. Here $i^{-1}$ means ordinary sheaf restriction; it is not the extraordinary restriction $i^!$.

statement_full_latex: Let $i:Y\hookrightarrow Z$ be a closed embedding and $j:U=Z\setminus Y\hookrightarrow Z$ its open complement. For sheaves of modules over any fixed ring $\Lambda$, restriction induces an equivalence \[ \operatorname{Sh}_\Lambda(Z)\simeq \mathcal C_{i^{-1}j_*}. \] It identifies all six functors with A6.001. In particular the right adjoint to restriction to the open part is $j_*$, and the right adjoint to extension from the closed part is the kernel of the specialization arrow. For a boundary pushout $Z=Y\cup_pX$ with $p:\partial X\to Y$, the unrestricted triples of page 039, with $G$ an arbitrary sheaf on the whole resolved $X$, are in general a larger category than $\operatorname{Sh}_\Lambda(Z)$. statement_full_latex: The following is a precise form of the data on 121/041--047. Fix a finite partially ordered set $I$. For each $i$ give a compact manifold with embedded corners $M_i$ of dimension $d_i$. For each $j<i$ give a possibly empty collective boundary hypersurface $H_{ij}\subset M_i$ and a locally trivial fibration $p_{ij}:H_{ij}\to M_j$ of manifolds with corners, whenever $H_{ij}\ne\varnothing$. A collective hypersurface is a disjoint union of boundary hypersurfaces with a specified common base. Require the following conditions. \begin{enumerate} \item Every boundary hypersurface occurs in exactly one $H_{ij}$. An intersection of several nonempty $H_{ij}$ can occur only when their lower labels form a chain. The intersection is a corner of the expected codimension. \item For $j<k<i$ one has \[ H_{ij}\cap H_{ik}=p_{ik}^{-1}(H_{kj}),\qquad p_{ij}=p_{kj}p_{ik}\quad\hbox{on }H_{ij}\cap H_{ik}. \] Restrictions of the fibrations to these corners are locally trivial. Their entire finite diagram over a sufficiently small open set in $M_j$ has a simultaneous local trivialization. This last condition specifies compatibility as a family, and not merely the separate local triviality of each arrow. \item Compatible collars are part of the datum. They commute on corners and preserve all the displayed maps: a collar for a lower face $H_{ij}$, restricted to $H_{ik}$ with $j<k$, projects by $p_{ik}$ to the corresponding collar of $H_{kj}$ in $M_k$; a collar for $H_{ik}$, restricted to $H_{ij}$, is vertical for $p_{ij}$. Their products give corner charts with independent nonnegative radius coordinates. \end{enumerate} Here and below an empty face contributes no condition. The fiber of $p_{ij}$ has dimension $d_i-d_j-1$. Its boundary consists exactly of the corners with labels $j<k<i$; the part of $\partial H_{ij}$ over $\partial M_j$ consists of the labels $k<j$. Thus \[ \partial H_{ij}= \bigcup_{k<j}p_{ij}^{-1}(H_{jk}) \ \cup\ \bigcup_{j<k<i}(H_{ij}\cap H_{ik}). \] In particular a fiber has empty boundary when $j$ is an immediate predecessor of $i$. For a chain $i>j_1>\cdots>j_r$ the total corner $H_{ij_1}\cap\cdots\cap H_{ij_r}$ has dimension $d_i-r$. The subscripts in the dimension formula refer to $i$, not to $j_1$.

statement_full_latex: A resolution datum as in A6.004 reconstructs the compact stratified space \[ X=\left(\coprod_{i\in I}M_i\right)\big/ \bigl(x\sim p_{ij}(x),\ x\in H_{ij}\bigr). \] Its strata are exactly the images of the interiors $M_i^\circ$. It has compatible conical control neighborhoods, with retraction $\pi_j$ and radius $\rho_j$ induced by the boundary fibration and its collar. Conversely, a compact finitely stratified space with such conical control data has a resolution datum, obtained by successively replacing cones on links by cylinders on the links, starting at the closed strata. These operations are mutually inverse when the collective faces, their common bases, and the collar data are retained. More precisely, the control data used in this statement include locally trivial charts $V\times C(L)$ over each stratum, compact links with the same structure recursively, and compatible radial trivializations on overlapping tubes. Transition maps preserve the cone rays and the radius, with the induced maps on links compatible recursively. This is the conical-atlas condition in Definition 1(v) of Albin--Leichtnam--Mazzeo--Piazza~\cite{ALMP2012}, \emph{The signature package on Witt spaces}, pp.249--250. No Witt condition or orientability is needed in this topological statement. The finite family formulation permits nonpure dimensions and codimension-one strata. The same constructions work in the PL category, and for finite definable conical control atlases and compatible definable collars in a fixed o-minimal expansion of a real closed field. In that version compact means definably compact and the quotients carry their definable-space topology. All chart and transition maps in the construction stay in the given structure.

statement_full_latex: For a compact surface $M$, the ordinary fundamental-groupoid functor \[ \Pi_1(\partial M)\longrightarrow\Pi_1(M), \] with its decomposition into connected components, determines the unmarked homeomorphism type of every component of $M$, including orientability, genus and number of boundary circles. For a connected component with nonempty boundary, let $b$ be the number of boundary circles and let $r$ be the rank of the abelianization of its fundamental group. It is orientable precisely when \[ \ker\bigl(\mathbb Z^b=H_1(\partial M;\mathbb Z) \longrightarrow H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\bigr)\ne0. \] In the orientable case its genus is $(r-b+1)/2$; in the nonorientable case its crosscap number is $r-b+1$. For a closed component, $H_1=\mathbb Z^{2g}$ determines the orientable genus $g$, whereas $H_1=\mathbb Z^{h-1}\oplus\mathbb Z/2$ determines the nonorientable crosscap number $h$. Thus the sphere and the projective plane are also distinguished. This is the precise useful surface interpretation of the ``1-special'' and ``2-special'' ordinary groupoids on 121/043. It does not assert that the manuscript defines those words: the page contains a sketch and no definition of ``admissible functor''. Corner flags and their attaching maps must still be kept when several surface pieces are glued.

statement_full_latex: An ordinary fundamental groupoid, up to equivalence, determines exactly the homotopy $1$-type: connected components and their fundamental groups. A diagram of ordinary groupoids retains the corresponding diagram of $1$-types, including its specified functors and natural transformations. It cannot in general recover higher homotopy within any piece, nor the homeomorphism type of a stratified space. This remains false for compact one-stratum smooth semialgebraic manifolds of fixed dimension: $S^4$ and $\mathbb{CP}^2$ have identical fundamental groupoids. In dimension two compactness and peripheral data are essential to A6.007. The once-punctured torus and the thrice-punctured sphere have equivalent fundamental groupoids and no manifold boundary, but are not homeomorphic. There is a precise positive homotopy statement. If a resolution diagram consists of aspherical pieces, all attaching maps and their coherence are retained, and its geometric realization is the homotopy colimit of the diagram, then the groupoid diagram determines that full homotopy type: take the homotopy colimit of the classifying spaces of the groupoids. Taking a colimit inside ordinary groupoids instead need not do so, even for a sphere with one marked point.

statement_full_latex: For compact finite PL resolution systems of dimension at most two, the following finite and groupoid data classify the blown-down stratified spaces up to a homeomorphism preserving the resolution labels: \begin{enumerate} \item the components of every resolved stratum, their dimensions, and the finite corner flags, including the cyclic incidence of arcs around each boundary circle and their common-base labels; \item for each compact surface component, its peripheral functor $\Pi_1(\partial M)\to\Pi_1(M)$, with the boundary components identified with those in the flag datum; \item for each one-dimensional boundary fibration over a resolved one-dimensional stratum, its finite covering monodromy, with its endpoint maps to the flags. \end{enumerate} Isomorphisms of these data must preserve the coherent diagrams, including the boundary-loop maps in item 2. The one-dimensional pieces themselves are compact intervals or circles, with their finite endpoints; zero-dimensional pieces are finite sets. For a trivial covering over an interval the covering datum is just the set of sheets and the two endpoint maps. For a circle it is a finite set with a permutation, up to simultaneous conjugacy and, when the base orientation is reversed, inversion. Thus ordinary peripheral groupoids determine the compact surface pieces, and a complete flag/covering diagram supplies exactly the remaining boundary assembly in dimension two. A6.008 proves that one cannot discard the flag incidence and retain only aggregate attaching groupoids. This statement does not classify mapping spaces or replace the angular condition of A6.006.

statement_full_latex: Let $r$ be a locally connected local equivalence relation on $X$ for which $\mathcal M_r=\operatorname{Sh}(X,r)$ is a Grothendieck topos and the inclusion is the inverse image of $\pi_r:\operatorname{Sh}(X)\to\mathcal M_r$. For a connected $p:\operatorname{Sh}(X)\to\mathcal T$, there is an equivalence $\mathcal T\simeq\mathcal M_r$ over $\operatorname{Sh}(X)$ if and only if \[ \operatorname{EssIm}(p^*)=\operatorname{Sh}(X,r). \tag{A.7.1} \] This is the exact additional descent condition; connected fibres alone do not imply it. The following geometric condition suffices. Suppose $\mathcal T$ is an \emph{\'etendue}, $p$ is connected and locally connected, $r=\operatorname{Lker}(p)$, and there is an epimorphic \emph{\'etale} localic atlas $\operatorname{Sh}(A)\to\mathcal T$ whose pullback is $\operatorname{Sh}(B)\to\operatorname{Sh}(X)$, such that the resulting map of locales $b:B\to A$ is simply connected in the following explicit sense: $b^*$ is fully faithful, and any sheaf on $B$ locally isomorphic to pullbacks by $b^*$ is globally such a pullback. Then (A.7.1) holds. In particular $\mathcal M_r$ is an \emph{\'etendue} in this situation.

Then the quotient construction is an equivalence from this category to the $2$-category of such presentations after replacing its Hom groupoids by their isomorphism classes. These are explicitly \emph{sheaf-detected} morphisms; a theorem for a different notion of foliated map is not being asserted without a comparison. The relation decoration can be omitted in the subclass with $r=\operatorname{Lker}(p)$. On the relation side it suffices to require locally simply connected effective charts: each chart relation is the kernel pair of its quotient map. Then the local kernel of the canonical quotient is the original relation, by \cite[Remark 6.5]{KockMoerdijk1992}. Without effectivity one must not assert that equality merely from equality of the invariant-sheaf categories. The same recognition criterion and equivalence hold relative to a Grothendieck topos $\mathcal E$, for internal locales, internal local relations and relative topoi, with the foregoing descent and simple-connectivity hypotheses imposed internally and stably under base change. statement_full_latex: Choose a nonzero $k$-linear functional $\ell:L\longrightarrow k$ and write $U=\operatorname{Hom}^{\mathrm{cont}}_L(A,L)$, where $A$ is a left $L$-module by $s$. Give $U$ the left $A$-action $(a u)(b)=u(ba)$. Then \[ \operatorname{Hom}_A(M,U)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_L(M,L), \qquad \phi\longmapsto\bigl(m\longmapsto\phi(m)(1)\bigr), \qquad \operatorname{End}_A(U)\simeq A^{\mathrm{op}}. \] The last isomorphism uses $\ell$ when $L\ne k$. Evaluation and coevaluation are \[ \operatorname{ev}_M(m\otimes\phi)=\phi(m)(1),\qquad \operatorname{coev}_M(1)=\sum_i m_i\otimes\phi_i, \] where $(m_i), (\phi_i)$ are dual $L$-bases under the first isomorphism. Their two triangle identities always hold as linear maps, and therefore hold in the module category when the maps are $A$-linear. statement_full_latex: Let $P$ be a unital analyser and let $k$ be a specified unital subring of its constant ring. A compatible $k$-plethory structure is exactly the following additional data and conditions: a $k$--$k$ biring structure on the $k$-algebra $P$, with coaddition and comultiplication realizing the finite decompositions in 3a) and 3b), with $\beta(c)(F)=F\circ c$; and the requirement that the induced map $P\odot_k P\longrightarrow P$, $F\odot G\longmapsto F\circ G$, and $k[T]\longrightarrow P$, $T\longmapsto T$, are biring morphisms. Here a biring includes additive and multiplicative counits, additive coinverse, coassociativity, cocommutativity, codistributivity, and the scalar map $\beta:k\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(P,k)$. None of these coalgebra identities is encoded by unspecified existence of decompositions alone. There is a useful sufficient criterion with no choice of additional operations: if the constant ring is a field $k$, $P$ acts faithfully on $k$, and 1)--3) hold with the unitality convention of 153/006, then there is a unique compatible $k$-plethory structure.

statement_full_latex: Let $R\subset S$ be any unital commutative inclusion. Form the explicit coefficient ring $C=\bigcup_d(R:_S D_d(R))$ of B.064, and assume that $R\to C$ is flat and epic. Put $Q=C/R$ and define the $R$-module \[ E=\left\{\left(r\longmapsto\sum_{i=0}^d c_i r^i+R\right): d\ge0,\ c_i\in C\right\} \subset\operatorname{App}(R,Q). \tag{B80.1} \] Thus $E$ is specified by coefficient and value relations in $R\subset C$, without choosing tensor presentations of integer-valued polynomials. For $A=\Omega(R,S)$ there is a canonical exact sequence \[ \begin{gathered} 0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_2^R(E,E) \longrightarrow A\otimes_R A\\ \xrightarrow{\theta_2} C[X,Y] \xrightarrow{\partial}\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(E,E) \longrightarrow0. \end{gathered} \tag{B80.2} \] The map $\partial$ is given explicitly below, with all connecting maps fixed by the evaluation sequence. In particular the two tensors on 153/004 exist uniquely exactly when \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Tor}_2^R(E,E)=0,\\ \partial\!\left(\sum_{i,j\ge0}\binom{i+j}{i} a_{i+j}X^iY^j\right)=0,\\ \partial\!\left(\sum_{i\ge0}a_iX^iY^i\right)=0 \tag{B80.3} \end{gathered} \] for every finite vector $(a_i)$ in $C$ satisfying $\sum_i a_i r^i\in R$ for all $r\in R$; missing coefficients are zero. If only flatness of $C$ is initially assumed, epicness is an additional necessary condition, and epicness together with (B80.3) is sufficient. This is an exact obstruction calculation for the flat-coefficient scope, not a classification of arbitrary nonflat coefficient extensions.

statement_full_latex: Let $R\subset S$ be any unital inclusion of commutative rings. The following construction uses only ideals, coefficient functions and finite linear relations associated with this inclusion. It imposes no finiteness, reducedness, flatness or domain hypothesis. First form \[ \begin{gathered} C=\bigcup_{d\ge1}(R:_S D_d(R)),\qquad \mathcal F=C[X],\\ E=\operatorname{im}\left(\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varepsilon} \operatorname{App}(R,C/R)\right),\\ \varepsilon\left(\sum c_iX^i\right)(r)=\sum c_ir^i+R. \end{gathered} \tag{B82.1} \] The first arithmetic test is that every $c\in C$ have a finite matrix presentation \[ \begin{gathered} c=Y M Z,\qquad M\in\operatorname{Mat}_{n}(R),\\ Y\in C^{1\times n},\quad Z\in C^{n\times1},\quad YM\in R^{1\times n},\quad MZ\in R^{n\times1}. \end{gathered} \tag{B82.2} \] This test is equivalent to epicness of $R\to C$. If it fails, the requested tensors are not uniquely determined. When it holds, define the following finite-depth syzygy invariants. Set \[ \begin{aligned} U_q&=\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(\mathcal F,\mathcal F),\\ V_q&=\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(\mathcal F,E) \oplus\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(E,\mathcal F),\\ W_q&=\operatorname{Tor}_q^R(E,E),\qquad U_q\xrightarrow{a_q}V_q\xrightarrow{b_q}W_q, \end{aligned} \tag{B82.3} \] where \[ \begin{aligned} a_q&=(\operatorname{Tor}_q(1,\varepsilon), \operatorname{Tor}_q(\varepsilon,1)),\\ b_q&=\operatorname{Tor}_q(\varepsilon,1) -\operatorname{Tor}_q(1,\varepsilon). \end{aligned} \tag{B82.4} \] The two terms of $b_q$ act on the respective summands of $V_q$; thus $b_qa_q=0$. Put \[ Z_q=\ker a_q,\quad T_q=\operatorname{coker}b_q,\quad K_1=\ker b_1/\operatorname{im}a_1. \tag{B82.5} \] There are canonical maps, explicitly constructed in the proof, \[ \begin{gathered} \delta_0:C[X,Y]=Z_0\longrightarrow T_1, \qquad \delta_1:Z_1\longrightarrow T_2,\\ K_2=T_2/\operatorname{im}\delta_1. \end{gathered} \tag{B82.6} \] The two polynomial tensors on 153/004 exist uniquely if and only if (B82.2) holds and \[ \begin{gathered} K_1=K_2=0,\\ \delta_0\left(\sum_{i,j\ge0}\binom{i+j}{i} a_{i+j}X^iY^j\right)=0,\\ \delta_0\left(\sum_{i\ge0}a_iX^iY^i\right)=0 \tag{B82.7} \end{gathered} \] for every finite coefficient vector $(a_i)$ in $C$ satisfying $\sum_i a_ir^i\in R$ for every $r\in R$. Missing coefficients are zero. All quantities in this test are defined before forming any tensor power of $\Omega(R,S)$; in particular it is not a test that presupposes the image or kernel of that tensor map. Its free-module implementation below uses only finite coefficient relations in homological degrees at most three. The criterion does not assert a uniformly terminating algorithm for arbitrary presentations of infinite rings, and it does not replace the separate higher-coherence conditions for a plethory by a binary test.

statement_full_latex: Orient a compact smooth $2n$-manifold $M$ and its boundary $B$ by the outward-normal-first convention. Write $r:H^i(M)\to H^i(B)$ for restriction and $\delta:H^{2n-i-1}(B)\to H^{2n-i}(M,B)$ for the connecting map. With ordinary cohomology in the first slot of each duality pairing, \[ \langle b,\delta a\rangle_M =(-1)^i\langle rb,a\rangle_B. \tag{C.7.1} \] Thus the degree-$n$ arrows $\rho$ and $\rho'$ in scan 022 are transposes with sign $(-1)^n$. For the whole graded triangle the sign is $(-1)^i$, not one scalar independent of degree. Using the relative class in the first slot instead gives the sign-free identity $\langle\delta a,b\rangle_M=\langle a,rb\rangle_B$. For an isolated hypersurface Milnor page let $H=H_n(M;\mathbb Z)$, $Q=H_n(M,B;\mathbb Z)$, $v:Q\to H$ be homological variation for positive monodromy, and $\epsilon=(-1)^n$. The pairing $(q,x)$ between $Q$ and $H$ is the oriented intersection number. In the Seifert convention \[ L(x,y)=-\epsilon\,(v^{-1}y,x), \tag{C.7.2} \] the intersection pairing $I$ represented by the middle map $u$ satisfies \[ I=L+\epsilon L^{\mathsf t},\qquad L(x,Ty)=-\epsilon L(y,x). \tag{C.7.3} \] In column-vector bases dual for $(q,x)$, these are $V=-\epsilon L^{-1}$ and $T=-\epsilon L^{-1}L^{\mathsf t}$. statement_full_latex: Let $S$ be an excellent strictly henselian trait of residue characteristic $p$, let $f:X\to S$ be separated of finite type, and let $x$ be a geometric closed point of the special fibre. Suppose that near $x$ the generic fibre is smooth and pure of dimension $n$, and that $f$ is smooth on the special fibre away from $x$. Take $\Lambda=\mathbb Z/\ell^a$ with $\ell\ne p$, or a finite field of characteristic $\ell$. Let $I$ be inertia, $P_w$ its wild pro-$p$ subgroup, and $I_t=I/P_w$. On the strict localization at $x$ put \[ K=(R\Psi\Lambda)_x,\quad R=R\Gamma_{\{x\}}(X_s,R\Psi\Lambda),\quad L=R\Gamma(X_s\setminus\{x\},\Lambda). \] There is an $I$-equivariant triangle \[ R\xrightarrow{u}K\longrightarrow L^{\rm triv}\longrightarrow R[1], \qquad R\simeq D_\Lambda K(-n)[-2n]. \tag{C.8.1} \] Consequently $K_t=K^{P_w}$ has the triangle in the continuous derived category of $\Lambda[I_t]$-modules \[ D_\Lambda K_t(-n)[-2n]\xrightarrow{u_t}K_t \longrightarrow L^{\rm triv}\longrightarrow. \tag{C.8.2} \] For a chosen $\sigma\in I_t$, canonical nearby/vanishing-cycle variation gives $V_\sigma:K_t\to D_\Lambda K_t(-n)[-2n]$ with $u_tV_\sigma=\sigma-1$. This choice is geometric; it is not the unique abstract lift furnished by the triangle. If wild inertia acts trivially, $K_t=K$ and (C.8.2) is the requested tame version for the whole fibre. For a bounded perfect tame complex, continuous group duality gives \[ R\Gamma(I_t,D_\Lambda K_t) \simeq D_\Lambda R\Gamma(I_t,K_t)(-1)[-1]. \tag{C.8.3} \] Hence the left term after derived tame invariants in (C.8.2) is $D_\Lambda R\Gamma(I_t,K_t)(-n-1)[-2n-1]$. For trivial $L$ the right term is $L\oplus L(-1)[-1]$. The shifts and twists $(-n)$ and $(-n-1)$ are therefore forced, rather than interchangeable conventions.

statement_full_latex: Let $X$ be a projective Cohen--Macaulay $k$-scheme, pure of dimension $r$, let $\omega_X$ denote its dualizing sheaf, let $Y$ be closed, and let $\widehat X$ be the completion along $Y$. For every coherent $F$ and every integer $p$ there are natural identifications \[ H^p(X,F)^\vee\cong\operatorname{Ext}^{r-p}_X(F,\omega_X), \qquad H_Y^p(X,F)^\vee\cong \operatorname{Ext}^{r-p}_{\widehat X}(\widehat F,\widehat\omega_X). \tag{C.13.1} \] Here $(-)^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_k(-,k)$ is the full algebraic dual, and the formal Ext is hyper-Ext of coherent modules on the formal scheme. The dual of $H_Y^p(X,F)\to H^p(X,F)$ is the completion map on the right. Moreover \[ R\mathcal Hom_X(\omega_X,\omega_X)\simeq\mathcal O_X, \qquad R\mathcal Hom_{\widehat X}(\widehat\omega_X,\widehat\omega_X) \simeq\mathcal O_{\widehat X}. \tag{C.13.2} \]

statement_full_latex: Assume the hypotheses of C.013, choose a very ample $\mathcal O_X(1)$, and fix $0<m<r$. Put $d=r-m>0$ and $U=X\setminus Y$. The following seven conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $H^p(U,F)=0$ for every coherent $F$ on $U$ and every $p\geq m$. \item $H^p(U,\mathcal O_X(-N)|_U)=0$ for $p\geq m$, $N\gg0$. \item For every coherent $F$ on $X$, $H_Y^p(X,F)\to H^p(X,F)$ is bijective for $p>m$ and surjective for $p=m$. \item Condition (3) holds for $F=\mathcal O_X(-N)$, $N\gg0$. \item For every coherent $F$ on $X$, the completion map \[ \operatorname{Ext}^q_X(F,\omega_X)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Ext}^q_{\widehat X}(\widehat F,\widehat\omega_X) \] is bijective for $q<d$ and injective for $q=d$. \item For $N\gg0$, $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(N))\to H^0(\widehat X,\mathcal O_{\widehat X}(N))$ is bijective and $H^q(\widehat X,\mathcal O_{\widehat X}(N))=0$ for $0<q<d$. \item For every finite locally free $E$ on $X$, the completion map $H^q(X,E)\to H^q(\widehat X,\widehat E)$ is bijective for $q<d$ and injective for $q=d$. \end{enumerate} The same assertions include $Y=\varnothing$ and $Y=X$; no nonemptiness hypothesis has been suppressed. statement_full_latex: The seven-condition chain with one global dimension $r$ is false for a projective Cohen--Macaulay scheme of dimension $r$ unless pure dimension is required or the comparison thresholds are made componentwise. A counterexample to conditions (1) and (6) of C.014 being equivalent under the literal mixed-dimensional hypothesis is \[ X=\mathbb P_k^2\amalg\operatorname{Spec}k,\qquad Y=\mathbb P_k^2,\qquad r=2,\quad m=1. \tag{C.23.1} \] Here is the full corrected chain without a purity assumption. Let $X$ be projective and Cohen--Macaulay over $k$, let $Y\subset X$ be closed, let $\mathcal O_X(1)$ be very ample, and let $m>0$. Write the finite decomposition into open and closed subschemes \[ X=\coprod_sX_s,\quad \dim X_s=s\ \hbox{purely},\qquad Y_s=Y\cap X_s,\quad U_s=X_s\setminus Y_s,\quad d_s=s-m. \tag{C.23.2} \] Omit the empty $X_s$, and let $\omega_s$ be the dualizing sheaf of $X_s$. Write $\widehat X_s$ for its completion along $Y_s$. The following seven conditions are equivalent. Negative sheaf cohomology and negative Ext groups are understood to be zero. \begin{enumerate} \item $H^p(X\setminus Y,F)=0$ for every coherent $F$ on $X\setminus Y$ and every $p\ge m$. \item $H^p(X\setminus Y,\mathcal O_X(-N)|_{X\setminus Y})=0$ for every $p\ge m$ and all sufficiently large $N$. \item For every coherent $F$ on $X$, the natural map $H_Y^p(X,F)\to H^p(X,F)$ is bijective for $p>m$ and surjective for $p=m$. \item Condition (3) holds for $F=\mathcal O_X(-N)$ for all sufficiently large $N$. \item For every $s$ and every coherent $F_s$ on $X_s$, the completion map \[ \operatorname{Ext}_{X_s}^q(F_s,\omega_s)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Ext}_{\widehat X_s}^q(\widehat F_s,\widehat\omega_s) \] is bijective for $q<d_s$ and injective for $q=d_s$. \item For every $s>m$ and all sufficiently large $N$, the map \[ H^0(X_s,\mathcal O_{X_s}(N))\longrightarrow H^0(\widehat X_s,\mathcal O_{\widehat X_s}(N)) \] is bijective and $H^q(\widehat X_s,\mathcal O_{\widehat X_s}(N))=0$ for $0<q<d_s$. For $s=m$, the same map on $H^0$ is required only to be injective for all sufficiently large $N$. There is no condition for $s<m$. \item For every $s$ and every finite locally free $E_s$ on $X_s$, the map \[ H^q(X_s,E_s)\longrightarrow H^q(\widehat X_s,\widehat E_s) \] is bijective for $q<d_s$ and injective for $q=d_s$. \end{enumerate} Thus C.014 is exactly the special case $X=X_r$ and $0<m<r$. In the mixed-dimensional case the surjectivity clause of (4) is automatic for large $N$ if no component has dimension $m$; it cannot in general be deleted when such a component is present.

statement_full_latex: Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a complete noetherian local Cohen--Macaulay ring of dimension $r$, with canonical module $\omega_A$. Put $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $a=V(\mathfrak m)$, $U=X\setminus\{a\}$, and let $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$, $Y=V(I)$ and $Y'=Y\cap U$. Let $P$ be a bounded complex with finite cohomology modules on $X$ and put $Q=R\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,\omega_A)$. For the injective hull $E_A$ of the residue field, write $\mathbb D=R\operatorname{Hom}_A(-,E_A)$. Completion with a hat below is along $Y$, not along a newly chosen closed point. There are natural isomorphisms \begin{align} \mathbb D P&\simeq R\Gamma_a(X,Q)[r],& \mathbb D R\Gamma_a(X,P)&\simeq Q[r],\tag{C.21.1}\\ \mathbb D R\Gamma(U,P)&\simeq R\Gamma(U,Q)[r-1],\tag{C.21.2}\\ \mathbb D R\Gamma_Y(X,P)&\simeq R\Gamma_a(\widehat X,\widehat Q)[r],\tag{C.21.3}\\ \mathbb D R\Gamma_{Y'}(U,P)&\simeq R\Gamma(\widehat U,\widehat Q)[r-1].\tag{C.21.4} \end{align} They identify the dual of \[ R\Gamma_a(X,P)\longrightarrow R\Gamma_Y(X,P) \longrightarrow R\Gamma_{Y'}(U,P)\longrightarrow \tag{C.21.5} \] with the formal localization triangle, with its arrows reversed and the displayed shifts. In particular, for perfect $F$ and bounded coherent $G$, take $P=R\mathcal Hom(F,G)$ and $Q=R\mathcal Hom(G,F\otimes^L\omega_A)$. When $A$ is Gorenstein and a trivialization $\omega_A\simeq A$ is chosen, these are exactly the swapped-argument Ext groups drawn on scan 006, with $X'=U$ and subscript $a$ denoting support at the closed point. The $r-1$ is forced by localization. More generally, for closed $Y\subseteq Z\subseteq X$ containing $a$, the dual of the localization triangle $R\Gamma_Y P\to R\Gamma_Z P\to R\Gamma_{Z\setminus Y}(X\setminus Y,P)$ is the triangle determined by the restriction \[ R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Z,\widehat Q_Z) \longrightarrow R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Y,\widehat Q_Y). \tag{C.21.6} \] Precisely, the dual of the relative term is \[ \mathbb D R\Gamma_{Z\setminus Y}(X\setminus Y,P) \simeq \operatorname{Cone}\bigl( R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Z,\widehat Q_Z)\to R\Gamma_a(\widehat X_Y,\widehat Q_Y)\bigr)[r-1]. \] Iteration proves the same assertion for every successive difference of a finite closed filtration, including all endpoint connecting maps. This is the complete localization induction visible in the last two rows of the page.

statement_full_latex: For the seven conditions in C.014, the following attributions follow from the opened primary texts. They distinguish the ambient scheme from the closed subscheme and do not replace a source hypothesis by Cohen--Macaulayness without proof. \begin{enumerate} \item SGA~2, XII, 1.1--1.4, pp.~109--111, supplies projective Serre duality and the equivalence of eventual negative-twist vanishing with depth at closed points. It is not the full complement/formal-completion equivalence for arbitrary $Y$. XII, Theorem~2.1, Corollary~2.2 and Lemma~2.3, pp.~114--115 (original margins 143--144), give comparison for an ample effective section regular on the coherent sheaf, in a projective family, with the stated fibrewise depth and flatness hypotheses. Over a field, depth $>d$ at closed points gives isomorphisms below $d$ and a monomorphism at $d$. In particular, for a pure Cohen--Macaulay $r$-fold, an ample Cartier divisor, and a vector bundle, the bound is $d=r-1$. This is a sufficient geometric hypothesis, not a converse for an arbitrary closed $Y$. The proof and its precise scope are C.018 with $c=1$. \item Hartshorne, \emph{Ample subvarieties of algebraic varieties} (1970), III, Theorem~3.4(b), p.~96, with proof on pp.~97--98, contains both directions of C.014(1)$\Longleftrightarrow$(7) when $X$ is a complete nonsingular variety. If $\dim X=r$ and the cohomological dimension bound is $\operatorname{cd}U\leq a$, its comparison is an isomorphism for $q<r-a-1$ and injective for $q=r-a-1$. Put $a=m-1$ to obtain exactly $q<r-m$ and the boundary injection in C.014. III, Proposition~3.1, p.~92, supplies the negative-twist test in the smooth quasiprojective case; III, Theorem~3.3, pp.~94--96, supplies formal duality. These statements use a nonsingular ambient variety. C.011--C.014 give the argument for a projective Cohen--Macaulay ambient scheme whose canonical module need not be invertible. \item Hartshorne, \emph{Cohomology of non-complete algebraic varieties} (1971), Proposition~2.9, p.~261, assumes $X=\mathbb P^r_k$ and condition $(I_s^*)$: for $i<s$, $\bigoplus_{v\in\mathbb Z}H^i(\widehat X, \mathcal O_{\widehat X}(v))$ is a finite free graded $k[x_0,\ldots,x_r]$-module generated in degree zero. For an integer $d\leq s$, the proposition gives both directions between $\operatorname{cd}U<r-d$, vanishing in those degrees for the single untwisted sheaf $\omega_X$, and the isomorphisms $H^q(X,\mathcal O_X)\to H^q(\widehat X, \mathcal O_{\widehat X})$ for $q<d$. It does not state an additional boundary injection. For the range $0<d<r$ considered here that injection for $\mathcal O_X$ is automatic, since $H^d(\mathbb P^r, \mathcal O)=0$; it is not a substitute for the vector-bundle boundary condition of C.014(7). Theorem~2.1, p.~259, proves $(I_s^*)$ when $Y$ is purely $s$-dimensional and smooth over a characteristic-zero field, or Cohen--Macaulay over a field of positive characteristic. Here Cohen--Macaulayness is a condition on $Y$, while the ambient scheme remains projective space. Proposition~2.2, p.~260, separately contains an injection at its boundary degree $s-\operatorname{hd}(F)$ for the comparison map constructed there. Proposition~1.1, p.~258, gives a different equivalent criterion for the next-to-top vanishing on a smooth projective ambient variety: the Lefschetz condition and intersection with every divisor. \item Speiser, \emph{Cohomological Dimension of Non-Complete Hypersurfaces}, Inventiones~21 (1973), \S2, Lemma, p.~147, gives both directions of the positive-twist test. In his notation, $V$ is a smooth projective $r$-dimensional variety over an algebraically closed field and $W$ is a nonempty connected closed subset. The bound $\operatorname{cd}(V\setminus W)\leq r-k$ is equivalent to the maps \[ H^q(V,\mathcal O_V(v))\longrightarrow H^q(\widehat V,\mathcal O_{\widehat V}(v)) \] being injective for $0\leq q\leq k-1$ and isomorphisms for $0\leq q\leq k-2$, for $v\gg0$. Put $k=r-m+1=d+1$: the boundary is exactly $q=d$, and Serre vanishing turns the remaining conditions into C.014(6). Thus the injection is printed explicitly in the lemma, even though it becomes automatic for sufficiently positive twists in positive degree. Theorem~C, pp.~147--148, gives the descent by one in the cohomological bound under a smooth hyperplane section, assuming $(I_k^*)$ with $k\geq2$; this is more specialized than the general equivalence in C.014. \end{enumerate} These attributions concern the sources actually opened. The exact clauses of Hartshorne (1968) and Ogus (1973) are the separate source-verification gate recorded in the unchecked file; neither paper is declared read on the strength of a later citation.

statement_full_latex: Let $S$ be a scheme over $\mathbb Q$. In the Lie-algebra version let $G/S$ be semisimple, with any isogeny type; in the group version let $G/S$ be reductive with simply connected derived subgroup. Let $D/S$ be its flag scheme and $T/S$ its torus determined by the based root datum, and let $W/S$ be the corresponding finite etale Weyl group. Put $(X,I')=(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak t)$ in the Lie-algebra version and $(X,I')=(G,T)$ in the group version, and set $I=I'/W$. There is a canonical adjoint quotient $f:X\to I$ and a diagram \[ \widetilde X\xrightarrow{p}X'=X\times_I I' \xrightarrow{q}X, \qquad \widetilde f:\widetilde X\to I', \] where $\widetilde X$ is the universal Borel Lie algebra or the universal Borel group over $D$, respectively. The maps $p$ and $q$ here have the indicated scheme-theoretic targets; $q$ is finite and $p$ is projective. The schemes $I$ and $I'$ are smooth over $S$, $f$ is flat with geometrically normal fibres, and $\widetilde f$ is smooth. The regular locus $X^{\rm reg}$ is the smooth locus of $f$. The map $p$ is an isomorphism over $X'^{\rm reg}$, and no larger open subset has this property. Fibrewise over $S$, the complements of the regular loci in $\widetilde X$ and $X'$ have codimension at least two and pure codimension three, respectively. If $S$ is normal and locally noetherian, then $X'$ is normal.

statement_full_latex: Use the group version of D.009 and assume that $S$ is connected, normal, and locally noetherian. Write $\xi$ for its generic point, $M=X^*(T)$ for the etale character-lattice sheaf, and $\pi:\mathcal B=\widetilde X\to D$ for the universal Borel group. Then pullback and the unit section give canonical decompositions \[ \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B) \simeq\operatorname{Pic}(D)\oplus H^1_{\rm et}(S,M), \qquad \operatorname{Pic}(T) \simeq\operatorname{Pic}(S)\oplus H^1_{\rm et}(S,M), \tag{D.10.1} \] and restriction and $p$ induce isomorphisms \[ \operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B) \simeq\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B^{\rm reg}) \simeq\operatorname{Pic}(G'^{\rm reg}). \tag{D.10.2} \] Pullback along $G'\to T$ is an isomorphism $\operatorname{Pic}(T)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(G')$. In particular the manuscript's sequences hold, and in this scope can be completed by zeros on the right: \[ \begin{split} 0&\to\operatorname{Pic}(D)\to\operatorname{Pic}(\mathcal B) \to H^1_{\rm et}(S,M)\to0,\\ 0&\to\operatorname{Pic}(S)\to\operatorname{Pic}(G') \to H^1_{\rm et}(S,M)\to0. \end{split} \tag{D.10.3} \] If $\Gamma$ is the finite monodromy group of $M$, then $H^1_{\rm et}(S,M)=H^1(\Gamma,M_{\bar\xi}) =H^1(\xi,M)$, a finite group. After etale sheafification this term vanishes, giving the relative Picard sheaf isomorphisms of 123/011. Finally \[ 0\to\operatorname{Pic}(S)\to\operatorname{Pic}(G) \to\operatorname{Pic}(G_\xi) \] is exact, and restriction $\operatorname{Pic}(G)\to\operatorname{Pic}(G^{\rm reg})$ is an isomorphism. The group $\operatorname{Pic}(G_\xi)$ is finite; it is zero when $G$ is semisimple simply connected, even for a nonsplit form.

statement_full_latex: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a simple complex Lie algebra, and let $\chi:\mathfrak g\longrightarrow\mathfrak t/W$ be its adjoint quotient. The following formulas determine $\operatorname{rank}(d\chi_e)$ for every nilpotent $e$. In the classical types let $\lambda=(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k)$ be its Jordan partition in the defining representation, and put $m=\lambda_1$. \[ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{type and condition}&\operatorname{rank}(d\chi_e)\\\hline A_r&m-1\\ B_r,\ C_r&\lfloor m/2\rfloor\\ D_r,\ k>2&\lfloor m/2\rfloor\\ D_r,\ \lambda=(2r-i,i),\ i\text{ odd}&(2r-i+1)/2\\ D_r,\ r\text{ even},\ \lambda=(r,r)&r/2. \end{array} \tag{D22.1} \] The orthogonal and symplectic partition parity conditions are understood; the two very-even $D_r$ orbits have the same rank. For the exceptional types, the following table lists every orbit whose rank is at least two. The rank is the number of displayed exponents. Every other nonzero nilpotent orbit has rank one; the zero orbit has rank zero. Complete weighted diagrams, representatives, and exact certificates for all $5+16+21+45+70=157$ orbits, including zero, are supplied in the accompanying machine-readable files.

For the typed quotient maps $\chi_{\mathfrak g}:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak t/W$ and $\chi_j:\mathfrak l_j\to\mathfrak t_j/W_j$, one has \[ \operatorname{rank}(d\chi_{\mathfrak g})_x =\dim Z(\mathfrak l)+ \sum_j\operatorname{rank}(d\chi_j)_{e_j}. \tag{D23.1} \] For a simply connected complex semisimple group $G$, the same formula determines the rank of $\chi_G:G\to T/W$ at every $g=su$: replace $\mathfrak l$ by $\operatorname{Lie}Z_G(s)$ and $e$ by $\log u$. statement_full_latex: Let $q:\widetilde G\to G=\widetilde G/Z$ be a central isogeny of complex semisimple groups, with $\widetilde G$ simply connected. Let $F_i=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_i)$ be its fundamental characters, $1\le i\le r$, and let $\omega_i|_Z$ be their central characters. For a lift $\widetilde g$ of $g$, set $b=(F_i(\widetilde g))$ and \[ \Gamma_b=\{z\in Z:\omega_i(z)F_i(\widetilde g) =F_i(\widetilde g)\text{ for all }i\}, \quad I_b=\{i:\omega_i|_{\Gamma_b}=1\}. \] For any basis $Y_1,\ldots,Y_{\dim G}$ of $\widetilde{\mathfrak g}=\operatorname{Lie}\widetilde G$, the exact rank at $g$ is \[ \operatorname{rank}(d\chi_G)_g =\operatorname{rank}\left( \operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho_i(\widetilde g) d\rho_i(Y_j)\bigr) \right)_{i\in I_b,\ 1\le j\le\dim G}. \tag{D24.1} \] This is a finite matrix formula for every element and every isogeny in every simple type. Fundamental representations and their central characters are determined by the root datum. If $\Gamma_b=1$ it reduces to D.023; in particular this holds for unipotent $g$.

statement_full_latex: Let $G=\mathrm{PGL}_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge3$, and let $Q=(T,B,T',B')$ be an ordered apposition quadruple. Its automorphism group is either $1$ or $C_2$. If $n$ is odd it is always trivial; in particular no inner-conjugacy class of quadruples is fixed by the outer involution. If $n=2k$ is even, put $m=n/2^{v_2(n)}$ and let $\omega(m)$ be the number of its distinct prime factors (with $\omega(1)=0$). Among the \[ C_n=\frac{(n!)^2}{n^2\varphi(n)} \] inner-conjugacy classes, precisely \[ F_n=\frac{(2^k k!)^2\,2^{\omega(m)}}{n\varphi(n)} \begin{cases}1,&4\mid n,\\[2pt]1/2,&n\equiv2\pmod4\end{cases} \tag{D25.1} \] have automorphism group $C_2$; the other $C_n-F_n$ have trivial automorphism group. The constructive test in the proof determines the stabilizer of each class, not only its aggregate number. For $A_3$ the two numbers are $8$ and $10$, out of $18$ classes. For $A_1$ the outer group is trivial and all stabilizers are trivial.

statement_full_latex: Let $S$ have six elements. A duad is a two-element subset, a syntheme a partition into three duads, and a total a partition of all fifteen duads into five synthemes. Let $S^*$ be the set of totals. Then $|S^*|=6$, the natural homomorphism $\mathfrak S(S)\longrightarrow\mathfrak S(S^*)$ is an outer isomorphism, and $S\longrightarrow S^{**}$ is a canonical bijection. The duality interchanges duads and synthemes, and gives a canonical bijection between the ten unordered $3+3$ partitions on either side. For each $s\in S$, $t\in S^*$ there is a unique $\operatorname{Stab}(s,t)$-equivariant bijection $S\setminus\{s\}\longrightarrow S^*\setminus\{t\}$. Here is an explicit completion of the undefined marginal term ``bihexagones'' on 119/155. A hexagon is a Hamiltonian cycle in $K_S$, and a bihexagon is a pair of edge-disjoint hexagons. The graph whose vertices are hexagons and whose edges are bihexagons has six connected components, each a Petersen graph. Its components are canonically $S^*$. Thus the duality can indeed be constructed from bihexagons. This supplies a precise construction; the one-word margin does not specify a unique historical definition of that word.

A biicosahedron with a distinguished edge $\varepsilon=\{a,b\}$ is exactly a square $Q$ on the other four vertices, together with an identification $\varepsilon\simeq\operatorname{rot}(Q)$. Choosing one of its two icosahedra is choosing one of the two diagonals of $Q$. An icosahedron with a distinguished face is exactly an ordered pair of three-element sets with a bijection between them. A biicosahedron with a distinguished biface is the corresponding unordered prism. The stabilizers are respectively $D_{10},\operatorname{AGL}_1(5)$, $D_8$, $\mathfrak S_3$, and $\mathfrak S_3\times C_2$.

statement_full_latex: For a square $Q$, write $D(Q)$ for its two diagonals, $C(Q)$ for its two opposite-side partitions, and $W(Q)$ for its two rotation directions. Then \[ W(Q)=D(Q)\wedge C(Q),\qquad\omega(Q)=C(Q) \] where the second $\omega$ is the sign orientation of the underlying four-element set. For a square on four of six points, let $\varepsilon$ be its complementary pair. Under E.003 its stabilizer preserves a unique square $Q^*$ and complementary pair $\varepsilon^*$ on $S^*$. Their torsors satisfy \[ D(Q^*)=C(Q),\quad C(Q^*)=D(Q),\quad W(Q^*)=W(Q),\quad \varepsilon\wedge\varepsilon^*\wedge W(Q)=1. \] Let $Q^\vee$ be the square of sides of $Q$. Define \[ \varepsilon\wedge Q^\vee = (\varepsilon\times Q^\vee)/((e,c)\sim(\bar e,\bar c)), \] where $\bar c$ is the opposite side. There are exactly two equivariant square isomorphisms $Q^*\simeq\varepsilon\wedge Q^\vee$, differing by the antipodal map. There is no equivariant isomorphism to the analogous twist of the original vertex square $Q$. Thus 119/157's displayed dual is essential. The formula on 156 is true if its notation $\varepsilon\wedge Q$ is defined to include this side dual. Reading its $\omega(Q)$ as the sign orientation of four vertices makes its first torsor equation false.

statement_full_latex: A set of nine points carrying twelve three-element blocks, any two \emph{distinct} blocks meeting in at most one point, is the affine plane $\mathbb F_3^2$, uniquely up to isomorphism. The quantifier must exclude equal blocks. Dually, partition a twelve-element set as $E=\coprod_{i=1}^4E_i$, with $|E_i|=3$. Conditions a) and c) on 159, namely four-element transversals and unique blocks through any pair from different classes, imply that there are nine blocks, that every point belongs to three, and that any two different blocks meet in exactly one point. They characterize the dual affine plane. Adjoining $\infty$ and the four blocks $E_i\cup\{\infty\}$ gives $\mathbb P^2(\mathbb F_3)$. Condition c) alone does not imply nine blocks, even if every block has four elements.

statement_full_latex: Let $V=\mathbb F_3^2$, let $E$ be its twelve lines, and let $I$ be its four directions. Then $\operatorname{Aut}(V,E)=\operatorname{AGL}_2(3)$ has order $432$, and \[ 1\longrightarrow V\rtimes\{\pm I\} \longrightarrow\operatorname{AGL}_2(3) \longrightarrow\mathfrak S_4\longrightarrow1 \] is nonsplit. The kernel is the equal-sign subgroup of $\mathfrak S_3\times\mathfrak S_3$ on any two chosen parallel classes. For each pairing $\alpha$ of the four directions, write $E=A_\alpha\amalg B_\alpha$ for the resulting two six-line sets. There is exactly one graph of an isomorphism $\mathfrak S(A_\alpha)\longrightarrow\mathfrak S(B_\alpha)$ that contains the translations and is normalized by the block-preserving part of $H_\alpha=\operatorname{Stab}_{\operatorname{AGL}_2(3)}(\alpha)$. It is the graph of an outer isomorphism; denote it by $G_\alpha$. The whole affine group permutes these three groups. Moreover \[ H_\alpha\simeq\mathrm{A}\Gamma\mathrm{L}_1(9),\quad |H_\alpha|=144,\quad |H_\alpha\cap G_\alpha|=72, \] and conjugation embeds $H_\alpha$ with index ten in $\operatorname{Aut}(G_\alpha)$, of order $1440$. The translations are a common Sylow $3$-subgroup, and \[ N_{G_\alpha}(V)/V\simeq D_8,\qquad N_{\operatorname{Aut}(G_\alpha)}(V)/V\simeq\operatorname{SD}_{16}. \] Thus ``order ten'' on 156 must be index ten; and the square-group normalizer assertion is true with $G_\alpha$, not with $\operatorname{Aut}(G_\alpha)$. Without the normalization condition there are nine translation-compatible outer graphs for each pairing, so an unqualified uniqueness assertion is false.

statement_full_latex: Consider an oriented disc $D$, a finite union $K$ of disjoint properly embedded arcs with distinct endpoints on $\partial D$, a nonempty $n$-element set $S\subset\partial D\setminus K$, and a root $s_0\in S$. Every component of $\partial D\setminus\partial K$ must contain at least one mark, and every such component outside the region containing $s_0$ must contain exactly one. These are the data and conditions on 003. Their isotopy groupoid is equivalent to the following explicit groupoid of word types: a rooted cyclically ordered $n$-set of marks, together with a partial pairing of its $n$ gaps, noncrossing, such that after cutting at the root no pair encloses an unpaired gap. Morphisms preserve the root, cyclic order, and pairing. Equivalently a type can be written as a linear word of $n$ positions with a specified cancellation matching: paired letters are the two occurrences of a private symbol with opposite exponents; every unpaired letter has its own private symbol; the pairing is noncrossing and encloses no unpaired letter. Renaming symbols and reversing the chosen name of a paired symbol changes no type. Unspecified equality patterns of ordinary free-group words are not the object classified by the page. Under the reading ``isotypique'' as a set of isomorphism types, take isomorphism classes of these same finite data. Under the reading ``isotopique'', retain their combinatorial isomorphisms, which are exactly the isotopy classes of homeomorphisms. If orientation is forgotten, allow order reversal; its possible reflection automorphisms must be retained for a groupoid equivalence. Neither reading identifies the raw groupoid of all homeomorphisms with a finite combinatorial groupoid.

statement_full_latex: A finite oriented combinatorial map without isolated vertices is a finite dart set $D$, a fixed-point-free involution $\alpha$ pairing its darts into edges, and a permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles are the cyclically ordered vertices. Its boundary permutation is $\tau=\sigma\alpha$; its faces are the cycles of $\tau$. Connectedness is transitivity of $\langle\sigma,\alpha\rangle$. Conversely these permutations reconstruct the oriented ribbon neighbourhood and, after capping its boundary components, the closed oriented surface, uniquely up to oriented homeomorphism. With one face, $|D|=2m$ and $c(\pi)$ denoting number of cycles, \[ g=\frac{m+1-c(\tau\alpha)}2. \] The following are equivalent: the graph is a tree; $g=0$; its boundary pairing is noncrossing. This is exactly the corrected content of 152/010--013. The point tree is an additional zero-dart object.

statement_full_latex: All the configurations above have explicit geometric realizations over their indicated fields. An $n$-cube with labelled coordinate directions is a product $\prod_{i\in I}P_i$ of two-element coordinate torsors; its dual cross-polytope has vertices $\coprod_iP_i$. Its orientation torsor is $\omega(I)\wedge\bigwedge_iP_i$, and its antipodal map has sign $(-1)^n$. For $n=3$, a cube is equivalently its four body diagonals and its orientation torsor, with automorphism group $\mathfrak S_4\times C_2$. The affine and projective planes in E.007 are realized over $\mathbb F_3$; they cannot be realized faithfully by nine distinct real points and straight lines with exactly the affine-plane incidences. The anharmonic ratios in 119/160 are the usual six transforms \[ \lambda,\quad1-\lambda,\quad\lambda^{-1},\quad (1-\lambda)^{-1},\quad\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda},\quad \frac{\lambda}{\lambda-1}. \] On $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_3)$ they all equal $-1$. statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-mag-equivalence} The following two structures are equivalent, by mutually inverse definitions on the same set \(M\). \begin{enumerate} \item Mag 1--4: \(\leq,\ll\) are partial orders, \(\leq\subseteq\ll\); every nonempty \(\{Z\leq Y:X\ll Z\}\) has a least element; \(\delta\) is symmetric, irreflexive and hereditary under the resulting \(\rho\); and \[ Y,Z\leq X,\ Y\ne Z\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y\delta Z. \tag{B.M4} \] \item The corrected strong Mag \(1'\)--\(4'\): \(\leq,\rho\) are partial orders; \(\delta\) is symmetric and irreflexive; there is at most one \(Z\) with \(X\rho Z\leq Y\); the exchange condition \[ X'\leq X\rho Y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists Y'\leq Y\ (X'\rho Y') \tag{B.E} \] holds; \(\delta\) is hereditary under \(\rho\); and (B.M4) holds. \end{enumerate} The inverse definition is \(X\ll Y\Longleftrightarrow\exists Z\ (X\rho Z\leq Y)\). For either structure define \[ X\bowtie Y\Longleftrightarrow \bigl(\forall A\in\widetilde X\setminus\widetilde Y, B\in\widetilde Y\setminus\widetilde X\bigr)\ A\delta B. \tag{B.MC} \] Every principal downset is a clique. The full family of clique downsets, or any atlas containing all principal downsets and closed under subfigures and finite compatible unions, is a prime atelier with At 1--7, C, D, D\(_0\), L3 and finite gluing. For the full family, arbitrary gluing, At 11 bis and At Fil also hold.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-gluing-not-L3} Take \(M=\{x,y,q\}\), incidence \(x<y\), refinement \(x\ll y,q\ll y\), and compatibility consisting of equality and the pair \(x,y\). The figures are \(0,\{x\},\{q\},\{x,y\}\). The lieux are \(x,q\), and \(U_y=\{q\}\). The prime core, L1, L2, CL(spac), At supp and D\(_0\) hold. No two nonempty figures are disjoint, so L2 and D\(_0\) have exactly their stated, mostly vacuous content. Every incidence cover of \(\{x,y\}\) contains \(\{x,y\}\) itself; the other nonzero figures are elementary singletons. Consequently all compatible local refinement data glue uniquely. This checks At 11, including arbitrary covers after deleting repetitions. For parents \(x\leq y\), the refinements \(x\ll x\) and \(q\ll y\) restrict respectively to \(x\) and \(0\) on their intersection. Those restrictions are disjoint, while \(x,q\) are not. Thus D and L3 fail, and so does C. The exhaustive code verifies every finite cover and all its refinement assignments. This also shows why CL(spac) alone must not be confused with the relative C axiom.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-fil} Let \(M=\{a_n,x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\), with discrete incidence, refinement generated by \(a_n\ll x_n\), and internal disjointness between exactly those pairs having different indices. This is a strong local magasin: the open-lieu set of either member of the \(n\)-th pair is \(\{a_n\}\). A full figure chooses at most one member of each pair. Restrict the atlas to those figures containing only finitely many \(a_n\), allowing arbitrarily many \(x_n\). It contains all principal figures and is closed under subfigures, bounded unions within the atlas and finite compatible unions. It therefore satisfies all the prime core, local and finite-gluing axioms proved above. Let \(F=\{x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) and \(G_k=\{a_0,\ldots,a_k\}\). These form an increasing family of refinements of \(F\); their restriction to each stratum \(x_n\) is eventually constant. Their union \(\{a_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) is omitted, and no admitted figure can bound it. Thus At Fil, At 11 bis and arbitrary gluing fail. For the last assertion use the disjoint cover of \(F\) by the singleton figures \(x_n\), with local refinements \(a_n\). This identifies the exact extra atlas closure needed by the otherwise valid gluing theorem.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-Sigma-gate} Assume the prime core and At 10. Let \(\Sigma\) be a replete class of posets containing all occurring principal deployments. Suppose At \(9_\Sigma\) states \[ X\bowtie Y\Longleftrightarrow \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (\forall p\in\ell(X)\setminus\ell(K), q\in\ell(Y)\setminus\ell(K))\ p\parallel q,\\ \widetilde K\in\Sigma, \end{array}\right. \qquad K=X\cap Y. \tag{B.Sigma} \] For compatible parents \(X,Y\), elementary refinements \(X'\ll X,Y'\ll Y\), and compatible restrictions to \(K=X\cap Y\), the exterior-lieu condition in (B.Sigma) for \(X',Y'\) is automatic. Consequently \[ X'\bowtie Y' \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \widetilde{X'\cap Y'}\in\Sigma. \tag{B.Gate} \] Thus At 12 follows exactly when these common-refinement deployments remain in \(\Sigma\). In particular it follows for unrestricted \(\Sigma\). For \(\Sigma\) equal to the empty poset and posets with a greatest element, it follows if elementary refinements restrict to empty or elementary figures on every elementary subfigure.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-Sigma-counter} Take the underlying set \(\{a,b,c,p\}\). We use seven elementary admissible families, with point objects denoted by their points: \[ \begin{array}{c|l} a,b,c,p & \{\{a\}\},\{\{b\}\},\{\{c\}\},\{\{p\}\}\\ k & \{\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b,c\}\}\\ x & \{\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b,c\},\{a,b,c,p\}\}\\ x' & \{\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b,p\}\}. \end{array} \] Incidence is closed-subfamily inclusion; refinement is ordinary set-figure refinement. Declare a pair compatible precisely when it is set-theoretically compatible and its common deployment is empty or elementary. The figures are all downward-closed cliques for this compatibility. The complete nontrivial data are \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} Z&\widetilde Z&\{W:W\ll Z\}&\{W:W\rho Z\}\\ \hline a&\{a\}&\{a\}&\{a\}\\ b&\{b\}&\{b\}&\{b\}\\ c&\{c\}&\{c\}&\{c\}\\ p&\{p\}&\{p\}&\{p\}\\ k&\{a,b,k\}&\{a,b,c,k\}&\{c,k\}\\ x&\{a,b,k,x\}&\{a,b,c,p,k,x,x'\}&\{p,x,x'\}\\ x'&\{a,b,x'\}&\{a,b,p,x'\}&\{p,x'\}. \end{array} \] The incompatible distinct pairs are exactly \[ (c,k),(c,x),(p,x),(p,x'),(k,x'),(x,x'). \] There are 21 figures: the sixteen subsets of the four point objects, and \[ \{a,b,k\},\quad\{a,b,k,p\},\quad\{a,b,k,x\},\quad \{a,b,x'\},\quad\{a,b,c,x'\}. \] Take \(\Sigma\) to be the class consisting of the empty poset and all posets having a greatest element. Every principal deployment is a figure. The table gives two partial orders, unique carriers for every stratum refining every figure, coincidence of incidence and refinement on compatible objects, and transitive internal refinement. Thus the prime At 1--7 hold. The lieux are exactly \(a,b,c,p\), and the open lieu sets of \(k,x,x'\) are respectively \(\{c\},\{p\},\{p\}\); hence At 8. Distinct points are disjoint, and ordinary support disjointness is exactly figure disjointness, giving At 9. Compatible distinct objects have disjoint open lieu sets, giving At 10. The explicit compatibility definition is exactly (B.Sigma), so At \(9_\Sigma\) holds. These assertions, including all figure carriers, are exhaustively checked in \texttt{finite\_axioms.py}. Now use compatible parents \(k\leq x\), with refinements \(k\ll k\) and \(x'\ll x\). Their restrictions to \(K=k\) are \(k\) and \(\{a,b\}\), which are compatible. But \(k,x'\) are incompatible: their common deployment \(\{a,b\}\) has two incomparable maximal elements and is not in \(\Sigma\). This refutes the proposed implication. The same program verifies D and the matching-overlap criterion for \emph{every} compatible figure-parent pair and every refining figure pair. Therefore At 11 also holds, by finite gluing. Adding At 11 and At D does not repair the implication.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-extension-unique} Let \(M=\{a,x\}\), let incidence be equality, let refinement have \(a\ll x\), and let internal disjointness be empty. The full figures are \(0,a,x\); two nonempty figures are compatible only when equal, and no nonempty figures are disjoint. Mag 1--4 hold: every principal deployment is a singleton, carriers are unique, and all orthogonality clauses are vacuous. The sole lieu is \(a\), and \(U_a=U_x=\{a\}\). Thus Mog L2, the local axioms, the prime core, C, D, all gluing and At supp hold. Every nonempty refinement has the same cosupport, so \(a\preceq x\). Take \(F=x\), \(G=G'=0\). Both choices \(F'=x\) and \(F'=a\) are subdivisions. Their deployment maps are isomorphisms of one-point posets, their restrictions over \(G\) are empty, and the deployment squares are cartesian. The complementary deployment map is an isomorphism. The mixed incidence condition is vacuous. Hence both satisfy At 14 bis, but they are different figures. Their boundaries are both empty, so At 14 ter's uniqueness also fails. This model satisfies At 14 bis \emph{existence for every possible diagram}: the finite certificate enumerates all six extension diagrams and all twelve gluing assignments.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-deployment-unique} Fix posets \(\widetilde G\subseteq\widetilde F\), with \(\widetilde G\) a downset, and a monotone map \(r:\widetilde G'\to\widetilde G\). A deployment square with inverse image \(\widetilde G'\), an isomorphism over \(\widetilde F\setminus\widetilde G\), and the intended mixed incidence rule is unique up to unique isomorphism over these data. Its poset is \[ E=\widetilde G'\amalg(\widetilde F\setminus\widetilde G), \] with the original orders on each piece, no exterior-to-interior relations, and \[ \xi\leq\eta\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r(\xi)\leq\eta \qquad(\xi\in\widetilde G',\ \eta\in\widetilde F\setminus\widetilde G). \] This is a uniqueness theorem for an abstract ordered deployment. An atelier can have several objects with this same deployment and carrier map, as Counterexample~\ref{SA21-B-extension-unique} shows. Requiring a coarsest extension is an additional property, not a consequence of the displayed deployment diagram.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-C-carriers} Let \(M=\{d,a,y,z\}\), with \(d<a,d<y,d<z\). Every pair is compatible except \(a,y\) and \(a,z\). The figures, written by their deployments, are \[ 0,\quad d,\quad da,\quad dy,\quad dz,\quad dyz. \] Primitive subdivision is equality together with \[ da\preceq dy,\qquad da\preceq dz,\qquad da\preceq dyz. \] This is a partial order. All nonempty figures contain \(d\), so no two are disjoint and C5 holds. C1--C3, including (B.P), are the explicit clique-downset construction. The incidence graph of \(M\) is connected, so C4 and C4 bis impose no additional condition. For \(da\preceq dy\) or \(da\preceq dz\), restriction sends the bottom, the subfigure \(d\), and the whole parent respectively to \(0,d,da\). For \(da\preceq dyz\), it sends \(0,d,dy,dz,dyz\) respectively to \(0,d,da,da,da\). These are the unique subfigures that subdivide the prescribed subfigure; they have exactly the strata refining it, and preserve all joins. Identity subdivisions restrict identically. This checks C6(a,b,c) completely. A subdivision \(da\preceq dy\leq dyz\) extends by \(da\preceq dyz\), and likewise for \(dz\); all other extension cases are identities. Hence C7\(_0\) holds, as does C8\(_0\). Nevertheless \(a\ll dyz\), and the strata refined by \(a\) in \(dyz\) are \(y,z\), with no least member. Thus the later At 5 fails. Final C8, the \emph{full gluing} axiom for subdivisions, is a different assertion and fails here: the subdivisions \(da\preceq dy\) and \(dz\preceq dz\) agree on \(d\) but cannot glue, because \(a,z\) are incompatible. The script \texttt{legacy\_subdivision.py} exhaustively checks all bounded joins, every C6 restriction and every C7\(_0\) extension.

statement_full_latex: \label{SA21-B-incidence-components} Let \(L\) be an arbitrary set. A multistrate in \(\operatorname{Fig}(L)\) is an elementary admissible family of subsets of \(L\), ordered by closed-subfamily incidence. If \(|L|\geq3\), the connected components of its comparability graph are exactly: \begin{enumerate} \item the isolated multistrate \(\{L\}\); \item for each \(p\in L\), the two-object component \[ \{L\setminus\{p\}\} \ <\ \{L\setminus\{p\},L\}; \] \item one component containing every remaining multistrate. \end{enumerate} The last component contains every point multistrate. For \(|L|=2\) there are just the isolated object and the two two-object components. For \(|L|=1\) there is one object and one component; for \(L=\varnothing\), there are no multistrates. Thus a finite \(n\)-point set has \(n+2\) components for \(n\geq3\), three for \(n=2\), one for \(n=1\), and none for \(n=0\).
