statement: The canonical cap-radius map is asserted to be a real-analytic diffeomorphism onto the open convex downward logarithmic domain defined by all strict weighted Strebel support inequalities, exactly the radii realizable by pairwise disjoint analytic pointed discs.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2b-image} The canonical cap radius map is a real-analytic diffeomorphism \[ (0,\infty)^I\longrightarrow\exp\mathcal L_Y, \qquad \mathcal L_Y= \left\{x\in\R^I:\ p\cdot x<K(p) \text{ for every }p\in[0,\infty)^I\setminus\{0\}\right\}. \] In particular its logarithmic image is open, convex, and downward closed. It is precisely the set of conformal-radius vectors realized by systems of pointed discs with pairwise disjoint analytic closures avoiding all the other marked points. The boundary support values are the weighted Strebel extrema \eqref{A2b-support}.

statement: For canonical squared lengths s and any disjoint comparison discs, the weighted logarithmic radius deficit is at most 2g−2+n, yielding 0≤K(s)−s·F(s)≤2g−2+n even with fixed cusp ends.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2-strebel-deficit} Put $c=2g-2+n>0$. For every $s\in(0,\infty)^I$ and every pairwise disjoint system of pointed conformal discs $E_i$ avoiding the other marked points, \[ \sum_{i\in I}s_i\bigl(\log r_i(E_i)-F_i(s)\bigr)\leq c. \] Consequently \[ 0\leq K(s)-s\cdot F(s)\leq c. \] The constants do not depend on the boundary lengths. Fixed cusp ends are allowed.

statement: When squared boundary lengths grow with limiting nonnegative direction p on a fixed marked curve, positive-weight caps converge to the corresponding Jenkins–Strebel discs and zero-weight radii vanish, so the limit depends on relative growth rather than being universally Koebe-shaped.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2-cap-limit} Fix $Y$ and its marked points as above. Let $s^{(m)}>0$ and $t_m\to\infty$ satisfy $s^{(m)}/t_m\to p\in[0,\infty)^I\setminus\{0\}$. For every $i$ with $p_i>0$, the pointed caps $D_i(s^{(m)})$ converge in the Carath\'eodory kernel sense to the Jenkins--Strebel disc $U_i(p)$ with circumference weights $2\pi\sqrt{p_i}$. Their normalized conformal maps converge locally uniformly, and \[ r_i(s^{(m)})\longrightarrow R_i(p). \] For $p_i=0$, the radii tend to zero. In particular the limit depends on the relative growth of the lengths and on $Y$; it is not universally a Koebe slit domain. No assertion of a fixed limit is made when the marked compactification itself is allowed to diverge.

statement: For a normalized pant, one dominant growing boundary has Koebe slit cap limit of radius 4, whereas three asymptotically equal growing lengths have the stated orange-slice cap limit of radius 4/(3√3).
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2-explicit-limits} Normalize a capped pant by placing its centres at $0,1,\infty$. If $L_0\to\infty$ and $L_1/L_0,L_\infty/L_0\to0$, then the cap at $0$ tends to $\C\setminus[1,\infty)$, its conformal radius tends to $4$, and its normalized conformal map tends to \[ k(u)=\frac{4u}{(1+u)^2},\qquad |u|<1. \] If instead $L_0/L_1,L_0/L_\infty\to1$ and the lengths tend to infinity, the cap at $0$ tends to \[ Q_0^\circ=\{|z|<1,\ \operatorname{Re}z<1/2\}, \qquad r(Q_0,0)=\frac4{3\sqrt3}. \] The other two limits follow by the permutations of $0,1,\infty$. This is the precise limiting sense in which the orange slices are valid.

statement: Canonical pant caps always satisfy r_0 r_1<1 although each individual radius has supremum 4, so the admissible radius set is not a product of independent intervals.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2-nonbox} For the pants normalization $0,1,\infty$, every genuine admissible cap system satisfies $r_0r_1<1$. Nevertheless the individual supremum of each of $r_0,r_1,r_\infty$ over such systems is $4$. The set of admissible radii is therefore not a Cartesian product of intervals.

statement: Removing arbitrary smooth collars gives the unique conformal hyperbolic metric solving Δu=exp(2u)−1 and ∂_n u=k_g with exact area and length formulas, and positivity follows from nonnegative boundary curvature but not from inward collar removal alone.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2-collar-general} Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected hyperbolic surface with geodesic boundary and $\chi(M)<0$. Let $M'\subset M$ be obtained by removing finitely many disjoint smooth open boundary collars, with $M'$ diffeomorphic to $M$. Write $k_g=g(\nabla_TT,n)$ on $\partial M'$, where $T$ is a unit tangent and $n$ is the outward unit normal. The unique conformally compatible hyperbolic metric with geodesic boundary is $g'=e^{2u}g$, where $u\in C^\infty(M')$ is the unique solution \[ \Delta_g u=e^{2u}-1,\qquad \partial_nu=k_g. \] Its area and boundary lengths are exactly \[ \int_{M'}e^{2u}\,dA_g=-2\pi\chi(M),\qquad L_{g'}(B)=\int_B e^u\,ds_g\quad(B\subset\partial M'). \] If $k_g\ge0$ everywhere and is positive somewhere, then $u>0$ everywhere. In general the sign of $u$ is not determined by the fact that a collar was removed.

statement: For collars of thickness εa_i(s), the first metric variation solves (Δ−2)h=0 with boundary derivative a_i−a_i'', and high-frequency positive analytic thickness on an equal-length pant makes the new conformal factor negative somewhere and positive elsewhere.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2-collar-shape} Let the boundary components of $(M,g)$ have arclength coordinates $s$, and choose smooth functions $a_i(s)>0$. In inward Fermi coordinates remove the collars $0\le r<\varepsilon a_i(s)$, for sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, and let $u_\varepsilon$ be as in Theorem~\ref{A2-collar-general}. After any smooth identification with $M$ which is the identity at $\varepsilon=0$, \[ u_\varepsilon=\varepsilon h+O(\varepsilon^2)\quad\hbox{in }C^2, \qquad (\Delta_g-2)h=0,\quad \partial_nh=a_i-a_i''. \] Here the prime is differentiation in boundary arclength. In particular, take the unique hyperbolic pant all of whose boundary lengths are $2\pi$. On one boundary set \[ a_1(s)=1+\tfrac12\cos(ns), \] and on the other two set $a_2=a_3=1$. For every sufficiently large integer $n$, and then every sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the resulting $u_\varepsilon$ takes a negative value at a point of the new first boundary. Thus even smooth analytic, everywhere inward collar removal need not increase the hyperbolic metric pointwise. The same metric takes a positive value somewhere.

statement: On the pant with all lengths 2π, collars with frequency 10^4 and thickness 10^−14[1+cos(10^4s)/2] on one boundary give u≤−(9991/20)10^−14 at s=π/10^4 while u is positive elsewhere.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A2-collar-explicit} Let $M$ be the hyperbolic pant with all three geodesic boundary lengths equal to $2\pi$. Label the boundaries $B_1,B_2,B_3$, and take an arclength coordinate $s\in\R/(2\pi\Z)$ on $B_1$, with origin at its shortest perpendicular to $B_2$. Set \[ n=10^4,\qquad \varepsilon=10^{-14},\qquad a_1(s)=1+\tfrac12\cos(ns),\qquad a_2=a_3=1. \] In inward Fermi coordinates remove the three collars $0\le r<\varepsilon a_i(s)$. They are disjoint, everywhere inward, and have analytic boundaries. On the retained pant let $g'=e^{2u}g$ be its conformally compatible hyperbolic metric with geodesic boundary. At the point of its first boundary with $s=\pi/n$ one has \[ u\le-\frac{9991}{20}\,10^{-14}<0. \] The same function $u$ is positive somewhere. Thus the general-shape counterexample of Proposition~\ref{A2-collar-shape} can be given with these fixed parameters, without an unspecified perturbation threshold.

statement: A nonconstant holomorphic germ fixing zero, real on the real axis and mapping the upper half-disc into the closed upper half-plane has positive derivative at zero and is therefore locally biholomorphic.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A3-boundary-chart} Let $f$ be a nonconstant holomorphic germ at zero with $f(0)=0$, real values on the real axis, and $\operatorname{Im} f(z)\geq0$ for $z$ in the upper half-disc. Then $f'(0)>0$. In particular the germ is locally biholomorphic, as required by Th\'eor\`eme 1 of cote 67/055--056.

statement: A continuous complex function holomorphic off a relatively closed rectifiable curve or locally finite union of rectifiable arcs extends holomorphically across it, without implying existence of welding for every interval homeomorphism.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A3-rectifiable} Let $U\subset\C$ be open and let $C$ be a relatively closed rectifiable curve in $U$, or locally a finite union of rectifiable arcs. Every continuous complex-valued function on $U$ which is holomorphic on $U\setminus C$ is holomorphic throughout $U$. In particular the continuous-function assertion of 67/061 is valid; this does not by itself assert existence of a welding for an arbitrary interval homeomorphism.

statement: Orientation-reversing quasisymmetric identifications of analytic boundary circles admit a unique conformal welding with quasiconformal seams, and any existing welding has the same uniqueness when its seam is conformally removable.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A3-welding} Let $X_1,X_2$ be bordered Riemann surfaces with analytic boundary, and identify selected boundary circles by orientation-reversing homeomorphisms that are quasisymmetric in analytic boundary coordinates. For finitely many such identifications, the topological quotient has a conformal structure for which the inclusions of the interiors are holomorphic and the seams are locally quasiconformal images of line segments. It is unique up to the unique conformal isomorphism restricting to the identity on every original piece. More generally, whenever a welding exists, the same uniqueness conclusion holds if its seam is conformally removable.

statement: Finite boundary-arc welding gives inverse cutting and welding equivalences when the quotient is an oriented surface and the vertex identifications admit uniformly quasiconformal sector charts, a condition satisfied by compatible smooth nondegenerate arc maps and finite positive angles.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A3-graph} Theorem \ref{A3-welding} extends to finite systems of orientation-reversing boundary-arc identifications, provided that the topological quotient is an oriented surface and the identifications are quasiconformal-compatible at the vertices: in a neighborhood of each vertex there is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism to a standard finite star of sectors which is quasiconformal on each incident open sector with one common finite bound. Cutting and welding are then inverse equivalences between these marked seam surfaces and their cut surfaces with pairing data. Smooth arc identifications with compatible nonzero derivatives and finite nonzero sector angles satisfy this condition.

statement: A disc cut along a Jordan slit has the stated prime-end uniformization without rectifiability, and suitably compatible quasisymmetric bank pairings produce a unique normalized quasislit welding, with removable slits giving uniqueness but not an automatic rectifiability conclusion.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A3-slit} Let $V$ be a Jordan domain and let $I$ be a Jordan arc joining $a\in V$ to $b\in\partial V$, with $I\setminus\{b\}\subset V$. No rectifiability is required for the conformal uniformization of the cut domain $V\setminus I$ by a disc. Its prime-end boundary consists of the outer boundary and two copies of the slit, with a single tip and two copies of its root. Specifying three positively cyclically ordered prime ends fixes the uniformizing map uniquely. For the converse in Lemma 4B and the Scholie of 67/072--073, take the three source points $1,\zeta,\bar\zeta$, $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/3}$, and the arcs $\beta=[1,\zeta]$, $\bar\beta=[1,\bar\zeta]$ in the source circle. Let $h:\beta\to\bar\beta$ identify the tip $1$ with itself and the two roots with each other. Assume the induced order-reversing involution on the combined arc $\beta\cup\bar\beta$ is quasisymmetric, with the endpoint compatibility of Proposition \ref{A3-graph}. Then there is a unique continuous map \[ f:\overline\D\to\overline\D \] which is conformal and injective on $\D$, has image $\D\setminus I$ there for a quasislit $I$ from $0$ to $1$, sends the source tip $1$ to $0$ and the source roots $\zeta,\bar\zeta$ to $1$, and realizes $h$ as its bank identification. Conversely, a quasiconformal image of the standard slit pair gives such pairing data. For an arbitrary slit whose welding exists, uniqueness holds whenever the slit is removable; one must not assert that every quasisymmetric welding produces a rectifiable slit.

statement: Geodesic cutting and canonical capping use analytic boundary diffeomorphisms whose welding exists uniquely without a separate rectifiability conjecture, and smooth diffeomorphisms suffice whereas merely differentiable homeomorphisms may not.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A3-L5} For the geodesic cutting and canonical capping operations of section 6, all boundary circle gluings are analytic diffeomorphisms. Their existence and uniqueness do not use a separate rectifiability conjecture. The same conclusion holds for smooth boundary diffeomorphisms, but mere differentiability of a homeomorphism without a nonvanishing derivative is not the same hypothesis.

statement: The cap at zero of the generalized pant with lengths (32,0,0) is not contained in the proposed orange-slice region, refuting that literal model when the other caps may degenerate to points.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A4-orange-extremal} Let $Q_0=\{|z|\leq1,\ \operatorname{Re}z\leq1/2\}$ in the sphere with centres $0,1,\infty$. The canonical cap $D_0$ for a generalized pant of boundary lengths $(32,0,0)$ is not contained in $Q_0$. In particular the literal model in the letter to Bers, which permits the other two caps to degenerate to points, is false.

statement: No three fixed pointed discs have independently concentric subdiscs describing every canonically capped pant, so the independent orange-slice model fails even apart from its spherical geometry.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A4-orange-jets} There are no three fixed pointed discs $Q_0,Q_1,Q_\infty$ whose independently concentric subdiscs describe all canonically capped pants. Thus the literal model in 67/019--020 is false, independently of its additional spherical description.

statement: For a negative-Euler marked surface with geodesic boundaries or cusps, capping together with all nonnegative lengths is an equivariant homeomorphism onto punctured Teichmüller space times [0,infinity)^n and is real-analytic on each boundary-type stratum.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A4-grafting} Let $S$ be a marked compact oriented surface of type $(g,n)$ with $n\geq1$ and negative Euler characteristic. Let $\mathcal T_B^{\geq0}(S)$ classify complete hyperbolic structures with each labelled end either a geodesic boundary of length $\ell_i>0$ or a cusp of length $\ell_i=0$, and with no nodes in the interior. Let $\mathcal T_{g,n}$ be its punctured Teichm\"uller space. Canonical capping gives a mapping-class-equivariant homeomorphism \[ \Phi=(\operatorname{cap},\ell):\mathcal T_B^{\geq0}(S) \longrightarrow\mathcal T_{g,n}\times[0,\infty)^n. \] Its restriction to each boundary-type stratum is a real-analytic diffeomorphism. In particular the positive-length part is a trivial principal $(\R_{>0})^n$-bundle over $\mathcal T_{g,n}$ by boundary lengths, not by all possible tangent radii.

statement: Multiplying labelled lengths defines an intrinsic equivariant [0,infinity)^n action on the capping bundle, with positive units acting freely on positive fibres and simultaneous scaling to zero giving a strong deformation retraction to the punctured locus.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A4-action} The multiplicative monoid $[0,\infty)^n$ acts continuously and intrinsically on $\mathcal T_B^{\geq0}(S)$ by \[ \lambda\cdot X=\Phi^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{cap}(X),(\lambda_i\ell_i(X))_i\bigr). \] It commutes with the mapping class action (and with a simultaneous permutation of end labels). On the positive-length part its group of units acts freely and transitively on each capping fibre. The zero vector gives the canonical capping retraction. The maps $X\mapsto\Phi^{-1}(\operatorname{cap}(X),(1-t)\ell(X))$ give a strong deformation retraction onto the punctured locus.

statement: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from 2, every faithful Klein-four action on P¹ is conjugate to {z,−z,1/z,−1/z}, with centralizer V_4 and normalizer S_4, giving inverse correspondences between Klein and S_4 subgroups.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A5-normalizer} Every faithful action of $V$ on $\mathbf P^1_k$ is conjugate to \[ V_0=\{z,\ -z,\ 1/z,\ -1/z\}. \] Its centralizer in $\operatorname{PGL}_2(k)$ is $V_0$, and its normalizer is isomorphic to $\mathfrak S_4$. The maps \[ V\longmapsto N(V),\qquad \Gamma\longmapsto \text{the unique normal Klein subgroup of }\Gamma \] are inverse bijections between Klein subgroups and subgroups isomorphic to $\mathfrak S_4$, in every characteristic different from $2$.

statement: The six fixed points {0,infinity,±1,±i} determine the Klein subgroup uniquely outside characteristics 2 and 5, while characteristic 5 has stabilizer order 120 and five such Klein subgroups, with the antipodal pairing restoring uniqueness.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A5-six-points} If $\operatorname{char}k\ne2,5$, a six-point set projectively equivalent to $S_0=\{0,\infty,\pm1,\pm i\}$ determines a unique Klein subgroup $V$ with $S(V)=S_0$, and its full projective stabilizer is $N(V)\simeq\mathfrak S_4$. In characteristic $5$, the same set is $\mathbf P^1(\mathbf F_5)$, its stabilizer has order $120$, and exactly five Klein subgroups have this fixed-point set. Retaining the antipodal pairing determined by $V$ restores the correspondence in characteristic $5$.

statement: A face of the oriented octahedron has stabilizer of order 3, whereas an unordered pair of opposite faces has an S_3 stabilizer complementary to V_4, so the claimed splitting belongs to the opposite-face pair.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A5-faces} A single face of the oriented octahedron has stabilizer of order $3$ in $N(V)$. An unordered pair of opposite faces has stabilizer $\mathfrak S_3$, complementary to $V$. Thus the splitting on 67/085 belongs to a pair of opposite faces.

statement: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from 2 with a chosen square root of −1, projective lines with an embedded four-element set are equivalent to the corresponding four-element sets plus a point away from the three pair-partition markings, including characteristics 3 and 5.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A5-groupoid} Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $\operatorname{char}k\ne2$, and fix a choice of $i^2=-1$. Let $\mathcal C_k$ be the groupoid whose objects are projective lines $X/k$ with an embedded four-element set $I$, and whose arrows are projective isomorphisms carrying the embedded set bijectively to the embedded set. For $I$, let $J(I)$ be its three partitions into two pairs and let $Z(J(I))$ be the projective line with those three labels as marked points. Then $\mathcal C_k$ is equivalent to the groupoid of pairs \[ (I,\zeta),\qquad \zeta\in Z(J(I))\setminus J(I), \] with arrows the bijections of $I$ whose induced maps of three-pointed lines carry $\zeta$ to $\zeta'$. The torsor-twist construction on 67/088--089 is an inverse. No exception at characteristic $3$ or $5$ is needed.

statement: Over Z[1/2,i], the unordered four-point moduli stack is [U/S_4] with the anharmonic S_3 action, coarse coordinate J=(λ²−λ+1)³/[λ²(λ−1)²] and generic inertia V_4, so the stack is not its affine-line coarse space.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A5-moduli} Set $R=\Z[1/2,i]$ and $U=\operatorname{Spec}R[\lambda,\lambda^{-1},(\lambda-1)^{-1}]$. The family version of Theorem~\ref{A5-groupoid} gives \[ \mathcal M_{0,[4],R}\simeq[U/\mathfrak S_4], \] where the action factors through $\mathfrak S_4/V\simeq\mathfrak S_3$ and the usual six anharmonic transformations of $\lambda$. Its coarse moduli space is $\mathbf A^1_R$, with coordinate \[ J=\frac{(\lambda^2-\lambda+1)^3}{\lambda^2(\lambda-1)^2}. \] In particular the groupoid theorem does not identify the unordered moduli stack with its coarse space: generic inertia is $V$.

statement: The ordinary arithmetic fundamental group of a stable marked curve does not recover a chosen nonzero normal tensor, already for a four-pointed rational example, and the ordinary geometric group also loses nodal inertia.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-ordinary-counterexample} The ordinary arithmetic fundamental group of a stable marked curve cannot reconstruct a chosen nonzero normal tensor, even for $(g,n)=(0,4)$ over $\Q$. Moreover its geometric version does not retain nodal inertia.

statement: For a field finitely generated over Q, the Kummer map K×→H¹(G_K,Zhat(1)) is injective and the Galois invariants of Zhat(1) vanish.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-kummer} For a field $K$ finitely generated over $\Q$, the Kummer map \[ K^\times\longrightarrow H^1(G_K,\widehat{\Z}(1)) \] is injective. Also $(\widehat{\Z}(1))^{G_K}=0$.

statement: A Galois-compatible outer isomorphism of the specified framed logarithmic groups is asserted to preserve the entire semi-graph of component anabelioids, including nodes, cusps and incidence.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-graphic} For the framed logarithmic realization above, every $G_K$-compatible outer isomorphism $\Delta_{Y,N}\simeq\Delta_{Y',N'}$ preserves the entire semi-graph of anabelioids: vertices, nodes, cusps, and incidence.

statement: After splitting the nodes and fixing normal-line bases, changing propagators from c_e to c'_e changes the arithmetic outer action by their Kummer-ratio cocycle, and graph- and component-trivial automorphisms are precisely the product of profinite Dehn twists, including self-nodes.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-normal-kummer} Fix a stable marked curve $Y/K$ as above. After a finite extension splitting its nodes and branches, choose bases for their normal lines. For two propagators $N=(c_e)$ and $N'=(c'_e)$, geometric transport identifies their admissible groups, and the difference of their arithmetic outer actions is the cocycle \[ \bigl(\kappa(c'_e/c_e)\bigr)_e \ \in Z^1\!\left(G_K,\prod_e\widehat{\Z}(1)\right). \] Changing that transport changes the cocycle by a coboundary. The group of graphic automorphisms that act identically on the underlying graph and on every component anabelioid is precisely the displayed product of profinite Dehn twist groups. This statement includes loops and self-nodes.

statement: For stable marked curves over fields finitely generated over Q, the specified framed logarithmic groups are asserted to recover the curves and their actual nonzero normal tensors through a bijection between geometric isomorphisms and Galois-compatible outer isomorphisms.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-anabelian} Let $K$ be finitely generated over $\Q$, and let $(Y,N)$ and $(Y',N')$ be geometrically connected stable marked curves with nonzero normal tensors as above. For the framed logarithmic fundamental groups, the natural map \[ \operatorname{Isom}_K\bigl((Y,N),(Y',N')\bigr) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}^{\mathrm{out}}_{G_K} \bigl(\Delta_{Y,N},\Delta_{Y',N'}\bigr) \] is bijective. Labels, if prescribed, must be preserved on both sides. In particular, the graph, component curves, marked points, and actual normal tensors are all recovered. The use of a framed logarithmic group is a hypothesis of this theorem and is the interpretation needed for the manuscript's normal propagator.

statement: Being procyclic with invariant conjugacy class and cyclotomic arithmetic action does not characterize node or cusp inertia because infinitely many subgroups satisfy it, while the stronger claimed reconstruction uses the arithmetic action on finite covers.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-procyclic} The condition of being isomorphic to $\widehat{\Z}$, with invariant conjugacy class and cyclotomic arithmetic action, does not put such subgroups in bijection with nodes and marked points. Even with all points rational, infinitely many subgroups satisfy it. The strongest reconstruction statement established here is instead the canonical recovery of the full finite graph and all its maximal node and cusp inertia groups in Lemma~\ref{A6-graphic}. It uses the arithmetic action on finite covers, not merely the proposed condition on an individual subgroup.

statement: For a smooth affine hyperbolic curve over a number field, a nontrivial geometric fundamental-group element lies in cusp inertia exactly when some closed subgroup projecting openly to Galois conjugates it by the cyclotomic character.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-cyclotomic-detection} Let $U/k$ be a smooth affine geometrically connected hyperbolic curve over a number field, with $\Pi=\pi_1(U)$ and geometric kernel $\Delta$. For $1\ne z\in\Delta$, the element $z$ belongs to a conjugate of a cusp inertia group if and only if there is a closed subgroup $N\subset\Pi$ whose image in $G_k$ is open and such that \[ nzn^{-1}=z^{\chi(n)}\qquad(n\in N). \] Here $\chi$ is the cyclotomic character pulled back from $G_k$.

statement: Hyperbolic geometric fundamental groups have infinitely many procyclic embedding classes, while simple loops admit peripheral, separating and nonseparating kinds whose mapping-class orbits are indexed by genus and puncture data rather than by only two or three conjugacy classes.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-three-classes} For every hyperbolic type $(g,n)$ in characteristic zero, there are infinitely many conjugacy classes of injective continuous homomorphisms $\widehat{\Z}(1)\to\Delta_{g,n}$. Thus the NB cannot literally assert that there are three such classes, or two when $n=0$. For geometric simple loops there is a meaningful three-way division into peripheral, separating essential, and nonseparating loops. This is a division into kinds, not three conjugacy classes. Under the mapping class group with unordered punctures, peripheral loops have one orbit when $n>0$, nonseparating loops one orbit when $g>0$, and separating loops have orbits indexed by unordered admissible pairs \[ \{(h,r),(g-h,n-r)\},\qquad 2h+r-1>0,\quad 2(g-h)+(n-r)-1>0. \] For labelled punctures their subsets must also be specified.

statement: The same open variety (P¹ minus {0,1,infinity})² has smooth proper normal-crossings compactifications with six and seven boundary components, so its augmented arithmetic fundamental group does not determine an arbitrary such compactification.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-blowup} Let $U=(\mathbf P^1_\Q\setminus\{0,1,\infty\})^2$. The same smooth variety, and hence the same augmented arithmetic fundamental group, admits two nonisomorphic smooth proper compactifications with strict normal-crossings boundary, containing respectively six and seven irreducible boundary components.

statement: Every smooth separated variety of finite type over a characteristic-zero field has a smooth proper compactification with reduced strict normal-crossings boundary and hence admits the stated tangential log compactification.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-SNC-existence} Every smooth separated finite-type variety over a characteristic-zero field has a smooth proper compactification with reduced strict normal-crossings boundary. Therefore every member of $\mathcal A$ has a tangential log compactification in the stated sense.

statement: For the stated proper log-regular fs model over k[[t]], finite étale covers of the generic interior equal Kummer-étale covers of the model and strict log special fibre, and the frame t defines the corresponding tangential Galois extension without replacing the log fibre by its ordinary singular curve.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-log-specialization} Let $k$ have characteristic zero, $R=k[[t]]$, $F=k((t))$, and let $S^{\log}$ be $\operatorname{Spec}R$ with the divisorial log structure of $t=0$. Let $\mathcal X^{\log}\to S^{\log}$ be a proper morphism of noetherian fs log schemes with $\mathcal X^{\log}$ log regular. Suppose its interior $U$ is contained in the generic fibre and is geometrically connected over $F$. Put \[ X_0^{\log}=\mathcal X^{\log}\times_{S^{\log}}s^{\log}, \] where $s^{\log}$ is the strict closed log point. Restriction gives equivalences \[ \operatorname{F\acute Et}(U) \simeq\operatorname{K\acute Et}(\mathcal X^{\log}) \simeq\operatorname{K\acute Et}(X_0^{\log}). \] Consequently there is an outer isomorphism \[ \pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(U)\simeq \pi_1^{\mathrm{k\acute et}}(X_0^{\log}) \quad\hbox{over}\quad G_F\simeq\pi_1^{\mathrm{k\acute et}}(s^{\log}). \] The frame $t$ gives a section $\sigma_t:G_k\to\pi_1^{\mathrm{k\acute et}}(s^{\log}) \simeq\widehat{\Z}(1)\rtimes G_k$. Pullback along that section defines a tangential specialization extension \[ 1\longrightarrow\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(U_{\overline{F}}) \longrightarrow \pi_1^{\mathrm{k\acute et}}(X_0^{\log}) \times_{\pi_1^{\mathrm{k\acute et}}(s^{\log})}G_k \longrightarrow G_k\longrightarrow1. \] In particular this applies to proper log-smooth saturated semistable pairs, with horizontal boundary included. It retains the logarithmic special fibre, rather than replacing it by the ordinary singular fibre.

statement: An isomorphism between interiors of smooth proper normal-crossings pairs with ample log canonical bundles extends uniquely to the pairs, so an isomorphism-anabelian interior class also recovers their boundary strata and tangential normal-torus data.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-canonical-compactification} Let $(X,D)$ and $(X',D')$ be smooth proper pairs over a characteristic-zero field $k$, with reduced strict normal-crossings boundaries. Suppose $L=\omega_X(D)$ and $L'=\omega_{X'}(D')$ are ample. Every isomorphism $U=X\setminus D\simeq X'\setminus D'=U'$ extends uniquely to an isomorphism of pairs. Consequently, on any isomorphism-anabelian class $\mathcal A$, the map \[ \operatorname{Isom}_k((X,D),(X',D')) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{G_k} \bigl(\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(U),\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(U')\bigr) /\operatorname{Inn}\bigl(\pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(U'_{\overline{k}})\bigr) \] is bijective for these compactifications. In particular their strata, normal-torus diagrams and the associated tangential fibre functors are recovered functorially.

statement: The displayed generators and relations present SL₂(Z) and GL₂(Z), with explicit involution matrices identifying the ordinary and extended once-punctured torus mapping-class groups.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-matrix-presentations} The presentations, with the involution relations made explicit, are \[ \operatorname{SL}_2(\Z) =\langle \sigma,\rho\mid \sigma^2=\rho^3,\ \rho^6=1\rangle, \] \[ \operatorname{GL}_2(\Z) =\langle r_1,r_2,r_3\mid r_1^2=r_2^2=r_3^2=1,\ (r_1r_2)^2=(r_2r_3)^3,\ (r_1r_2)^4=1\rangle. \] We may take \[ \sigma=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \rho=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad r_1=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\ r_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\ r_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. \] In particular these identify the ordinary and extended once-punctured torus groups.

statement: For the four-punctured sphere, the pure group is F_2≅Γ(2)/{±I}, the full group is V_4⋊PSL₂(Z), and the distinguished-point subgroup and full quotient by V_4 are PSL₂(Z), so the manuscript formula depends on which marking convention its superscript denotes.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-four-punctures} For the four-punctured sphere, \[ \operatorname{PMod}(S_{0,4})\simeq F_2 \simeq \Gamma(2)/\{\pm I\}, \qquad \operatorname{Mod}(S_{0,4}) \simeq V_4\rtimes\operatorname{PSL}_2(\Z). \] The subgroup fixing one specified puncture is $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\Z)$, and the quotient of the full group by its displayed normal $V_4$ is also $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\Z)$. Thus the formula with $+!$ is false if that symbol consistently means the pure group; it is correct if the second superscript means the distinguished-point subgroup. The exact diagram intended by the main part of 051 is \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccc} 1&\longrightarrow&F_2&\longrightarrow& \operatorname{Mod}(S_{0,4})&\longrightarrow&S_4&\longrightarrow&1\\ &&\Vert&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\ 1&\longrightarrow&\Gamma(2)/\{\pm I\}&\longrightarrow& \operatorname{PSL}_2(\Z)&\longrightarrow&S_3&\longrightarrow&1 . \end{array} \]

statement: The stated binary-dihedral quotient of SL₂(Z) has order 12 and free kernel F₂, descends to the four-puncture projective sequence, and differs from ordinary reduction modulo 2.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-binary-S3} There is an exact sequence \[ 1\longrightarrow F_2\longrightarrow\operatorname{SL}_2(\Z) \longrightarrow\widetilde{S}_3\longrightarrow1, \] where $\widetilde{S}_3$ is the binary dihedral group of order $12$. It can be obtained as a quotient of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\Z/4\Z)$, as suggested by the partially erased formula on the sheet. The quotient by $\{\pm I\}$ gives the lower row of Proposition~\ref{A6-four-punctures}. This is not the ordinary reduction-modulo-$2$ sequence, whose kernel contains $-I$.

statement: The stabilizer B∞ of a primitive integral line identifies the SL₂(Z)-sets SL₂(Z)/B∞, P¹(Z), and P¹(Q), with a reduction map to P¹(F₂), as point sets rather than schemes.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-projective-line} With \[ B_\infty=\left\{\ \pm\begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix} :n\in\Z\right\}, \] there are bijections of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\Z)$-sets \[ \operatorname{SL}_2(\Z)/B_\infty \simeq\mathbf P^1(\Z)\simeq\mathbf P^1(\Q). \] Reduction gives the displayed surjection $\mathbf P^1(\Z)\to\mathbf P^1(\mathbf F_2)$. These are point sets; the quotient written on the sheet is not an identification with the entire scheme $\mathbf P^1_{\Z}$.

statement: For an oriented surface of negative Euler characteristic, forgetting an additional fixed marked point gives the Birman exact sequence with point-pushing kernel π₁, including pure, extended, and boundary-fixed versions.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-birman} Let $S=S_{g,n-1}$ be an oriented surface with $2g-2+(n-1)>0$, and let $p$ be an additional marked point. There are exact sequences \[ 1\longrightarrow\pi_1(S,p)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Mod}(S,p)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}(S) \longrightarrow1, \] and their pure and extended versions. Here the middle group fixes $p$; forgetting one point is not a map from a group that is allowed to interchange that point with all the others. The same form holds with boundary fixed pointwise. The positivity condition is essential.

statement: Pants and Lego moves present mapping-class groupoids, while closed extended mapping class groups admit finite involution presentations, without thereby identifying arithmetic automorphisms of the full Teichmüller tower.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-presentation-types} The three presentation mechanisms anticipated on 050 have rigorous realizations, with different conventions. The pants and Lego mechanisms give complete mapping-class \emph{groupoid} presentations by local moves and their relations. Closed extended mapping class groups of every genus $g\ge1$ admit finite presentations on orientation-reversing involutions; generation by three such involutions is known. These assertions do not by themselves identify an arithmetic automorphism group of the full Teichm\"uller tower.

statement: For a smooth geometrically connected variety in characteristic zero, all marked smooth proper SNC compactifications form a nonempty cofiltered category whose canonical pro-object is functorial in the interior and is reconstructed whenever the augmented arithmetic fundamental group is Isom-fully faithful.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-model-system} Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $U/k$ be smooth, geometrically connected, separated and of finite type. Define $\mathcal C_k(U)$ as follows. An object is a smooth proper integral $k$-scheme $X$, with a specified dense open immersion $j_X:U\hookrightarrow X$ whose reduced complement $D_X$ is a strict normal-crossings divisor. A morphism from $X$ to $Y$ is a $k$-morphism $f:X\to Y$ satisfying $f\circ j_X=j_Y$. Then: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)] \item $\mathcal C_k(U)$ is essentially small, nonempty and cofiltered. There is at most one morphism between any two objects. Every morphism is proper and satisfies $f^{-1}(j_Y(U))=j_X(U)$. \item Its inverse system, with its marked common interior, \[ \mathfrak C_k(U)=\bigl((X,D_X)\bigr)_{X\in\mathcal C_k(U)}, \qquad U\longrightarrow\mathfrak C_k(U), \] is independent, up to canonical pro-isomorphism, of the choice of a small skeleton. For any fixed model $X_0$, restricting to all models dominating $X_0$ gives the same pro-object. The same holds after fixing any finite collection of initial models. \item Every $k$-isomorphism $\varphi:U\to V$ extends uniquely to an isomorphism of these pro-systems with their marked interiors. Thus, on any class $\mathcal A$ for which the augmented arithmetic fundamental group is fully faithful on isomorphisms, that group reconstructs $\mathfrak C_k(U)$ functorially. The reconstructed object retains the schemes, boundaries and transition maps, not just the abstract indexing partially ordered set. \end{enumerate} Here an isomorphism of marked pro-systems includes the isomorphism of their interiors and commutes with the displayed maps from those interiors. The theorem makes no selection of one compactification.

statement: Regular proper SNC models over k[[t]] in characteristic zero form a cofiltered system whose finite Kummer-étale cover categories, including those of strict special log fibres, agree compatibly with finite étale covers of the common generic interior and its framed arithmetic specialization.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-model-specialization} Let $k$ have characteristic zero, put $R=k[[t]]$ and $F=k((t))$, and fix a smooth geometrically connected separated finite-type $F$-scheme $U$. Consider proper integral regular $R$-schemes $\mathcal X$ containing $U$ as a dense open, with reduced complement $D_{\mathcal X}$ a strict normal-crossings divisor. Give them their divisorial log structures, and give $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ the log structure of $t=0$. Their morphisms are $R$-morphisms restricting to $\operatorname{id}_U$. This category is nonempty and cofiltered. Every such model is flat over $R$, and it has a canonical morphism of log schemes to $S^{\log}$. For every model, write $\mathcal X_0^{\log}$ for its strict closed log fibre. The equivalences \[ \operatorname{F\acute Et}(U) \simeq\operatorname{K\acute Et}(\mathcal X^{\log}) \simeq\operatorname{K\acute Et}(\mathcal X_0^{\log}) \] are compatible with every transition map. In particular, if $f:\mathcal X'\to\mathcal X$ is one, then \[ f_0^*:\operatorname{K\acute Et}(\mathcal X_0^{\log}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{K\acute Et}(\mathcal X_0'{}^{\log}) \] is an equivalence. The comparisons between any two models are independent of common refinement, up to the unique natural isomorphism compatible with restriction to $U$. They preserve the maps to $G_F$ and, for the same chosen frame $t$, the tangential specialization extensions over $G_k$ of Theorem~\ref{A6-log-specialization}.

statement: Two regular proper SNC models over Q[[t]] can have nonisomorphic special-fibre schemes while their strict special log fibres have equivalent augmented and uniformly framed Kummer-étale cover data.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-special-fibre-counterexample} Over $R=\Q[[t]]$, there are two proper integral regular models of the same smooth geometrically connected generic open, both with strict normal-crossings reduced boundary, whose special fibres are not isomorphic. Nevertheless their strict special log fibres have equivalent finite Kummer-\'etale cover categories over $G_{\Q((t))}$ and the same tangential arithmetic extension over $G_\Q$ for the fixed frame $t$. Thus even these augmented and framed cover data do not reconstruct a chosen special-fibre scheme. This does not contradict reconstruction of the complete marked model system.

statement: For proper integral log-regular models over a complete mixed- or equal-characteristic DVR with characteristic-zero fraction field, the model-independent tame covers of the interior equal the Kummer-étale covers of each model and strict special log fibre, yielding a uniformizer-dependent extension over the residue Galois group.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-tame-specialization} Let $R$ be a complete noetherian discrete valuation ring, with fraction field $F$ of characteristic zero and residue field $k$ of characteristic $p\geq0$. Give $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ the divisorial log structure of its closed point. Let $U/F$ be a smooth geometrically connected separated finite-type variety. Suppose that $\mathcal X^{\log}\to S^{\log}$ is a proper morphism of noetherian fs log schemes, that $\mathcal X^{\log}$ is integral and log regular, and that its interior is identified with $U$. Write $\mathcal X_0^{\log}$ for its strict closed log fibre. Then restriction gives equivalences \[ \operatorname{Tame}_{\mathcal X}(U) \simeq\operatorname{K\acute Et}(\mathcal X^{\log}) \simeq\operatorname{K\acute Et}(\mathcal X_0^{\log}). \] They commute with pullback from $S^{\log}$. If $\mathcal Y^{\log}$ is any other model satisfying these same hypotheses for the same $U$ and $R$, then \[ \operatorname{Tame}_{\mathcal X}(U) =\operatorname{Tame}_{\mathcal Y}(U) \quad\text{as full subcategories of }\operatorname{F\acute Et}(U). \] Consequently the special-log-fibre cover categories are canonically equivalent through this common category. The comparisons are independent of a common refinement, whose existence is not assumed. They are unique up to the natural isomorphism normalized by their restriction to $U$. For an actual log morphism of models fixing $U$, its pullback is this equivalence. Let $G_F^t$ be the quotient of $G_F$ classifying finite extensions tame over $R$, and let $\Pi^t(U)$ be the fundamental group of the common tame-cover category. There is a natural surjection $\Pi^t(U)\to G_F^t$. A uniformizer $\varpi$ supplies a section \[ \sigma_{\varpi}:G_k\longrightarrow G_F^t, \qquad G_F^t\simeq\widehat{\Z}^{(p')}(1)\rtimes G_k, \] where all primes are retained when $p=0$. If $\Delta^t=\ker(\Pi^t(U)\to G_F^t)$, the resulting tangential extension \[ 1\longrightarrow\Delta^t\longrightarrow \Pi^t(U)\times_{G_F^t}G_k \longrightarrow G_k\longrightarrow1 \] is independent of the chosen model. For $p>0$ we do not identify $\Delta^t$ with the full geometric \'etale fundamental group, nor do we replace $G_F^t$ by $G_F$.

statement: There are nonisomorphic hyperbolic curves over F₁₆ with isomorphic fundamental groups augmented over its Galois group that both arise as good reductions of curves over Q(ζ₁₅), so characteristic-zero Isom-anabelian reconstruction does not specialize unchanged.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-frobenius-counterexample} The characteristic-zero Isom-anabelian property used in the compactification definition is not preserved unchanged under arithmetic specialization. There are two nonisomorphic hyperbolic curves over $k=\mathbf F_{16}$ whose augmented \'etale fundamental groups are isomorphic over $G_k$. Both are good reductions of hyperbolic curves over the number field $\Q(\zeta_{15})$.

statement: Replacing tame covers by all finite étale covers invalidates the log-specialization equivalence even for a smooth proper relative curve with SNC boundary and hyperbolic generic interior.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-wild-counterexample} The first equivalence of Theorem~\ref{A6-tame-specialization} is false with $\operatorname{F\acute Et}(U)$ in place of the tame subcategory, even for a smooth proper relative curve with strict normal-crossings boundary and hyperbolic generic interior.

statement: The Galois character on a stable node inertia group is the cyclotomic character multiplied by the branch-interchange sign, becoming cyclotomic over the branch-splitting field, whereas marked-point inertia has the ordinary cyclotomic character.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-node-character} Let $e$ be a geometric node of a stable curve in the framed logarithmic interpretation of Theorem~\ref{A6-anabelian}, over a characteristic-zero field $K$. On the subgroup of $G_K$ stabilizing $e$, let $\varepsilon_e$ be the character which is $1$ when the two branches are preserved and $-1$ when they are interchanged. The character on its node inertia group is \[ I_e\simeq\widehat{\Z}(1)\otimes\varepsilon_e, \qquad \gamma\longmapsto\chi_{\rm cyc}(\gamma)\varepsilon_e(\gamma). \] In particular the invariant-conjugacy-class condition does not by itself make the character cyclotomic. It becomes cyclotomic after passing to the branch-splitting field. Marked-point inertia has the ordinary cyclotomic character on its point stabilizer.

statement: Testing finite covers on every DVR trait over the base defines a functorial intrinsic tame Galois category with a surjection to the tame base Galois group, and it equals the model-defined tame category whenever a proper log-regular model exists.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A6-intrinsic-tame} Let $R$ be a complete noetherian discrete valuation ring, let $F=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ have characteristic zero, and let $U/F$ be nonempty, smooth, geometrically connected, separated and of finite type. A test trait is a discrete valuation ring $A$, not a field, with an $R$-algebra structure, together with an $R$-morphism \[ f_A:\eta_A=\operatorname{Spec}\operatorname{Frac}(A)\longrightarrow U. \] The ring $A$ need not be excellent, henselian, or of finite type over $R$; the structure map need not be local. In particular, tests for which a uniformizer of $R$ becomes a unit in $A$ are included. Give $T_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$ the divisorial log structure of its closed point, denoted $T_A^{\log}$. Define $\operatorname{Tame}^{\rm tr}_R(U)$ to be the full subcategory of $\operatorname{F\acute Et}(U)$ consisting of covers $V\to U$ such that, for every test trait, $f_A^*V\to\eta_A$ is the generic fibre of a \emph{finite Kummer-\'etale cover} of $T_A^{\log}$. Then the following hold. \begin{enumerate} \item With the restriction of any geometric fibre functor on $U$, $\operatorname{Tame}^{\rm tr}_R(U)$ is a Galois category. It is closed in $\operatorname{F\acute Et}(U)$ under finite limits, finite sums, subobjects and quotients. Its fundamental group $\Pi^{\rm tr}_R(U)$ is a quotient of $\pi_1(U)$. \item Pullback along an $F$-morphism $U'\to U$ between such varieties preserves these categories. Pullback of tame covers of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ gives a natural surjection $\Pi^{\rm tr}_R(U)\twoheadrightarrow G_F^t$. \item Whenever a proper integral noetherian fs log-regular model $\mathcal X^{\log}\to(\operatorname{Spec}R)^{\log}$ with interior $U$ exists, one has equality of full subcategories \[ \operatorname{Tame}^{\rm tr}_R(U) =\operatorname{Tame}_{\mathcal X}(U) \subseteq\operatorname{F\acute Et}(U). \] Consequently the equivalence with finite Kummer-\'etale covers of the strict special log fibre in Theorem~\ref{A6-tame-specialization} realizes this intrinsic category. \end{enumerate}

statement: Modules with an involution and injective multiplication by 2 are equivalent to pairs of 2-torsion-free modules glued by a submodule of their reductions modulo 2 meeting each summand trivially, without commutativity or finite-generation assumptions on the coefficient ring.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A7-gluing-modules} Let $R$ be a ring, not necessarily commutative, and use left $R$-modules. The category of pairs $(M,\sigma)$ with $M$ an $R$-module, multiplication by $2$ injective on $M$, and $\sigma^2=1$, is equivalent to the category of triples $(P,Q,m)$, where $P,Q$ are $2$-torsion-free $R$-modules and \[ m\subset(P/2P)\oplus(Q/2Q),\qquad m\cap(P/2P)=m\cap(Q/2Q)=0. \] Morphisms of triples are pairs of module maps preserving $m$ after reduction modulo $2$. No Noetherian or finite-generation hypothesis is required. In the proof, localization at $2$ is valid because the integer $2$ is central; equivalently, $M[1/2]=M\otimes_{\Z}\Z[1/2]$.

statement: The displayed involution over Z[x,y,z]/(x²+yz−1) has noninvertible rank-one eigenspaces despite the ring being a 2-torsion-free domain, while Dedekind hypotheses or connectedness with 2 invertible give sufficient conditions for invertibility.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A7-domain-counterexample} The assertion following 67/091 that the two eigenspaces of a nontrivial involution on a rank-two projective module are invertible is false even over a $2$-torsion-free domain. Thus the supplied correction ``needs $\operatorname{Spec}R$ connected (e.g. a domain)'' is insufficient. A counterexample is \[ R=\Z[x,y,z]/(x^2+yz-1),\qquad M=R^2, \qquad \sigma=\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\z&-x\end{pmatrix}. \] The categorical statement in Proposition~\ref{A7-gluing-modules} remains valid. Its eigenspaces are invertible under either of the sufficient hypotheses: $R$ is a Dedekind domain and $M$ is finite projective of rank two; or $2$ is invertible in $R$, $\operatorname{Spec}R$ is connected, and $M$ is finite projective of rank two. In these two cases we require $\sigma\ne\pm1$.

statement: Over a PID with nonzero 2 and residue field κ=R/2R, nontrivial rank-two involutions have one split conjugacy class and nonsplit classes indexed by κ× modulo global units, giving two classes over Z and four over the indicated imaginary quadratic PID.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A7-PID-count} Suppose $R$ is a PID, $2\ne0$, and $\kappa=R/2R$ is a field. Conjugacy classes of involutions $\sigma\in\operatorname{GL}_2(R)$ with $\sigma\ne\pm1$ consist of one split class and a set of nonsplit classes canonically indexed by \[ \kappa^\times/\operatorname{im}(R^\times\to\kappa^\times). \] For $R=\Z$ there are two classes in total. For $R=\Z[(1+\sqrt{-11})/2]$ there are four classes in total, three of them nonsplit. The struck surjectivity proviso on 67/100 is therefore necessary for the assertion that there is just one nonsplit class.

statement: The rectangular and rhombic uniformizations Eₐ and E′ₐ classify pointed real elliptic curves with unique positive parameters, real automorphism groups {±1}, and exactly two real forms for every complex elliptic curve with real j-invariant.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A7-real-classification} For $a>0$ define real elliptic curves by their complex uniformizations and the indicated conjugation: \[ E_a:\quad \C/(\Z+i\sqrt a\,\Z),\qquad E'_a:\quad \C/\bigl(\Z+\tfrac{1+i\sqrt a}{2}\Z\bigr), \qquad \sigma[z]=[\bar{z}]. \] These two disjoint families, with the parameter $a$ unique in each, are the complete list of origin-marked real elliptic curves up to real isomorphism. Their real origin-preserving automorphism groups are $\{\pm1\}$. A fixed complex elliptic curve has real forms if and only if its usual modular invariant $j$ is real, and then has exactly two real isomorphism classes. Outside the square case they are either $\{E_a,E_{1/a}\}$ or $\{E'_a,E'_{1/a}\}$ with $a>1$. For the square lattice they are $\{E_1,E'_1\}$. For the hexagonal lattice they are $\{E'_3,E'_{1/3}\}$.

statement: The hexagonal quadratic-form ratio is 3, and the real elliptic families have the usual modular values j(i√a) and j((1+i√a)/2), invariant under a↦1/a and not proportional to log a.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A7-ratio-j} With $Q$ the quadratic form used on 67/093 and 099, the hexagonal ratio is $3$, not $\sqrt3$. The usual modular invariant is \[ j(E_a)=j(i\sqrt a),\qquad j(E'_a)=j\left(\frac{1+i\sqrt a}{2}\right), \] and is unchanged by $a\mapsto1/a$ in either family. It is not $c\log a$ for either tentative nonzero constant in 67/097.

statement: Rectangular real elliptic curves have two real components and H¹(R,E)=Z/2, rhombic curves have one component and vanishing H¹, and their real structures and the unique nontrivial rectangular torsor yield annulus, Möbius-band, and Klein-bottle quotients.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{A7-real-topology} The real locus and the first Galois cohomology group are \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} E & E(\R) & H^1(\R,E)\\\hline E_a & (\R/\Z)\times(\Z/2\Z) & \Z/2\Z\\ E'_a & \R/\Z & 0. \end{array} \] The quotients of the complex curves by their standard real structures are respectively an annulus and a M\"obius band. The unique nontrivial $E_a$-torsor has no real point; its antiholomorphic involution is $[z]\mapsto[\bar{z}+1/2]$, and its quotient is a Klein bottle. These torsors together with the two pointed families classify all smooth projective geometrically connected genus-one curves over $\R$.

statement: The source claims that rational codimension-two cycles on every smooth connected projective complex fourfold are numerically equivalent exactly when their rational Betti classes agree.

statement_full_latex: \label{thm:B1a-betti} Let $X$ be a smooth connected projective complex variety of dimension four. Two codimension-two cycles with rational coefficients on $X$ are numerically equivalent if and only if their rational Betti classes agree.

statement: Numerical triviality of a rational cycle on a smooth projective variety is preserved and reflected by arbitrary extension of the ground field.

statement_full_latex: \label{lem:B-basechange-num} Let $X/k$ be smooth projective, $K/k$ a field extension, and $z\in\mathrm{CH}^r(X)_{\Q}$. Then $z$ is numerically trivial if and only if $z_K$ is numerically trivial.

statement: The source claims that numerical and geometric ℓ-adic homological equivalence coincide for rational codimension-two cycles on every smooth projective fourfold in characteristic zero.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{thm:B1a-etale} Let $k$ be any field of characteristic zero, $X/k$ smooth projective of pure dimension four, and $\ell$ any prime. Numerical and geometric $\ell$-adic homological equivalence coincide for codimension-two cycles with rational coefficients on $X$.

statement: An algebraic Lefschetz decomposition with negative definiteness on hA¹prim and positive definiteness on homological primitive codimension-two classes forces numerical–homological equality, and the criterion follows conversely from that equality plus numerical positivity.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{prop:B1b-criterion} Fix a Weil cohomology on smooth projective varieties over a field $k$. Let $X/k$ be a smooth projective fourfold and $h$ an ample divisor class. Suppose that its algebraic classes in $H^4$ admit the orthogonal decomposition \[ A^2=\Q h^2\oplus hA^1_{\mathrm{prim}}\oplus A^2_{\mathrm{prim}}, \] that the intersection form is negative definite on $hA^1_{\mathrm{prim}}$ and positive definite on $A^2_{\mathrm{prim}}$. Positivity here is on the $\Q$-vector spaces of \emph{homological} algebraic classes, before dividing by numerical equivalence. Then numerical and homological equivalence coincide in codimension two. Conversely, if the decomposition exists, numerical primitive positivity together with numerical--homological equality implies this criterion.

statement_full_latex: \label{thm:B3-raynaud-flatness} Let $f:X\to S$ be quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and let $F$ be a quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module. statement_full_latex: \label{thm:B3-trace} Let $X$ be a proper scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field $k$, let $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$, and let $c=(c_1,c_2):C\to X\times_kX$ be a correspondence with $C$ proper. statement: The pliant cone of numerical codimension classes is full-dimensional, salient, nef, and functorial with ample complete intersections in its interior, and on smooth varieties it lies successively in the basepoint-free, universally pseudoeffective, and nef cones.

statement_full_latex: \label{thm:B3-positive-cones} Let $X$ be a projective variety over an algebraically closed field. Here $N^k(X)_\R$ is the dual of the numerical group $N_k(X)_\R$; on singular $X$ the cap map to $N_{\dim X-k}(X)_\R$ need not be an isomorphism.
