statement_full_latex: \label{B:Witt-localization-witness} Use standard $p$-typical Witt coordinates and write $[f]=(f,0,0,\ldots)$. For every commutative ring $A$, every $f\in A$, every $N\geq0$, and every $w=(w_i)_{i\geq0}\in W(A)$, one has \[ ([f]^Nw)_i=f^{Np^i}w_i. \tag{\(*\)} \] Consequently, for $A=\mathbb F_p[f]$, with $f$ an indeterminate, the canonical map \[ W(A)_{[f]}\longrightarrow W(A_f) \] is injective and is not surjective. An explicit element outside its image has coordinates $v_i=f^{-ip^i}$. The same conclusions and witness hold for the perfect domain $A=\mathbb F_p[f^{1/p^r}:r\geq0]$. In contrast, the vector with coordinates $w_i=f^{-i}$ does lie in $W(A)_{[f]}$. Thus this particular illustrative vector in \cite[Remark~18.3]{BBertapelleGonzalezAviles2022} must be replaced when using the standard-coordinate convention explicitly fixed in that source, Section~2.3, pp.~8--9. The localization inequality and the corrected Greenberg theorem remain valid.

statement: The specified perfect-field, perfect-scheme, and ind-rational sites support a derived Greenberg localization formalism with comparison under explicit acyclicity conditions, representing smooth commutative groups by proalgebraic Greenberg groups and finite flat groups by degree-zero finite étale and degree-one connected pro-unipotent cohomology.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{B:perfect-Greenberg-cohomology} Let $R$ be a complete discrete valuation ring with fraction field $K$, uniformizer $\pi$, and perfect residue field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$. Equal and mixed characteristic are both allowed. Fix a coefficient map $W(k)\to R$. For a finite product $L$ of perfect field extensions of $k$, put \[ R(L)=\varprojlim_n \bigl(W_n(L)\otimes_{W_n(k)}R/\mathfrak m_R^n\bigr), \qquad K(L)=R(L)[1/\pi]. \] For $R=k[[t]]$ with its specified coefficient field, these are $L[[t]]$ and $L((t))$. For $L$ a field, $R(L)$ is a complete discrete valuation ring with residue field $L$. Let $S_{\mathrm{pa}}$ be the étale site on finite products of perfect field extensions of $k$, $S_{\mathrm{pf}}$ the pro-fppf site on quasi-compact quasi-separated perfect $k$-schemes, and $S_{\mathrm{ir}}$ the pro-étale site on ind-rational $k$-algebras. Here rational algebras are finite products of perfections of finitely generated field extensions, and ind-rational algebras are filtered unions of rational subalgebras. In the pro-fppf site, coverings are finite jointly surjective families flat of profinite presentation in the perfect sense. The inclusions induce premorphisms \[ h:S_{\mathrm{pf}}\to S_{\mathrm{pa}},\qquad \widetilde h:S_{\mathrm{pf}}\to S_{\mathrm{ir}},\qquad \mathsf a=R\widetilde h_*Lh^*: D(S_{\mathrm{pa}},\mathbf{Ab})\to D(S_{\mathrm{ir}},\mathbf{Ab}). \] These premorphisms are not assumed to have exact inverse image on arbitrary sheaves of sets. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $\mathcal P'_{\mathrm{fc}}$ consist of commutative proalgebraic groups representable as extensions of perfections of abelian varieties by perfect affine groups, with finite étale component group. Restriction to $S_{\mathrm{pa}}$ is fully faithful on this category, and its derived counit is an isomorphism: \[ Lh^*(P|_{S_{\mathrm{pa}}})\simeq P \quad\text{in }D(S_{\mathrm{pf}},\mathbf{Ab}). \] \item The functors $R(-),K(-)$ induce premorphisms $\pi_R:R_{\mathrm{fppf}}\to S_{\mathrm{pa}}$ and $\pi_K:K_{\mathrm{fppf}}\to S_{\mathrm{pa}}$. Define \[ \mathcal R_R(F)=\mathsf aR\pi_{R,*}F,\qquad \mathcal R_K(F)=\mathsf aR\pi_{K,*}F,\qquad \mathcal R_x(F)= \operatorname{fib}\bigl(\mathcal R_R(F)\to\mathcal R_K(F|_K)\bigr). \] They give a functorial localization triangle. Call $Q\in D(S_{\mathrm{pa}},\mathbf{Ab})$ $h$-acyclic if its unit $Q\to Rh_*Lh^*Q$ is an isomorphism. If $R\pi_{R,*}F$ is $h$-acyclic, then \[ R\Gamma(L_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},\mathcal R_R(F)) \simeq R\Gamma(R(L)_{\mathrm{fppf}},F). \] The analogous assertion holds over $K$. If both unit conditions hold for $F$ and $F|_K$, the analogous comparison holds with support on the closed fibre. Under this unit hypothesis, if both $F$ and $\mathcal R_R(F)$ are bounded below, there is the spectral sequence \[ E_2^{ij}= H^i(L_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},\mathcal H^j\mathcal R_R(F)) \Longrightarrow H^{i+j}(R(L)_{\mathrm{fppf}},F). \] For algebraically closed $L$, this reduces to $\mathcal H^q\mathcal R_R(F)(L)=H^q(R(L)_{\mathrm{fppf}},F)$. \item If $G/R$ is a smooth commutative group scheme of finite type, write $G_n=G\times_RR/\mathfrak m_R^n$ and \[ \mathbf G=\varprojlim_n \bigl(\operatorname{Gr}_{R/\mathfrak m_R^n}(G_n)\bigr)^{\mathrm{perf}}. \] Then $\mathbf G\in\mathcal P'_{\mathrm{fc}}$ and \[ 0\longrightarrow U_G\longrightarrow\mathbf G \longrightarrow G_k^{\mathrm{perf}}\longrightarrow0 \] is exact, with $U_G$ connected pro-unipotent. Consequently $\pi_0(\mathbf G)=\pi_0(G_k)$, and $\mathcal R_R(G)\simeq\mathbf G[0]$. The unit condition in the preceding clause holds. \item If $N/R$ is finite flat and commutative, then $\mathcal H^0\mathcal R_R(N)$ is finite étale and agrees with $\mathcal H^0\mathcal R_K(N_K)$, $\mathcal H^1\mathcal R_R(N)$ is connected pro-unipotent, and $\mathcal H^q\mathcal R_R(N)=0$ for $q\geq2$. The object $R\pi_{R,*}N$ is $h$-acyclic. \end{enumerate}

statement: Finite exponential and logarithm biject nilpotent and unipotent elements in Q-algebras, and their pointwise versions biject locally nilpotent endomorphisms with locally unipotent module automorphisms compatibly with intertwiners.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:explog} For an associative unital $\mathbb Q$-algebra $R$, exponential and logarithm give inverse bijections between nilpotent elements $x\in R$ and unipotent elements $1+y\in R$, where $y$ is nilpotent. For a $K$-module $M$ they also give inverse bijections between locally nilpotent $u\in\operatorname{End}_K(M)$ and automorphisms $U\in\operatorname{Aut}_K(M)$ for which $U-1$ is locally nilpotent. The formulas are interpreted vector by vector in the latter case. They commute with every intertwining $K$-linear map.

statement: Exponential bijects nilpotent derivations with algebra automorphisms whose difference from the identity is nilpotent, preserving the nilpotency index, and the same correspondence holds locally nilpotently.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:unipotent} Exponential induces a bijection \[ \{D\in\operatorname{Der}_K(A):D\text{ is nilpotent}\} \longrightarrow \{U\in\operatorname{Aut}_{K\text{-alg}}(A):U-1\text{ is nilpotent}\}. \] It preserves the nilpotency index. The same statement holds with both occurrences of ``nilpotent'' replaced by ``locally nilpotent.''

statement: For an ideal I with Iq=0, exponential and logarithm terminating before degree q identify filtration-raising derivations with I-preserving automorphisms acting trivially on the associated graded algebra.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:filtered} Let $I\subset A$ satisfy $I^q=0$, with $q\geq1$, and put $I^0=A$. Define \begin{align*} \mathfrak g_I&=\{D\in\operatorname{Der}_K(A):D(I^k)\subset I^{k+1}\text{ for all }k\geq0\},\\ G_I&=\{U\in\operatorname{Aut}_{K\text{-alg}}(A):(U-1)(I^k)\subset I^{k+1}\text{ for all }k\geq0\}. \end{align*} Then $G_I$ is exactly the group of $K$-algebra automorphisms preserving $I$ and inducing the identity on $\operatorname{gr}_I(A)$, and \[ \exp:\mathfrak g_I\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }G_I, \qquad \log:G_I\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathfrak g_I \] are inverse bijections. Both defining series terminate before degree $q$. This supplies a valid replacement for the last corollary of cote~68, scan~046, using the deleted condition on scan~045.

statement: An algebra automorphism has differential order at most n exactly when its difference ideal has vanishing (n+1)st power, and among these differential automorphisms precisely the globally unipotent ones are exponentials of nilpotent derivations.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:differential} For $U\in\operatorname{Aut}_{K\text{-alg}}(A)$ put $J_U=(U(a)-a:a\in A)\subset A$. For every integer $n\geq0$, $U$ is a differential operator of order at most $n$ if and only if $J_U^{n+1}=0$. In particular the differential automorphisms are exactly the automorphisms inducing the identity modulo some nilpotent ideal. Among them, exactly those with $U-1$ globally nilpotent are exponentials of nilpotent derivations.

statement: For a nilpotent difference ideal J, an automorphism is a globally nilpotent exponential exactly when its induced conormal action on J/J² is uniformly unipotent, with the displayed explicit nilpotence exponent.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:conormal} Suppose $J=J_U$ and $J^q=0$. The ideal $J$ is $U$-stable, and the induced map $U_1$ on $J/J^2$ is linear over $B=A/J$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $U$ is the exponential of a globally nilpotent $K$-derivation; \item $U-1$ is globally nilpotent; \item $U_1-1$ is globally nilpotent on $J/J^2$. \end{enumerate} If $(U_1-1)^r=0$, then \[ (U-1)^{\,q+(r-1)q(q-1)/2}=0. \] Thus the other differential automorphisms are exactly those whose conormal action has no uniform unipotence exponent. This includes conormal actions that are locally unipotent with unbounded exponents.

statement: Automorphisms of a square-zero algebra B⊕M inducing the identity on B are uniquely pairs of a derivation B→M and a B-module automorphism of M, are differential of order at most one, and are nilpotent exponentials exactly when the module automorphism is uniformly unipotent.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:squarezero} Let $B$ be a commutative $K$-algebra, $M$ any $B$-module, and $A=B\oplus M$ with multiplication $(b,m)(c,n)=(bc,bn+cm)$. Every $K$-algebra automorphism of $A$ inducing the identity on $B=A/M$ is uniquely \[ U_{d,\sigma}(b,m)=(b,d(b)+\sigma(m)), \quad d\in\operatorname{Der}_K(B,M),\quad\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}_B(M). \] Composition is $(d,\sigma)(e,\tau)=(d+\sigma e,\sigma\tau)$. All these automorphisms have differential order at most one. They are exponentials of globally nilpotent derivations precisely when $\sigma-1$ is globally nilpotent.

statement: Scaling ε by 2 on dual numbers is differential but not a nilpotent exponential, and εd/dε on Q[ε]/(ε³) maps into a nilpotent ideal without being locally nilpotent, disproving the weaker unfiltered hypotheses.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:counterexamples} On $A=\mathbb Q[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$, the automorphism $U(\varepsilon)=2\varepsilon$ is differential of order one but is not an exponential of a nilpotent derivation; it acts as multiplication by $2$ on $J_U/J_U^2$. On $A'=\mathbb Q[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^3)$, the derivation $D=\varepsilon\,d/d\varepsilon$ has $D(A')\subset I=(\varepsilon)$ but is not locally nilpotent. Thus identity on $A/I$ does not imply identity on $\operatorname{gr}_I(A)$, and merely requiring $D(A)\subset I$ does not make the exponential finite. The correct replacements are Theorems~\ref{C:filtered}, \ref{C:differential}, and \ref{C:conormal}.

statement: A linear map intertwines exponentials of locally nilpotent operators at time one exactly when it intertwines the operators, equivalently every scalar extension and all formal additive-group parameters.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:intertwine} Let $M,N$ be arbitrary $K$-modules, $u\in\operatorname{End}_K(M)$ and $v\in\operatorname{End}_K(N)$ locally nilpotent, and $f\in\operatorname{Hom}_K(M,N)$. Then \[ f\exp(u)=\exp(v)f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad fu=vf. \] The equivalence also identifies intertwining at time $1$ with intertwining for every parameter over every commutative $K$-algebra, and with intertwining of the formal additive group actions.

statement: For tensor-product module functors, formal additive-group actions correspond to arbitrary endomorphisms and ordinary actions to locally nilpotent endomorphisms, while global nilpotence suffices exactly when every locally nilpotent operator is globally nilpotent.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:module-actions} For any $K$-module $M$, let $\mathcal M(R)=M\otimes_K R$ and $\widehat{\mathbb G}_a(R)=\operatorname{Nil}(R)$. Natural $R$-linear additive-group actions on $\mathcal M$ satisfy \begin{align*} \operatorname{End}_K(M)&\simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{grp}}(\widehat{\mathbb G}_a,\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal M)),\\ \operatorname{LNil}(\operatorname{End}_K(M))&\simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{grp}}(\mathbb G_a,\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal M)), \end{align*} by $u\mapsto[\lambda\mapsto\exp(\lambda u_R)]$. Here $\operatorname{LNil}$ means locally nilpotent endomorphisms. Restricting the second map to globally nilpotent endomorphisms is bijective exactly when every locally nilpotent endomorphism of $M$ is globally nilpotent. Finite generation of $M$ is sufficient, but is not necessary.

statement: For arbitrary module functors, formal exponential fibres are cosets of the displayed kernel and its image is governed separately by unipotence, scalar-linearity, and logarithm-extension obstructions, whereas ordinary exponentials are injective with image characterized by uniform nilpotence and linear logarithms.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:functor-criterion} For an arbitrary $\mathcal O$-module functor: \begin{enumerate} \item The map $u\mapsto\bar e_u$ from $E$ to formal additive-group actions has fibers exactly the additive cosets of $\ker\delta$. A formal action $\rho$ belongs to its image if and only if all three following tests hold: each $\rho_R(\lambda)$ is unipotent for nilpotent $\lambda$; its finite logarithm is $R$-linear in the parameter $\lambda\in\operatorname{Nil}(R)$; and the resulting morphism $\ell_\rho\in H$ has zero class in $\operatorname{coker}\delta$. In particular the formal exponential map is bijective if and only if $\ker\delta=0$ and these three tests hold for every formal action. \item The map from globally nilpotent elements of $E$ to ordinary additive-group actions is always injective. Its image consists exactly of those actions for which there is one integer $r$ with $(\rho_R(\lambda)-1)^r=0$ for all $R,\lambda$, and whose logarithms satisfy \[ \log\rho_R(a\lambda)=a\log\rho_R(\lambda) \quad(a,\lambda\in R). \] It is bijective exactly when every ordinary action passes these two tests. \end{enumerate} These criteria distinguish failure of uniqueness, failure of unipotence, failure of scalar linearity, and failure to divide the formal parameter. They apply without representability, exactness, or finiteness assumptions on $\mathcal M$.

statement: The reduced-ring module functor makes distinct endomorphisms have the same formal exponential, and the differential-form functor has a square-zero additive action involving dλ that is neither an ordinary nor formal exponential of the required kind.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:functor-counterexamples} Both maps asked about on cote~68, scan~044, fail to be bijective for general module functors. The manuscript poses a question here, not an assertion of bijectivity. \begin{enumerate} \item For $K=\mathbb Q$ and $\mathcal M(R)=R_{\mathrm{red}}$, the distinct endomorphisms $0,1\in E$ have the same formal exponential. \item For $K=\mathbb Q$ and $\mathcal M(R)=R\oplus\Omega_{R/\mathbb Q}$, the formula \[ \rho_R(\lambda)(a,\omega)=(a,\omega+a\,d\lambda) \] defines an ordinary additive-group action, with $(\rho_R(\lambda)-1)^2=0$ for every $R,\lambda$. Neither it nor its restriction to the formal additive group is an exponential of the required form. \end{enumerate}

statement: Compatibility of a module functor with all truncated polynomial extensions ensures formal exponential classification, while polynomial-extension compatibility classifies ordinary actions by naturally locally nilpotent endomorphisms, including the stated tensor, product, and internal-Hom examples.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:functor-basechange} Let $\mathcal M$ be an arbitrary $\mathcal O$-module functor over the commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra $K$. \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose that for every $K$-algebra $R$ and every $n\geq1$, the canonical map \[ \mathcal M(R)\otimes_R R[t]/(t^{n+1}) \longrightarrow\mathcal M(R[t]/(t^{n+1})) \] is an isomorphism. Then $u\mapsto\bar e_u$ is bijective. \item Suppose instead that for every $R$, the canonical map \[ \mathcal M(R)\otimes_R R[t]\longrightarrow\mathcal M(R[t]) \] is an isomorphism. Then ordinary additive-group actions correspond exactly to natural endomorphisms $u$ for which each $u_R$ is elementwise locally nilpotent. The map from the globally nilpotent elements of $E$ is therefore bijective exactly when all these natural locally nilpotent endomorphisms are globally nilpotent in $E$. \end{enumerate} The first hypothesis holds for \[ \mathcal M(R)=\operatorname{Hom}_R(P\otimes_KR,Q\otimes_KR) \] with arbitrary $K$-modules $P,Q$, without finite generation or projectivity, and for arbitrary product functors $\mathcal M(R)=\prod_{j\in J}R$. Both hypotheses hold for every tensor-product functor $M\otimes_KR$. For the internal Hom functor the second hypothesis also holds when $P$ is finitely generated.

statement: The formal exponential tests are independently necessary: natural actions can fail local unipotence at square-zero scalars or can have a uniformly unipotent scalar-linear logarithm that does not extend across the required parameter-division map.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:functor-separate-obstructions} The distinct tests in Theorem~\ref{C:functor-criterion} cannot in general be omitted. \begin{enumerate} \item There is a natural formal additive-group action whose value at a square-zero scalar is not even locally unipotent. \item There is a natural formal action which is uniformly unipotent of exponent two and whose logarithm is $R$-linear in its nilpotent scalar parameter, but which is not a formal exponential because its logarithm has nonzero class in $\operatorname{coker}\delta$. \end{enumerate}

statement: A sheaf derivation over Q that is uniformly nilpotent on neighborhoods exponentiates to a scheme automorphism fixing the reduction, with commuting derivations exponentiating by composition, while elementwise nilpotence on a single affine ring is insufficient for this conclusion.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:sheaf-globalization} Let $X$ be a scheme over $\mathbb Q$, and let $D$ be a derivation of the sheaf $\mathcal O_X$. Suppose each point has an open neighborhood $V$ and an integer $r$ such that $D^r=0$ as an endomorphism of $\mathcal O_X|_V$. The local finite exponentials glue to an automorphism $E_D$ of $X$ inducing the identity on $X_{\mathrm{red}}$. If $X\to S$ is a morphism and $D$ is an $S$-derivation, this is an $S$-automorphism. If $D,D'$ satisfy this hypothesis and commute, then $D+D'$ satisfies it and \[ E_0=\operatorname{id}_X,\qquad E_{D+D'}=E_D\circ E_{D'}. \] Thus the plus sign between automorphisms in the transcription of scan~044 must be composition. Elementwise local nilpotence on the ring of one affine open is a weaker hypothesis and does not imply identity on its reduction.

statement: Positive finitely supported functions attain their maximal rearrangement pairing exactly for nested level sets, majorization is detected by all such pairings or finite-set indicators, and in a finite universe the dominated set is the stated convex hull.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:majorization} For nonnegative finitely supported functions on a set, the maximum scalar product over rearrangements is $R(f,g)$. It is attained exactly when all positive level sets of the two functions are mutually nested. Moreover $f'\preceq f$ is equivalent to $R(f',h)\leq R(f,h)$ for every nonnegative finitely supported $h$, and to this inequality only for indicator functions of finite subsets. On a finite universe the set $\{f':f'\preceq f\}$ is the convex hull of the functions lying coordinatewise below a permutation of $f$.

statement: The cone-system axioms force pairwise prétassé and the two-factor convolution peak inequality, but do not imply three-factor peak inequalities or two-factor convolution majorization.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:pretasse-cones} For the preceding system, every pair $(f,g)\in S^2$ is pr\'etass\'e. In particular the two-factor peak inequality \[ f'\preceq f,\quad g'\preceq g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \|f'*g'\|_\infty\leq\|f*g\|_\infty \] holds. This does not imply the corresponding inequality for three factors, or two-factor majorization.

statement: The printed chain-system axioms fail to imply Condition K even with surjective structural map, exact two-torsion kernel, nonempty chains containing the whole group, all singletons, and full cardinality coverage.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:K-counterexample} Axioms a)--d) of cote~68, scan~017, do not imply Condition~K of scan~021. This remains false when $\rho$ is surjective, its kernel is exactly the specified copy of $G[2]$, every chain is nonempty, every chain contains $G$, every singleton occurs, and every cardinality from $1$ to $|G|$ occurs.

statement: Under the system axioms, tassé generating indicator pairs, all tassé pairs, and all convolution-majorization inequalities are equivalent and imply Condition K, with full cardinality coverage needed only to recover pairwise tassé from Condition K.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:K-repair} Assume the system axioms and that $S$ contains an indicator of every possible finite cardinality. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item every pair of generating indicators, from any two labelled chains, is tass\'e; \item every pair in $S^2$ is tass\'e; \item for every $n\geq2$, $f_i\in S$ and $f_i'\preceq f_i$ imply $f_1'*\cdots*f_n'\preceq f_1*\cdots*f_n$; \item Condition~K: for the same data, $\|f_1'*\cdots*f_n'\|_\infty\leq\|f_1*\cdots*f_n\|_\infty$. \end{enumerate} The cardinality assumption is needed only for (4)$\Rightarrow$(2); (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2)$\Leftrightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(4) holds without it. Thus a)--d) provide compatibility of the proposed extremizers, while extremality of generator pairs is an additional mathematical condition.

statement: With the literal full two-torsion kernel, nonzero systems satisfying the printed axioms exist exactly when all involutions commute, whereas specifying any exponent-two subgroup as kernel allows every ambient group and the axioms do not themselves force kernel surjectivity.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:group-classification} Suppose $G[2]$ means the full set of elements whose square is $e$, and the displayed $i:G[2]\simeq\ker\rho$ is a group isomorphism. With finite subsets and empty families allowed, a nonzero system satisfying all the displayed data and all lettered axioms exists if and only if the elements of $G[2]$ commute pairwise. Surjectivity of $\rho$ does not change this answer. For finite groups satisfying this condition, all fibers can also be required nonempty. If instead $G[2]$ is interpreted as a specified subgroup $H\leq G$ of exponent two, every ambient group $G$ admits such a system with $\ker\rho\simeq H$. This includes the choice $H=\{e\}$ for every group. In either interpretation, the requirement that $i$ map \emph{onto} $\ker\rho$ is not forced by the chain, reflection, convolution, alignment, and kernel-covariance axioms, even with full finite cardinality coverage and $i$ still injective into the kernel.

statement: Integer intervals indexed by twice their midpoint give a nonempty system covering every finite cardinality on Z, and the construction descends to even-order cyclic groups with the displayed doubled indexing group and two-torsion kernel.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:integer-system} For $G=\mathbb Z$, a nonempty system representing every finite cardinality is obtained with $\widetilde G=\mathbb Z$, $\rho=1$, and $\mathcal A(k)$ consisting of all finite integer intervals whose midpoint is $k/2$. Its kernel is $0=G[2]$. The same chain, reflection, and convolution construction descends to cyclic groups of even order $N$ with indexing group $\mathbb Z/(2N)$, $\rho(k)=k\pmod N$, and $i(N/2)=N$, after including the whole group in every chain.

statement: On Z/3Z with the printed trivial exact kernel, the chain and convolution axioms forbid two-element generating sets and therefore full cardinality coverage, regardless of surjectivity or the remaining axioms.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:C3-coverage-obstruction} Let $G=\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ and retain the printed exact-kernel condition $\ker\rho=G[2]=0$. Any system satisfying the chain and convolution axioms has no two-element generating set in any family. Consequently it cannot have full cardinality coverage. Surjectivity of $\rho$ and the remaining printed axioms do not remove this obstruction.

statement: Prétassé and tassé are generally asymmetric but symmetric on abelian groups, always satisfy reversal by inversion and factor exchange, and prétassé also has symmetry for individually inversion-translation-invariant functions.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:symmetry} Neither pr\'etass\'e nor tass\'e is a symmetric relation on arbitrary groups. Both are symmetric on abelian groups. On every group their universally valid reversal is \[ (f,g)\text{ has the property} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\check g,\check f)\text{ has the property}. \] For the pr\'etass\'e property, symmetry also holds whenever each function is invariant under inversion followed by some left translation.

statement: Graded determinant lines have symmetry sign (−1)ᵃᵇ compatible with units, exterior products, block permutations, and complement changes, whereas the cited printed sign (−1)ᵃ⁺ᵇ fails those requirements.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:graded-determinant-sign} Let $S$ be any scheme. Let $\operatorname{Pic}^{\mathbb Z}(S)$ be the groupoid whose objects are pairs $(L,a)$, with $L$ an invertible $\mathcal O_S$-module and $a:S\to\mathbb Z$ locally constant, and whose arrows are degree-preserving $\mathcal O_S$-linear isomorphisms. Set \[ (L,a)\otimes(M,b)=(L\otimes M,a+b),\qquad \symbf{1}=(\mathcal O_S,0). \] With the ordinary tensor associator and unit maps, the formula \[ c_{(L,a),(M,b)}(l\otimes m)=(-1)^{ab}m\otimes l \] defines a symmetric monoidal Picard groupoid. The functor \[ E\longmapsto\operatorname{Det}(E) =(\textstyle\bigwedge^{\operatorname{rk}E}E,\operatorname{rk}E) \] on finite locally free modules and their isomorphisms, equipped with the exterior-product maps for direct sums, respects this symmetry. It respects all finite block permutations and, on finite free modules, the change-of-complement condition of scan~056. The replacement $(-1)^{a+b}$ printed in the commutativity formula of Knudsen--Mumford, p.~20, fails these unit and exterior-product requirements already over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Q$.

statement: Properness and finite Tor dimension with perfect coefficients do not ensure determinant base change on an ordinary fibre product, since the two displayed determinant lines can even have different degrees.
statement_summary_status: one-sentence restatement checked against complete source statement; not itself a proof check
statement_full_latex: \label{C:determinant-ordinary-basechange} The assumptions ``$p:X\to Y$ proper of finite Tor dimension, $Y$ noetherian, $F$ perfect on $X$, and $g:Y'\to Y$ a morphism of noetherian schemes'' do not imply the ordinary-fibre-product comparison displayed on p.~46 of \cite{ROOT_KnudsenMumford1976}. statement_full_latex: \label{C:determinant-basechange-repair} Let $R\to S$ and $R\to A$ be homomorphisms of commutative rings, and put $B=A\otimes_R S$. For a perfect $S$-complex $F$, consider the classical comparison in $D(A)$ \[ \beta_F:A\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}F \longrightarrow B\otimes_S^{\mathbf L}F, \] where the target is restricted along $A\to B$. Then $\beta_F$ is a quasi-isomorphism for every perfect $S$-complex $F$ if and only if $\operatorname{Tor}_i^R(A,S)=0$ for all $i>0$. More generally, let $p:X\to Y$ be a quasi-compact, quasi-separated morphism of schemes, let $g:Y'\to Y$ be any morphism, and form $X'=X\times_Y Y'$ with projections $g'$ and $p'$. Suppose that $X$ and $Y'$ are Tor independent over $Y$: on affine charts over an affine open of $Y$, all higher Tor modules of their two coordinate algebras vanish. For every $E\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_X)$ the canonical map \[ Lg^*Rp_*E\longrightarrow Rp'_*Lg'^*E \] is an isomorphism. If $Rp_*E$ is perfect, this gives an isomorphism of their graded determinants as well. In particular, flatness of either $p$ or $g$ supplies the Tor-independence hypothesis. When $p$ is proper of finite Tor dimension, $Y$ is noetherian and $E$ is perfect, $Rp_*E$ is perfect, so this is a corrected version of the printed determinant comparison.

statement_full_latex: \label{C:determinant-trace-splitting} Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $m\geq1$, and set $\mathfrak s_m(R)=\ker(\operatorname{tr}:M_m(R)\to R)$. statement_full_latex:
\label{A:nodal-q-test}
Take two labelled projective lines, each with node at $0$ and external
marks at $1,\infty$, over $\mathbb Q$. Set
$N=q\,\partial_z\otimes\partial_w$, $q\in\mathbb Q^\times$.
The labelled underlying curve has no automorphisms. Its geometric
tangential group is $\widehat F_3$, presented as the amalgam of the
two three-punctured-sphere groups along their inverse node generators.
Writing it as $\widehat F(c,a,b)$, a twist fixes the left subgroup
$\langle c,a\rangle$ and conjugates the right subgroup
$\langle c,b\rangle$ by $c$. The outer actions for $q,q'$ are
isomorphic over $G_{\mathbb Q}$ if and only if $q=q'$. Indeed any
such isomorphism is graphic and identity on the labelled components,
so it is $T^u$; the necessary and sufficient equation is
$\kappa(q'/q)=(1-\chi)u$, which forces $q'/q=1$.
Thus the bare geometric group loses $q$, but its specified arithmetic
tangential action does not. This rules out using the former
independence as a counterexample to 049(a).
